div.head: RATES.
div.p: THE RATES.
'A Record Collection Satisfac
torily Performed.

The Borough Collector's report for the last half-year's work of his department says : The continuance of the war and the large increase in the rates, together with the shortage in the staff, have made the collec- tion generally much more difficult than in pre- vious half-years, but taking the large amount collected, very much larger than any rates pre- viously raised in Warrington, I think the re- sells will be considered very satisfactory. The total amount collected, including water meters, was £78,554 75.; the sum allowed for composi- tion was £4,773 ss. Bd.; empty property was .2.895 13s. 5d.; assessments that were reduced was .£lO5 4s. 5d.; the amount deducted for other allowances totalled £147 is. 7d.; arrears on rates came to £129 4s. 6d.; arrears on water meters to £665 7s. 2d.; and the loss in collection was £8 Os. Id. The amount collected is £9,691 more than in the last half-year; the composition is 4330 more, simply because the 'rate in the .2 is more; the empties are £52 more, partly due to the higher rate and partly to the insertion in the rate-book of new properties which did not come fully into occupation; and the assessments reduced are .2180 less. _Allowances "Very Small Indeed."

"The allowances on the improvement rate are mostly for Corporation properties not charge- able to the rate, and a rebate to the L. & N.-W. Railway Company in respect of an item rated in error in full instead of under the partial exemption clause. The allowances on the other rates are very small indeed; the total includes deductions of .27 for properties demolished or closed as uninhabitable, and £l7 13s. 2d. for houses occupied by the War Refugees and by the British Red Cross Society. The arrears carried forward are somewhat less than last half-year, being (apart from a water meter account due on a date under „discount allow- ance) £129 4s. 6d., as against £136 4s. 4d. last half-year, and £194 3s. id. the corresponding period last year.
A Record!

"Finally, the loss in. collection, including As. Bd. on water account in three small bank- ruptcy cases, is only .28 Os. Id. This latter sum is a record, and means that even including the loss in bankruptcy, which is something I could not avoid, as the water rate' is not a preferen- tial debt, we have collected £78,554 with a loss of only .28 Os. id. A penny in the .2 on the poor rate has worked out at £1,185 (estimate £1,190), and the improvement rate at £1,093 (estimate £1,086). May I further say that these results, although so satisfactory, have not been attained without very considerable effort on the part of the collectors, for, as I can per- oonally testify, the present high rates are press- ing very heavily upon many members of the community; I am, however, not submitting any names for excusal this half-year, as there seems nor cases' especially calling for remission. , Relief for Cottage Property Owners.

"I have had unfortunately to take proceed- ings in 26 cases, as against an average of about 21 in previous half-years. The movement for the increase of cottage rents which was so wide- spread last year, had a renewal in April last, 'when the increase of Is. 4d. in the in the rates was announced. To this latter increase must now be added the extra cost of upkeep and repairs, and lately the increase in mort- gage interest which is being demanded and obtained. To give some relief to the cottage property owners and to prevent rents from being unduly raised against the tenants, the Assess- ment Committee have decided to adopt a new scale of assessment, and have authorised the Clerk to the Guardians to prepare a new valua- tion list."

div.head: •,Would Suit Him.
div.p: •,Would Suit Him.

"Work," observed the reflective dead-beat— "work is all right if you can get the sort to suit your individual needs. I, for instance, wouldn't object to calling out 'the stations on an Atlantic liner."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDA f, OCTO tER 30, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDA f, OCTO tER 30, 1915.
STORIES FROM THE TRENCHES
TANNER-HIGHLANDER_
Year's Training In Verse; The Recent
Advance In Prose.

Private Benjamin Oldroyd, whose wife lives at 86, Wellington-street, has written a long description of the part he took in the re,,tytit advance in France. He is in a Highland regi- ment, which he joined at the outbreak of war. being at the time engaged at the Mersey-street tannery. He has had three narrow escapes. He writes:—

"Our battalion was in reserve in a back line of trenches and we just waited for the first line to get over the parapet of s the trench and then thigi fun began. I think there was every kind of shell known bursting around us as we made our way to reinforce the front line. There was plenty of gas used on both sides, but our gas did the most damage. When we got to the German trenches we got the bombs to work and bombed every dug-out along the trenches, and any Germans that tried to get away they just got the steel. But they were glad enough to give themselves up, coming to- wards us with their hands up, shouting Camarade,' meaning 'Comrade.' We gave them Camarade.' We hunted them through three lots of trenches and straight through the village. A lot hid themselves in the cellars of the houses, but not for long . . . .they were edher, shot or bayoneted. We got them on the run and kept them on the run beyond the village, where they had a good length of barbed wire already laid. There they took refuge, and we dug ourselves in about 50 yards away from their position. I shall never forget digging my- self in. They poured rapid rifle fire into us all the time we were digging, and their artillery were also shelling us. I never worked so hard in my life. Our Captain was standing behind us tell- ing us to dig for our lives, when he was shot. He only lived about five minutes. Another officer took command and he was shot; also a sub-lieutenant, all in the space of 20 minutes. We held this position from Saturday till Mon- day, when we were relieved by the Guards, and very soon got a good feed and a sleep, which we were badly in need of."

div.head: TWELVE MONTHS TRAINING FOR THE
div.p: TWELVE MONTHS TRAINING FOR THE
FRONT.
Private Oldroyd has spent some of his leisure writing verses. From one set on the above sub- ject, we have selected the following

'Twas on the 7th of September, in nineteen fourteen, I volunteered for the Army, to fight for King and Queen. I went to Bank Quay Station, and thought 1 owned the earth, As I smiled at the ticket collector, when he gave me a ticket forrYerth. I never will forget that day, if I live for a hundred years, As the train steamed out of the station, and eyes were dim with tears; ' • Handkerchiefs were waving, as far as the eye could see, And a prayer went up, "God bring you home, along with victory."

The time we had, as the train sped on, I never shall forget, A merrier crew I never saw, I can hear them singing yet. To get to my destination, I had to change my train; At good old Carlisle Station, I was soon on my way again. At last I reached the barracks, which I ever will bear in mind, Where the old Black Watch were stationed, the regiment I joined. They showed 13ie my sleeping quarters, which happened to be the floor. But I give you mY word I curled up like a bird and soon went off in a snore.

At last when morning light broke in, I went for a wash and shave, In came the orderly corporal, who began to roar and rave, "The cookhouse will soon be blowing, it's time you were on parade, Show a leg you lot of lubbers, you're not in the Boys' Brigade !"

An officer came along the line, and said with the nicest of smiles, We want a hundred transfers to make up the 11th Argyles. So out to the front I doubled, I wasn't a bit partic, With being caged up in the barracks I was . getting fairly sick. So off we went that very night, and you'll say it's a tidy trot When you consider the distance, from Perth to Aldershot; We landed on Saturday morning, hungry and tired were we, And we waited for our dinner, like waiting for a jubilee.

The way they marched us round that square, and doubled us round the lanes, The doctors' shop was soon full up with a squad of aches and pains; Some of them got their tickets, and some of them got M.D., And some of them did a " moonlight " to Scot= land, the land of the free. We were still dressed up in our civies, some of them tattered and torn, When we made a move a few miles away, to a place they called MOOT. They put us under canvas, to shelter us from the rain, And every day knee deep in mud, we tramped o'er 's Plain.

-At last they gave us a uniform, which filled us all with woe, We looked like a lot of dressed-up dolls, stuck up in a waxwork show. The tunics they were red ones, which made us look quite stout, When we stuck up a couple of well-worn Shirts to make our chest swell out. Well, to get along with my story, the winter was coming on, We were. told we were going to wooden huts, a palace to gaze upon, . • The name of the place was shot, but soon It appeared to me The proper name to give the place was Mud- shot, by the sea.

I never will forget that place, and the dinners of stews and stews, Where I worked for Sergt. Harty, looking for four by two's. To make a platform round the huts was a very good idea, - But I made more toast inside my hut, which happened to be quite near. At last the job was finished, which vexed me quite a lot, And back to my platoon I went, to do the turkey trot; What with kit inspections, and physical drill as well,' And the roar of the S.M.'s rusty voice, we wished we were in .

We got our kilts at Bramshott, we had pined for them many, a day, But now for a packet of Woodbines, I'd be glad to give mine away. Then came the great inspection, some nine or ten miles away, At a place called r-- Common, Oh, what a lovely day! I never saw it snow so bad as it did on this fatal . day. The wind was as strong as a lion, and nearly blew us all away, Lord Kitchener said, as be sat in his car,'" I cannot stop, tong to-clay'; .Just issue a tot of rum per man, and take thel poor devils away !"
Then we made another move to a place called --stoke, Where we spent many a happy day. bad mAniy a laugh and joke. * * * *

At last we left for -den, just two days' march away. And we never will forget that march, if we live till we're old and grey; But still we all kept cheery, and tried to do our best, . And every now and then they fell us out fo,r a smoke and rest. We broke our journey at N , to rest our bones for the night, And they found us some tidy billets, which gave us great delight.
We were up at eight next morning, and soon on on the roads once more, But we soon showed signs of weariness, our feet were tired and sore.

We toddled along to the tune of the 'pipes, which we fancied we could hear, But the pipes couldn't cure the blisters of the mey. who .fell to the rear; But, after all, putting jokes on one side, that march is past and gone, And our regiment stands, as it always will, the good old "Second to None." At last we marched into 'the camp, weary and tired were we, And some of us preferred our bed, instead of waiting for tea. Next morning the doctor was busy, attending to our feet, And Palmer used up as much iodine as would paint a blooming street.

We finished our training at den, and soon were fully equipped, And at midnight from one Friday across to Belle France we were shipped; We stopped for some time at a rest camp, and soon heard the roar of the guns, And we gave our rifles an extra rub and swore what we'd do for the Huns. Well! they soon got us into the trenches—an occasion we'll never forget— For a German shell like a foundry fell, killed • the best pall I ever met. To put the "tin hat" on my story, and putting all jokes on one side, We will struggle for Britain's glory and good old Warrington's pride.

div.head: WHY THEY HOLD BACK!
div.p: WHY THEY HOLD BACK!
Sapper Pye Thinks Young Men Do Not
Realise.

Sapper J. Pye, who is serving with the Expeditionary Force in France, writing under date October 16th, to Mr. Benjamin Farrar, Secretary of the Wycliffe P.S.A., says: "Please give my best regards to the brethren at your next meeting. Our company are at present working in the trenches. We are billeted in an old barn about two miles farther back, and we march up to our work in the morning and come down again at night. The enemy gave us a fine reception the first day we landed here. They started to shell the village, but they did no damage. The shells passed over our billet. •
"Stuck to the Enemy Like Glue.'

"A small village through which we pass on the way to the trenches has hardly a house standing—it is a sight worth seeing! You could hardly realise the damage the enemy have done to property. Our boys stick to them like glue, and give them back more than they get. I think we are playing them out on this front, and with a little time and patience we shall finish their career. I sincerely hope that all the single young men of Warrington who are not on munitions work, and who have nobody depending on them, will come forward and give us a helping hand. There is another winter coming on, and surely they must think about our brave soldiers, who have already spent one winter in the trenches, fighting for the mothers and sisters of the country, whilst many have stood idly by, watching developments. If They Only Saw -!

"I am quite sure that if the young fellows not yet 'listed could only see the sacrifices that France and Belgium have made in this great conflict, they would at once realise what is at stake. Our Allies are doing their utmost at present, and I hope more recruits will enlist, so that we can keep the ball a-rolling. I am quite sure that the majority of the Warrington people do not like the idea of conscription . . . for the simple reason that they do not want to lose their liberty, if the country can get volunteers instead of conscripts. I am sure that it is not because of faint-heartedness that the young fellows are holding back, but because of the fact that they do not realise the gravity of the situation."

div.head: ON HOSPITAL SHIP.
div.p: ON HOSPITAL SHIP.
Homecoming Of The Wounded—And
Burials At Sea.

Mr. B. Farrar, of Willfs-street, has received the following letter from a Warringtonian on board H.M.T. S.S. Northland : " Your letter of September sth reached me at Lemnos on the 19th inst., just as we were embarking the wounded, and the sights of these poor suffering ones would indeed touch any one possessed of human sympathy. They are hor- rible in the extreme, and already we have laid many of the brave ones out and committed their bodies to the deep. "But now as they near home their faces brighten up with expectation of seeing the dear old country once again. And now that we are through the Bay of Biscay they have com- menced to count the hours. Ah, but lam afraid that in many cases their own mothers will find difficulty in recognising their sons in the maimed, broken and crippled men aboard our ship. But worse indeed it will be for the relatives of those whom we have buried at sea.

"These burials at sea are indeed a pathetic sight. The body is covered with the Union Jack. The ship's ensign is lowered to half- mast. The ship herself is stopped and the pass- ing bell tolled. Then the body is lowered into the sea, with the words 'We here commit the body,to the deep; until the day of resurrection, when the sea shall give up her dead.' And then the ship sails silently away again. I hope SOOII to see this terrible conflict ended, and then it will indeed be a happy day when we are bring- ing home the troops. Please convey my brotherly love to all members of the P.S.A. and accept same yourself.—Sincerely yours, M. Roy McConville."

div.head: SOUTH AFRICAN ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE SOUTH AFRICAN ELECTIONS.
Win For Botha's Policy.
CAPE Tows, October 27th

The new Parliament, which will probably meet in about three weeks' time, consi'sts of :-- South African. Party, or Ministerialists 54 Unionists Nationalists -27 Independents ... ... 5 . Labour ... ... 4

The Unionists and Independents will all support General Botha's Imperial and "one- stream" policy. This means that the elec- torate has returned 99 out of the 130 members of the House pledged to back the Botha Ad- ministration during the period of the war. The strength of the South African Party and the Nationalists is pretty much as was anticipated. The, surprise of the election was the Labour rout, particularly on the Rand, which has given. the Unionists at least six seats more than was expected by the most sanguine.—The "Times" correspondent.

div.head: IVar Letters and Photographs.
div.p: IVar Letters and Photographs.

We invite our readers to submit to us letters received from their soldier friends. We shalll also be glad to receive photo- graphs .of soldiers who have been killed, wounded, mentioned in dispatches or other- wise become a source of interest to the public.
The letters will be carefully edited so that nothing will appear in print that ought not to appear.
The photographs, when suitable, will be published in "The Examiner," which has an established reputation as a picture paper.
All letters and photographs are returned after use, undamaged, to the owners.

div.head: VOLUNTEER REGIMENT.
div.p: VOLUNTEER REGIMENT.
New Committee To Stimu!ate
Interest.
HOW THE " OVER-AGED "
CAN HELP.

A fairly well-attended public meeting was held in the Town Hall on Wednesday evening for the purpose of forming a committee in connec- tion with the Warrington area of the Lanca- shire Volunteer Regiment. The Mayor (Alder- man Peter Peacock) presided, and was sup- ported by Platoon-Commander F. A. Frost (of the Grappenhall Platoon of the Knutsford Battalion of the Cheshire Regiment), Mr. A. T. Hanoway and Mr. E. Bohane (who came down from headquarters).

TO ENCOURAGE THE TRAINING CORPS. The Mayor, in opening the meeting, said that it was held with a view to encouraging the Training Corps. The Warrington Corps was very strong at its inception, but for various reasons the members fell away until to-day they had not got more than a hundred. Some weeks ago he invited all the principal tradesmen and manufacturers in Warringten to meet him, with a view to getting their active support and sym- pathy with the movement, which, he felt sure, ought to• appeal to all. As a result of that meeting he thought that he might advertise a public meeting, and hence the gathering that night. The Warrington area was composed of the borough itself and the surrounding dig- tricts, and if that movement was to go on and be successful—as he felt sure it Would—they wanted a committee representative of tire neighbourhood concerned. All Possible Help Needed.

Anybody who had read the newspapers these last few days would realise that whatever people might have thought of the Training Corps in the past, they now appreciated the fact that the country would need all the assistance it could get before the present disastrous war was con- cluded. It was highly desirable that the lead- ing people in Warrington should give their active support to the Training Corps move- ment, in addition to giving their financial sup- port also, later on. He did not think Warring- ton would be behind in the matter of making the movement a real success. (Hear, hear.) At any rate Warrington was to have her chance. The corps was one of those organisations which those who could not join the Army should join, in order that they might make themselves fit for any service that might be reauired of them. possibly before very long. His ,Worship added that he had received a letter from Mr. W. Peter Rylands saying that. whilst he was frightfully busy, he was nevertheless prepared to act as honorary commandant for the Warrington Corps: (Applause.)

div.head: OFFICIAL RECOGNITION IN SIGHT.
div.p: OFFICIAL RECOGNITION IN SIGHT.

Mr. Bohane then addressed the meeting. The War Office, he said, had given authority to the Central Association of Training Corps for those bodies to be recognised in accordance with the terms of the Hague Convention. He was afraid that the red brassard which the members of the corps now wore on their arms had, in the near past, been somewhat ridiculed, but it had come to stay. Having explained how the age limit for membership had been raised until it now stood at forty years, the speaker went on to say that a great many men had left the corps, up and dowi} the country, and had joined the Army proper. The Warrington Corps had not been behind other corps in that respect. and, in the past, had been the means of training several men for the Army, and thus had rendered a great service to the nation. The corps con- sisted of men who realised that at the present moment they had a duty in life and that was— though they might be beyond the age for ser- vice abroad—to make themselves fit to defend the hearths and homes of the country in case of invasion.

div.head: If Invasion Came
div.p: If Invasion Came

The volunteer would appreciate the absolute uselessness, of the ordinary man in the street in the event of an invasion,:belie ever so good a shot. Ire would simply become one of 'a rabble, not knowing what to do, or how to do it. In Lancashire the volunteer movement had been allowed to fall somewhat into the background. Lancashire had to bow to the neighbouring county of Cheshire, which had a wonderful volunteer force. But Lancashire, he was sure, was not going to remain behindhand, but was going to "buck up" and show Cheshire what she could do. (Hear, hear.) Lancashire was going to be second to no other county; he said that with authority, and with enthusiasm. , (Applause.) Only the previous evening a Bill, backed by Lord Newton, as representing the War Office, was presented in Parliament, deal- ing with voluntary training corps, and his Lordship drew attention to the fact that the voluntary training corns of the country had done more for recruiting than all the speakers on the war. Warrington men must not for a moment think of allowing the corps to, die out. especially when the movement was within sight of getting that official recognition which it 'desired. When the commandant came round he wanted him to be able to say that Warrington had done well, and that the men of the town were doing their duty not only to the town to which they belonged, but also to the County of the Red Rose, of which they were all so proud.

div.head: WORK THE WOMEN CAN DO.
div.p: WORK THE WOMEN CAN DO.

Mr. F. A. Frost also briefly addressed the meeting, remarking that the Cheshire corps were nearly 10,000 strong. If Lancashire was going to overtake the adjoining county she would have to start soon and keep on peffging away at it, or she would not do it, for the Cheshire. men had taken up the movement most enthusi- astically. The Grappenhall section started with nine or ten men, and now it had getting on for forty members. Ile had been told on very good authority that the time would soon come when they would be recognised as a limb of the Army, and would have some capitation grant. The members of the corps might get what he would , call metaphorical smacks in the eye, but they would come out on top—their King and country would want them! (Hear, hear.) The women of the,country could help the* in vement enormously, by persuading their menfolk who were over military age, or for Gther reasons could not join the Service, to enrol in a Volun- teer Corps. Wives should say to their husbands, "Look here, you have some spare time.

div.head: Wife's Question.
div.p: The Wife's Question.

"Are you going to prepare to protect 'me from the ravages of the Huns? Or are you going to let them treat me as they treated the women of Belgium?" He could not understand the apathy of so many of the women of the country.. There was one way in which the volunteers could 'be of real service. They' had no doubt noted that the bridges and the canals were guarded by old warriors who had rejoined the Colours. Those men had had military experience and could do the same duty as they were doing at home on the other side of the Water. They could guard the lines of communication just as well as they weKe guarding the waterways and the bridges of the main roads at home. If the Volunteer Corps were strong enough they could relieve those old soldiers of the duty they were at present doing; they could also relieve the men who were now employed in guarding German prisoners, whose numbers he was glad to say kept on the increase, and in fact was getting so big that the country would soon be pretty full of them. (Laughter and applause.) These men had to be looked after; they were not fit tG look after themselves. (More laughter.) For Home And The Family.

The troops at Aresent employed in watching them could be better employed looking afttn. other Germans who ware not yet prisoners. No man was so poor as not to have the privilege of protecting his wife and children, and the poor man's wife was just as dear to him as was the rich man's to him. •He had heard on good authority that the Volunteer Corps would be wanted. He did not say that he was told so in so many words, but a nod was as good as a wink to a blind horse. He hoped Warrington would stick to the corps like grim death. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: AREA COMMITTEE APPOINTED.
div.p: AREA COMMITTEE APPOINTED.

The meeting then proceeded to the appoint- ment of an area committee, it being explained that the existing corps committee would still remain in office. The following were appointed on the new committee: The Mayor, Alderman Tinnion, Councillor 11... Roberts, Messrs. J.
Fulton-Smith, W. Ashton, P. Bennett, G. H. Smith, W. Furness, B. S. Newcombe and Sykes. Mr. Rossiter was elected secretary and Mr. T. M. Broadbent treasurer.

div.head: MEETING'S CONDOLENCES.
div.p: THE MEETING'S CONDOLENCES.

• The Mayor then moved a vote of condolence with Sir Jas. de Hoghton on the loss of his son at the Front. The very morning after Sir James received the tidings of his son's death, said the Mayor, he was at Preston pressing forward the volunteer movement. The vote was carried in silence_

div.head: ALDERMAN BENNETT'S APPEAL.
div.p: ALDERMAN BENNETT'S APPEAL.

Alderman Bennett said that the Warrington Volunteer Training Corps would never justify its existence unless it made itself stronger numerically than it was at present. He went on to refer to the local Cadet Corps, remarking that there were very many youths between school age and military age who might derive real advantage from undergoing a course of military training. Turning to the war in general, the position seemed to him to get blacker and blacker as the days went by. They had not yet begun to see the beginning of the end. In heaven's 'fame let them begin to organise; let them take time by the forelock. There were hundreds of men in the town who were on munition ivork and could not join the Army. Could not an appeal be made to those men to join that corps and undergo some sort of training? The volunteer Movement was a patriotic one, and those who took part in it could afford to disregard the people in the street who felt inclined to laugh at them as they passed by and sneeringly referred to them as toy soldiers. If England were only organised, if her people only realised their duty sufficiently. there was not a shadow of doubt that she would come out the conqueror, and that the war would be brought to a speedy close.

div.head: MORE CANVASSERS WANTED.
div.p: MORE CANVASSERS WANTED.

The Mayor, who was accorded a vote of thanks for presiding mentioned, in closing the meeting, that up to that night only twenty names had been received of people who were willirig to do canvassing work in connection with "the pink forms." He thought more ought to come forward and play a part in help- ing to save, if possible, the voluntary system of which they had been so proud for many years. His Worship added that he required no thanks for his services that evening. He had merely done his duty by trying to impress their duty upon other people. (Applause.)

div.head: BRAVE LATCHFORD BOY.
div.p: BRAVE LATCHFORD BOY.
Plucky But Unsuccessful Attempt At Rescue.

The story of a Warrington boy's gallant attempt to save the life of a five-year-old child was told at an inquest held at the Police Station, Warrington, on Tuesday morning, by Mr. S. Brighouse, on the body of John Wright, the son of George Wright, of the 3rd Cheshire Regiment, and 14, School-street, Warrington. Little John Wright left home last Sunday afternoon to go for a walk with his elder brother, Samuel, aged seven years, and it was whilst on this walk that he attempted to pick up a cigarette on the canal bank, and accident- ally fell into the Old Quay Canal near the Black Bear Bridge, Latchford. Thomas Miller, aged 15 years, of 3, Beatrice-street, Latchford, made a brave attempt to save his life, but by the time he had brought Wright to the bank life was practically extinct. Giving his evidence at the inquest, Thomas Miller said that 4.45 on Sunday afternoon he was in Myrtle-grove, when a little girl came and told him that there was a little boy in the canal. He ran to the canal and saw a little boy float- ing on the water. The head was just under. He took off his clothes, and diving into the water, brought the boy to the bank. When he came out of the water a little girl told him that three other boys had been with Wright. The witness and some other boys got some whter out of Wright, but the latter never breathed or spoke again. Dr. Jago was sent for and on his , arrival life was pronounced extinct,
The Coroner (to the witness): Where did you learn to swim?

Miller: At schdol, sir. Addressing the jury. the Coroner said that he thought that the conduct of Miller ought to be brought to the notice of the Royal Humane Society. He was only a small boy, but he divested himself of his clothing and jumped into the canal to try and save the boy. The canal was Bft, to loft, deep, and he might very easily have lost his life. Many boys and men, bigger than he, would have been afraid to go in. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." Miller was brought bactic into the witness box, and addressing him, the Coroner said that appearances were very deceptive; one would not have thought that he (Miller) would have done this, but it was very brave of him. It was a very courageous act on his part., "Your father ought to be proud of you; tell him I say so;' concluded Mr. Brighouse.

div.head: FATAL FALL.
div.p: A FATAL FALL.

An inquest was held on Tuesday at the Police Station, Warrington, by Mr. S. Brighouse, on the body of Jane Timmins, aged 69 years, who died at the hospital at 8.30 on Sunday evening. Benjamin Timmins, a general labourer, resid- ing at 88, Hoyle-street, Warrington, said that for a long time his wife had been suffering from fainting fits. It was her usual custom to come and meet him on Saturdays as he .was coming from work. On Saturday, 16th inst., as he was walking along Bewsey-street, he noticed his wife against the rails at Wycliffe Schools. A young man and a young woman were supporting her. Her head was bandaged, and she said that she had fallen in the- street as a result of a fainting fit and had been to the Infirmary. On Tuesday night he .called in a doctor, who ordered her removal to the Union Hospital. Nurse .Lawson said that after Mrs. Timmins had been admitted she grew worse, until she died on Sunday night. Dr. Jagger, resident medical officer, gave cvi- denc9 to the effect that the cause of death was due to injuries caused by the fall, and, second- arily septiccemia. ' A verdict was returned accordingly.

div.head: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
div.p: THE FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.
" OLIVE BRANCH " LODWE. Warrinoton District (A1.t..)
Valuable Services Acknowledged.

At the above lodge on Saturday evening an interesting event took place in the form of a presentation to P.G. John. J. Cook, who has recently passed through various offices in the ledge. N.G. John A. Brown presided, being sup- ported by Lodge G.M. Wm. Hammon, V.G. Richard Whitfield, Wm. Toft (minute secre- tary). P.G. Arthur Cotterill (treasurer), and P.P.G.AL Alban Boyle (lodge secretary). ,

, During an interval in the transaction of the ordinary lodge business, P.G. John Brown was requested to make the presentation of a Past Grand's framed certificate to Bro. Cook, and in doing so he complimented him in gaining the confidence and esteem of his brother members by his energy and ability in carrying out his duties. He • expressed the- hope that his ex- ample would be followed by the younger ,seo- tion of the Lodge. By discharging the duties connected with the office of N.G. 'members did lot of good to their , fellow, members, and at the same. time gained • practical e'xperience in the 'management of lodge affairs. He-, hoped P.G. Cook would be spared long to take a still greater interest in Oddfellowship. He had much pleasure in asking him, to accept the pre. sent on behalf of the officers and members of the "Olive Branch" Lodge. (Applause.) P.P.G.M. Boyle and' P.G.: Cotterill also spoke in ,complimentary terms regarding the valuable services rendered by P.G. Cook.

P.G. Cook, in acknowledgment, said that his ambition had always been to obtain a Past Officers' certificate, and he was pleased to find that the lodge considered he had discharged his duties in so satisfactory a manner hs to earn their appreciation. He thanked them most sin- cerely for that token of regard and esteem. (Applause.)

div.head: FARM AND GARDE.
div.p: FARM AND GARDE.
FARMERS' SONS.
There has lately been a little newspaper dis- cussion on the position of farmers' sons and the way in which they are handicapped at

their start in life. Farming is a business which demands a large capital in proportion to profits, and farmers with several sons who can start them all well in his own profession are very few and far between. It is, says the
Estates Gazette," often the case_ that _a_man

has enough Money to run one good-sized farm, and no more. He knows his sons cannot all be farmers, and acts accordingly. As they leave school they are pp.cked off to the towns as clerks or shop assistants, &c. Perhaps one may fly at higher game and enter one of the learned professions, but all are made to understand that however they may delfre it, they cannot be farmers for want of capital. Frequently the eldest stays at home, and becomes a middle- aged man before, in the course of Nature, he succeeds to his father's holding. Even then there is a division of the father's estate, and he is saddled with a debt to his brothers and sisters, to whom he pays a heavy annual sum for interest In this way we get what is, in one writer's views, the greatest hindrance to progress in British farming, which is "short- age of capital." Often a young man takes a farm too big for his pocket, and finds it im- possible to make the best of it. Should bad times come upon him, the struggle to keep his
head above water is. too severeTand even if he survives it the best years of his life are gone before he can attain a solid footing.

div.head: WOMEN AT THE PLOUGH.
div.p: WOMEN AT THE PLOUGH.

In a letter to the "Times" Mr. Jesse Collings relates the following: "Some time ago I accom- panied the British Dairy Farmers' Association on a visit to rural France. We were examining a large cheese factory, when my attention was called to a woman in a neighbouring field who was holding the plough drawn by a pair of fine horses. I was asked by soixte of the farmers whether I would like to see such a sight in England. My reply was that I should be delighted to see it if the conditions were equal. On inquiry of the manager of the cheese fac- tory, who was intimately acquainted with the woman, we found that she was farming her own land, and had done so ever since the death of her husband. He told us that she was very well-to-do, and in addition to the land and stock, which were her own, she had a consid- erable sum invested in French Rentes, and that she carried on the work for the love of it. Since the war began more and more women in France are engaged in agriculture. The secret of the industry of the French peasants is that they own the land they till." We accompanied the B.D.F.A. on the visit referred to by Mr. Collings, and saw the inci- dent which he describes. It is quite a modern view that there is any "degradation" in the fact of a woman taking part in agricultural labour. In what respect is work in the fields worse than work in the factory? Our factories are crowded with women workers at all times, and the conditions therein are far lees satisfac- tory, more unwholesome hygienically and mor- ally than those which obtain on the farm. Naturally it is not right that either women or young boys should be put to tasks that entail too great a demand on their strength, but un- less labour generally is held to be a degrada- tion there is no valid argument against em- ployment of women on the farm in tasks suited to their powers.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
LI LI ES.

These lovely flowers form one of the most beautiful objects to be seen in any garden, and the majority are very easy to grow and quite hardy. Lilies can be grown in almost any 'border, but this is ~not always the place for them. Loam, grit, Jeat or leaf-mould suit the majority. Some require a little lime; some require partial shade, and others like plenty of. sun.
Lilies, on the whole, are rather expensive, but some are cheap and can be increased by the small bulbs from the base.

First among lilies must come Lilium Aura- turn, and its varieties. This lily is a beautiful shade, creamy white, spotted crimson, with a band of yellow running down each petal; it has huge blooms, sometimes touching twelve inches across, and plenty of them: This lily likes to be planted among rhododendrons or other low-growint, shrubs and likes to have the surface. mulched ° annually to encourage the stem roots. It objects to lime. I may say that . Dr. Bennett, of Padgate-lane, has a fine specimen of the above lily his garden. I should say it carried thirty blooms this season. Plant about eight inches deep. It grows from four to six feet according to soil. Next comes Lilium Speciosum. This lily is very easy to grow and quite hardy; in fact, I saw some in bloom this season in the small front gardens in Winwick-road just past the Blue Coat School. There are several vartuties, ranging from white to crimson, but all are very beautiful. This lily is best seen under glass. It makes a capital pot plant. Plant in the spring, same time as Auratum, eight to ten inches deep, in good light, rich soil, putting a handful of sand under and around the bulb to preserve it; this applies to all lilies.

Lilium Candidum or Madonna.—No garden should be without this beautiful lily, with its large snow-white blooms. It will give seven to thirty blooms on a stein, and last well when cut. It will grow anywhere, but is seen best in good, heavy soil, though it does very well in light soil containing lime. A sun-loving lily; plant from four inches to six inches deep; should- be planted in autumn. If planted in spring it might be liable to disease; bulbs, top size, 4d. each. Lilium Croceum or Orange Lily.—Another favourite on account of its easy culture and beautiful orange flowers. Any soil will suit; likes plenty of sun: Plant four inches to six inches deep. These bulbs cost about 4d. each.
Lilium Chalcedonicum.—Another very orna- mental lily, with large, bright, scarlet flowers and an easy doer. It will grow in any soil, but likes a -stiff, loamy soil the best. Plant

Lilium Martagcm.—The old Turk's cap lily; various colours, ranging from white to pink. It likes a stiff soil and will grow also in woods. It should be planted about six inches deep and likes lime.

Lilium Tigrinum or Tiger Lily.—Too well known to need describing and will grow any- where. The are sever's' varieties, but Splendens and Fortunei are the best; also double forms, which are beautiful. Fortunei has woolly stems, and Splendens larger spots on the flowers. Plant six inches to eight inches deep; height, four feet. Bulbs about 3d. each; double-flowered, 4d. Lilium Longiflorum.—This lily is best seen under glass, but can be grown in the garden and likes a light, rich soil. Longiflorum Gigan- teum is the best for outside; plant eight inches deep. Height, three feet; flowers white, trumpet-shaped.

Lilium Elegans.—A very beautiful dwarf lily growing from one foot to eighteen inches high. There are many varieties, varying in colour from pale yellow, apricot to deep crimson, and all give satisfaction. Grow same as Orange Lily. Makes a grand pot plant.

There are other lilies, but the above are the cheapest and best, and can be got from the local seed§men at reasonable prices. All can be planted from now onwards till November, with the exception of Auratum and Speciosum, these two being the least hardy.

div.head: BULBS IN POTS.
div.p: BULBS IN POTS.

A great point in the pot culture of hyacinths and other bulbs is often overlooked, namely a good supply of roots before placing them in the greenhouse or room window. To ensure success, this abundance of roots is all important. One often hears those who sell the bulbs blamed for their failure, when it is in truth the fault of the grower.' 'Very often one may see persons potting up hyacinths, tulips, and such like, and at once transferring them to the greenhouse, with the result that the bulbs either refuse to flower or rot. Now that the bulbs are procur- able they should be potted as soon as possible so as to give them a -long season to become well rooted. When potting do not fill the pot with soil and then push the bulb into it, but make a hole with the fingers into which the bulb may be put and the soil pressed firmly round it. If the former plan is followed the compost is made too firm, and when the roots begin to move the bulb is pushed up out of the soil. After potting stand the pots on a firm base and cover the whole with cocoa fibre, leaf soil or sand. Ashes direct from the furnace must not be used. as the sulphurous matter contained in these injures the bulbs and prevents them flowering. Tinder this covering the bulbs may remain for some six weeks, or at all events until on ex- amination it is found that growth is well on the move, when as many as are forward enough may be moved to a cool frame so as to become inured to the light. When this has been done the bulbs may be brought into the greenhouse or stood in the window so that abundance of air mily reach them. Given the above treatment the foliage will be short and sturdy. Care must be taken that the bulbs do not suffer from want of water, while over-watering must be guartl4 against.

div.head: MICHAELMAS DAISIES.
div.p: MICHAELMAS DAISIES.

When our autumn flowers begin to wane then it is that the Michaelmas daisies are at their best. Even long after the early frosts have destroyed the blooms of the Japanese anemones., blackened the dahlias, and despoiled the early flowering chrysanthemums, the starry flowers of the Michaelmas daisies spread a halo over the garden. The kinds, including, the double forms, are now very numerous, but to our idea the large single flowered forms. are the best, and devoid of that lumpiness found in the double flowered varieties. There are now 8° many that are weeds and of no value that those who contemplate planting should visit 'a garden where they are largely grown and wake a selection when the plants are in flower, at the same time taking into account their vary- ing heights and habit of growth. These Michaelmas daisies seed finely, and should a good variety appear it is a very easy matter to get together a stock by division. Two of the best varieties are the blue flowered Climax and its white counterpart, both of which flower late.—" Wick," in "Farm and Home."

div.head: RESTRICTIONS.
div.p: RESTRICTIONS.

Sir,—Why- your correspondent "Citizen" should desire the Central Colitrol Board to extend its operations to Warrington is not disclosed in his interesting letter. Rather he unconsciously supports the view that his for- tunate town well deserves its exemption from the drastic restrictions under whic4 the Mersey area is suffering. lle says: "The vast majority of the workmen are ideal in their behaviour and in their sense of responsibility, but there is a minority—a small minority— who require strong measures." Is it fair and right that this "vast majority" of patriotic, single-minded toilers should be harassed and inconvenienced for the sake of a handful of shirkers? These few individuals can be dealt with very stringently under the Munitions Act without any interference with the rights of the general public. I can tell "Citizen" that in our area the Control Board restrictions have only resulted in irritating everybody, without decreasing drunkenness to any extent or helping the production of muni- tions.. J. E. SIMPSON. Liverpool, October 25th, 1915.

div.head: FOR " JACK " AND
div.p: FOR " JACK " AND
"TOMMY."
Liberal Women Comfort-Makers

• Hold Another Social. A highly enjoya7le whist drive wasP held at the Crosfield Memorial Hall on Thursday even- ing, under the auspices of the Warrington -Women's Liberal Association, and in aid of the fund for providing materials for the Liberal women of Warrington fo work up into comforts for our soldiers and sailors. There was a good attendance. .

At the close of the card games the prizes were presented by Mrs. P. O'Brien, who was sub- sequently accorded 4 vote of thanks on the pro- position of Mrs. E. Osborne, the hon. secretary of the Liberal Women's Association, and the lady who has worked so hard to make the com- forts-making movement the undoubted success that it has been--and will be.

div.head: "WONDERFUL AMOUNT OF SELFSACRIFICE."
div.p: "WONDERFUL AMOUNT OF SELF- SACRIFICE."

Mr. O'Brien returned thar•..s for the vote of appreciation accorded his wife, and said that all present knew the good work that the mem- bers of the Association had accomplished and wore accomplishing. For months past they had been collecting money and working up the materials purchased therewith, the result being that many hundreds of soldiers and sailors had benefited. The work had entailed a wonderful amount of self-sacrifice both on the part of Mrs. Osborne and her committee and of the workers, but it was a sacrifice that had been mot un- grudgingly made. (Hear, hwr.) Another winter was ahead of the brave lads in France and on the high seas, and that .meant another winter's work for .the needlewomen at home, and he was assured that the Liberal women of n.rrington would go on working this winter ,of .as they did last. After fifteen or sixteen mor Ns of terrible war the people of this country had no need to wear long faces or to get into pessimistic moods concerning the result, for the British lads and their gallant Allies were proving their worth, and were going to win. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: Great Britain Wiii Conic Out On Top.
div.p: Great Britain Wiii Conic Out On Top.

He had absolute confidence in the fighting men from this country, and also in those who were directing the affairs of State, and he be- lieved that Great Britain would come out on top and that her soldiers and sailors would maintain the glorious traditions of the past and that the country would emerge from this, the greatest of all struggles in the history of the world, as trumphantly as ever she had come out of the great wars in which, in the past, she had been involved. He wanted them to be full of confidence. He had had a letter from a son of his who had been out in the North Sea. and who wrote: "If you saw the Fleet to-day you would be amazed at the tremendous improvement. Good as it always was and the admiration of all the world, its past condition is nothing to what it is to-day." (Applause.) Mr. O'Brien went on to urge his hearers not to allow them- selves to become members of the All-is-Lost party.

div.p: REDUCTION IN CLOTHING.

In union there is strength . but a man never fully realises it till he forms a matrimonial alliance with a strong-minded woman.
The Explanation.
Prof. William James, Harvard's brilliant psychologist, often illustrated a truth with a story.
"The most ghastly superstition," Prof. James said recently, "has often its base in a ludicrous fact. It is like the case of Jones.

" Jones,' said a man, 'tells me that his wooden leg pained him horribly last night.' "'Nonsense!' was the reply. How could his wooden leg pain him?' "'His wife,' the man explained, hit him over the head with it.'"

div.head: NOT AN UNMIXED EVIL.
div.p: NOT AN UNMIXED EVIL.

"We have been able to have our usual meet- ings and anniversary service, and have not dropped anything, although I am rather sorry to say that the attendances at all except one of the meetings, as well as the attendance at the anniversary service, have not been as good as they were last year. Probably the war has had something to do with it." Thus did the Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth, the secretary, report to the annual meeting of the Warrington Branch of. the English Church Union, which annual meeting was held in the Patten Hall. on Monday evening, and was but sparsely attended. The reverend secretary Went on to report that the strength of the branch was about the same as in the previous year. It was difficult, he added, to get people nowadays to realise ,that there were other things to think about besides the war. It was no use getting morbid. People must have some little change of mental diet, and a good diet for Churchpeople was for them to attend the meetings regularly. It would help them considerably.

div.head: REV. W. J. STANTON'S FORTHCOMING
div.p: REV. W. J. STANTON'S FORTHCOMING
DEPARTURE.

The secretary's viva voce report having been approved, the appointment of officers. for the ensuing year was proceeded with, the Rev. W. J. Stanton—who presided over the meeting—being re-elected chairman.

The Secretary, in proposing Mr. Stanton's re- election, said that he had been chairman for the last five years or so, and had done a tremendous amount of good work for the branch. Mr. Siddell was the seconder.

Returning thanks, the newly re-elected Chair- man said that he had thought it would be neces- sary for him to retire from the branch alto- gether, owing to the fact that he was shortly leaving this neighbourhood, and was going to live in Staffordshire. He had, however, con- sented to take the chair for another year, though it would not be so easy for him to attend the meetings. Still he would do his best, And would come whenever he possibly could. He would always do his utmost to further the work of the Union wherever and whenever he could. • Mr. C. Sawkins Burgess, who was unable to be present, was re-elected vice-president and treasurer, and the following were chosen to form the committee: Miss Margaret Wood, the Rev. J. M. Buckmaster, and Messrs. W. H. Stans- field and E. Hall Coates.
The Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth was unani- mously re-elected secretary, on the proposition of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Siddell.
STRIFE QUICKENS RELIGIOUS LIFE.

The Chairman then addressed the meeting at considerable length, touching upon a variety of subjects, including, of course, the war. How, he asked, had the war affected this country from the religious aspect? They heard a great deal of the effect it had had in Russia and France, and also in Italy—countries which were very differently situated to this ceuntry as regards religious feeling. Russia was, pre-eminently. the religious country; France and Italy had been of late years the irreligious countries of Europe. In the two last-named countries the war had led to a most remarkable religious re- vival. It seemed to have quite done away with the antagonism to religion of the secular authorities in France; it seemed to have turned the nation back from what he might call free thought to the religious -verities. It seemed also to have had a wonderful effect on those serving in the French Army. and the same, too, he thought, was true of Italy, where, owing to the unfortunate relations which of late years existed between the Papacy and the kingdom, the people had come to be more and more against the Church. One Gaih War Has Brought To Italy.

He had heard it stated by a friend of his in Rome that it was perfectly marvellous to see how, since the declaration of war, the whole attitude of the Italian authorities and the Army had changed—how the authorities had found the need for religion and how the soldiers instead of being discouraged from doing so were now encouraged to go to church. Could it be said that the war had had an effect 'on the religious life of the people of this nation, similar to that which it had had in France and Italy? He was very much afraid that it could not. It was true that just after the declaration of war there was a cer- tain quickening of religious interest, and the special intercession services _ held throughout the length and breadth of the land were very well attended, but he was afraid that the early effect had passed off. War was a thing which cut both ways, affecting not only the nation which was the aggressor, but also the nation which was defending principles, and it was never true that one side was wholly wrong and the other side was wholly right. And so, he thought, they must realise that the war was sent as a very terrible punishment for them all; as an infliction which must give them cause for true searchings of the heart and very genuine .self-examination as to their conduct as a nation in the past. It was a very clear call to repentance and humiliation.

div.head: Grounds For National Humiliation.
div.p: Grounds For National Humiliation.

They would find great grounds for national humiliation if they considered how the mar- riage laws had been tampered with; the fear- flu l state of immorality to be found in the towns and villages; of the thousands, nay, •myriads, who never gave a thought to God in this professedly Christian country; and the pleasure-seeking and the open flaunting of God's Holy Day. For all those things the nation was now being called to strict account. Having contrasted the former opposition offered to religion by the civil authorities of France and Italy with the happier relationships existing between Church and State in this country, the speaker went on to say that he (lid not altogether believe that want of opposi- tion was a sign of health, forlit too often bred indifference and utter lukewarmness, which were much more fatal things than violent opposition. The duty of the Christian people of this country was to try and bring back the lads and lasses to that Catholic faith which alone could support.and -sustain them in times of trial, storm and stress.

div.head: 111611 SIIERIFFS EXAMPLE.
div.p: 111611 SIIERIFFS EXAMPLE.
Abandoned Official Dinners Provide
Nursing Funds.

The High Sheriff of Lancashire (Mr. Edward Graham Wood) has thought it right to dis- continue for the remainder of his year of office the official dinners at which it is customary for the High Sheriff to entertain the Grand Jury, and instead to make a contribution to the funds of the Red Cross Society and the Order of St. John of Jerusalem. In sending a cheque for £5OO, Mr. Wood stated that he re- garded economy in both public and private life as a first obligation, not only as necessary for the successful prosecution of the war, but with a view to enabling the ,gerieral body of citizens to pay something of their debt to our wounded soldiers and sailors.

habitants given to fire and sword; the nation of " kultur " indulging in the barbarities of the Huns; the descendants of Luther standing by while their ally massacres thousands of Armenia Christians; justice perverted and Nurse Cavell brutally done to death. Now surely is a judg- ment, a time of discerning, and surely for the sake of the German people themselves we are doing a right thing to try and crush this insane ambition and militarism ,that has its issue in the denial of all democratic rights, in atrocity, in shame. The Lord of Hosts hath a day. It is a day of judgment, a day when in the fieice light of His presence all evil will stand revealed. The world would not suffer and shudder so much at the grim tragedies of war if God were not present in His world refining our spirits, giving us a horror of evil in every form, and day by day asking us to give the verdict, as judgment after judgment has to be made. But the day of the Lord of Hosts is also a day of realised ideals. All natiolo shall turn to the Lord, Isaiah cries. The basis of life will be seen to be spiritual and not material.

div.head: CHURCHES AND THE WAR,
div.p: THE CHURCHES AND THE WAR,
"THE DAY."
Striking Sermon At IN'esieyan
Intercession Service.
" RIGHT WILL WIN."

There was a large congregation at Bold-street Wesleyan Church, Warrington, on Sunday evening, when the Rev. Percy Meson preached the last of a series of sermons on "The World- War." It was also an intercession service, the roll of honour containing the names of 120 soldiers and sailors connected with the church being read, the congregation standing. After the sermon the choir sang the " Hallelujah " chorus, and at the close the congregation sang the National Anthem—altogether a most im- pressive service. _ _ _
The Rev. Percy meson preached on "The Day," taking for his text Isaiah ii., 12. "The Lord of Hosts hath a day."
CONFLICTING IDEALS.

On this day of intercession, he said, for those who are standing between us and nameless horrors of war, it will be well for us if, in God's presence, we can be assured that right must triumph: For years now our enemies have been accustomed to toast "The Day "—the day of their triumph and the triumph of militarism. Their faith is, as one. of their Professors puts it, that "Divine Providence has made us one of the greatest nations on earth, and we trust its guidance to lead us on in the future." But the Kaiser is an anachronism. He is.a -relic of Old Testament times. His god is a bloodthirsty Eastern monarch, and his day a day of blood and fire. His soldiers go to battle singing with a literal meaning "A safe stronghold our God is still." The Kaiser's day is not the day, how- ever.

div.head: Spirit That Will Win.
div.p: The Spirit That Will Win.
A short time ago a British regiment went into action singing "There is a green hill far away?' Picture it! A regiment of war-worn soldiers

div.head: Ploughshares for Swords.
div.p: Ploughshares for Swords.

Then he goes on—and this in the middle of strife—" Men shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more" —in the midst of turmoil, the vision of peace. But between the turmoil and the peace, still the clash of arms and the tramp of armed men. But in the day of the Lord of Hosts the vision will be realised. And have we not had the same vision of "the day"? I remember very well toward the beginning-of the war one notable man saying, "This may very well be the great- est and possibly the last of the wars of the Lord, for it is a Titanic struggle between the people and the war lords, between brotherhood and autocracy." It is the same vision of the day of the Lord; when the true ideals of. Chris- tianity will be realised. And though this is no time to • cry "Peace, peace!" yet for the strengthening of our souls in this warfare let. us not lose sight of the ideal which must be realised, because God is fighting for it. In the midst of the woful clash of events let us catch

div.head: By permission of the proprietors of " Punch.
div.p: By permission of the proprietors of " Punch.

before. battle singing this, one hymn which,. per- haps of all others., Most clearly expresses the tender, unworldly, unpractical idealism Of Christianity. "0 dearly, dearly has.He loved, and we must love Him too, And trust in His redeeming blood, and try
Ris works to do."

I don't suppose that the singers were particu- larly religious men. The point is that the men were able to Eking of Divine Love at the Moment when they were about to fling themselves upon the enemy. And be assured that in this ghastly catastrophe which civilisation has brought upon itself, it is that spirit which is going to win, for it means that these men, maybe uncon- sciously at times but nevertheless really, feel that they are battling for the right; that their warfare is but one of the fronts in the great world war between good and evil. In reality they are amongst the conquering heroes for whom the Lord of Hosts is mustering his spiritual hosts to battle, and the day will come at last.

Having illustrated, the fact that for the, Prophet Isjtiah "the day" of. the Lord ofllostS was primiifily a "day of judgment "z--" God will judge the nations "—the preacher proceeded All life and history is but a series of judg- ments, of discerning times. Calvary was the greatest time of judgment, the greatest discern- ing time the world has, yet, seen. It was like a scorching4lame throwing up the inviSiolc. ing on the heart of the wAld. It revealed the spirit that was in the world. Think of the men who stood thus revealed—Pilate, Judas, Peter, the howling mob of Scribes and Pharisees, the thief on the Cross—and to-day is a judgment. Saved Through Evil.

A French officer writes: "The German is -saving the world because he has shown us what evil is." "Never in his life," says a German, "had he seen- the reality of evil in so tangible a form as in this war." It is. the ,discerning time and men are seeing the spirit of evil that is in militarism. It has been there in Germany's heart for a long time, and now in this day of judgment it is being seem for what it is. We ought to have seen it before—in the swagger of the military, through the streets of the German towns, in 'the restraint 'that made men afraid to say what they thought, in the philosophy that said that power was everything. Neitzsche, the apostle of the superman, hates the thought of democracy and popular rights, as much as. the Kaiser does. He hold's the patient, toiling. ' industrial millions in contempt. A masterful autocracy, a tribe of men with no tender quali- ties—this is the Tace. to zultivate— But _now. is, the judgment, the discerning time, now the spirit that is within is revealing itself, and God's verdict will be seen—Louvain and its in-

div.head: HEROIC SERBIA.
div.p: HEROIC SERBIA.

the glimpse of .the fair far horizon, where the day is dawning. • The prophet in his darkness sees not only the dawn but the fnlness of the day. He talks- of the later day, of the time when the day will have come to its full issue. Let us be at least as daring as he was. Let us catch -a vision of the peace that Christianity came to bring. In the-midst of the tottering kingdoms let us seek to see and belong to the kingdom of God and His Christ. For the day is essentially the day of God's triumph. A Parable of Mighty Issues.

Whatever the issue of this war—and no one of us can say with certainty what it will be—in the end the Lord of Hosts will have His day of triumph. We may have te"-brace ourselves for disaster after disaster, but God's purpose can- not be defeated. In our hearts, firmly and quietly, most of us are saying to-day, "It may be a long time yet, but we shall win through." Which thing is a parable of mightier issues. In the great world war against evil the struggle may go on for ages yet, but in the end the Lord of Hosts and His conquering heroes will win through. As with every' dawn someone awakes saying "This is my day"; as with every dawn comes someone's chance, some soul gets its wish, some will shows what it can do, so God -will I.ave His day, the day on which His justice and power will find scope and triumph. Suddenly and simply like any dawn that comes, the great decision and victory of Divine justice shall at last break out of the long delay of ages. Life will be governed by new conditions. Right will win against might. Israel in her affliction thinking of that day, conceived of it as being the day when she would return to her country and her God. Early Christianity could not see how God was going to triumph under existing circninstances, so they said- that two things would happen in e•innertion with it. the return of Christ and the end of the world. But all were sure it would oome. The Lord God omnipotent would reign. The " Hallelujah " chorus would be sung on "the day," the day of the triumph of the right. In our present European war we were told the other (lay that the more men enlisted, the more speedily would the war be over and victory secure.. A Conquering Voluntary Army.

The greater army of the Lord of Hosts is also a voluntary army" and the same is true. the more conquering heroes God has to lead the more speedily will the day of the Lord of Hosts dawn. The day will come, the God of battle will triumph, but it will come only in so far as we as individuals let the day dawn in our own lives. And once more we say that the surest way to hasten the end Of this ghastly European struggle, is- also the surest sway to hasten-the great day of the LoYd.- We must ally ourselves with all• that is true and right, and have the victory in our own souls. In one sense

from Belgium, so as to take up arms against Germany. This Christian woman, arrested on August sth, held prisoner for months, has been tried by German court-martial on October 7th and Bth, sentenced to death at five o'clock on October 11th, and brought out for execution at two o'clock next morning! She was to die by shooting at the hands of soldiers. If the latest accounts are to be relied upon, the soldiers Nizre more merciful than their masters. Only one is said to have fired at her, but did not kill her, whereupon the officer in command killed her himself with a pistol! Her body was immedi- ately buried in the prison where she fell! Words fail to characterise this deed, or to estimate its unspeakable iniquity! One thing at any rate is certain, that however Unanimous our nation may be as to the righteousness of its attitude towards Germany in this most ter- rific strife, now the whole civilised world will rise up in condemnation of a deed so monstrous in its unparalleled guilt! urely. Germany itself will repudiate the deed and punish the perpetrators! That is demanded of her, as a great nation, still claiming to be ranked among Christian peoples. It may be, let us hope it will be, that now Christian Germany may rise up in condemnation of their horrid crime, and of the state of war which has led up to it; and that it may begin to pause in its career of wide and wholesale brutality and insensate hatred. Whatever other name may live in history, out of this most awful of all wars, Miss Cavell's name will live!

div.head: REV. E. DOWNHAM ON HELP INDESCRIBABLE.
div.p: REV. E. DOWNHAM ON HELP INDESCRIBABLE.

Preaching on Sunday morning at St. Paul's Church from the text 2 Thess., ii., 16-17, " Now our Lord Jesus Christ Himself, and God, even our Father, which hath loved us, and hath given us everlasting consolation and good hope through grace, comfort your hearts." The Rev. E. Downham said: Lo, Christ is with us. He has said "I am with you always." This is comfort and help indescribable. Of late we have had an example of the perfection of His presence. The heart of every English- man has been stirred by the story of deep devotion to duty, and of heroism contained in the death of Miss Edith Cavell. The murder of this lady reveals the horrible brutality of the Germans, and proves conclusively to the world that we are fighting not only against a hostile nation, but against a nation possessed with the spirit of an anti-Christ. But more than all this, the death of this Christian woman—this faithful daughter of the: Church - of England—is, I say, an example of the per- fection of Christ's presence. The last hours of Miss Cavell are made known to us in the letter

of the British Chaplain. He says: "We par- took of the Holy Communion together, and she received the Gospel message of consolation with all her heart. At the close of the little service I began to repeat the words ',Abide with me,' and she joined softly in the end." What a testimony to the comfort and hope that come to to the soul through faith in Christ. Read the hymn and accept it as the confession of her faith. .
I need Thy presence every passing hour; What but Thy grace can foil the tempter's power?. Who like Thyself my guide and stay can be? Through cloud and sunshine, Lord, abide with me. •

As a writer has said, "There is a companion- ship where there is no voice. Is it- not written, 'ln Thy presence there is fulness of joy'? Reveal Thy presence, Oh! my God. I want Thyi presence even more than Thy power." Just so. In the time of trouble it is enough that Christ is with us. As Francis Thompson has said:—
When the nations lie in blood, and their kings
a broken brood, Look up, 0 most sorrowful of daughters, Lift up thy head, and hark, what sounds are
in the dark, For His feet are coming to thee on the waters.
Yes, Christ comes to us on the waters of suffering and sorrow. He spet..._s, saying: "It is I, he not afraid." "Peace—be still."

div.head: "THE WILL TO LOVE."
div.p: "THE WILL TO LOVE."
Is it Transcended By "The Will
To Power" ?

"The Will to Power and the Will to Love" wassthe subject of an address given by Mrs. Q. Watts, of Manchester, at the Friends' Meeting House, Warrington, .cfn. Sunday.. evening. In her opening remarks the speaker said that to- day there were two great • forces at work—the will to power and the will to love. Since the beginning of the war they had heard very much of the will to power. It was the universal law af the_ nations. We",ourselves.claimed to: be mistress of the seas, and say that we must remain so, and this will to power was not only in our international life, but was also in our commercial, social and private life. The inter- national power consisted of Dreadnoughts, sub- marines and war. In the national life the relationship between employer and employe was made up of strikes and lockouts. The result both in international and national life was that everyone was dreading the power that could be exercised over one another—and the result was, war! In the national life there were glaring instances which stood out to-day with startling emphasis.

div.head: Drink Traffic.
div.p: The Drink Traffic.

One was the glaring failure of the government with the drink traffic. In spite of the excel- lent example of our Allies; in spite of the ex- ample of the King and the call of Lord Kitchener, we were to-day faced with the ter- rible fact that the money spent in the first six months of the year was six millions more than was spent in the first six months of last year. Continuing, Mrs. Watts said that power was often used for good, but it all depended on the root from which the power came. We had tried to regulate war according to rules, but every day these rules were broken by either one side or the other. Why? Because war was the devil's game, and cannot be regulated. Much had been done in our national life; we had regulated hours of labour, we had workshop regulations, we had seen to the education .of our children, but already these were being swept away by this terrible evil of war. Mrs. Watts contended that evil could only be overcome by the will to love. Christ never called for revenge. He said "Love your enemies." Love must enter their international life. If they refused to accept the love of Christ, to whom would they turn? Would it be power? They had seen the great evils which followed the will to power.

div.head: WIFE'S MAINTENANCE.
div.p: WIFE'S MAINTENANCE.
Former Warring ton Publican's Domestic Troubles.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court en Wednesday a separation order was sought against James Riches (55), an Army- pensioner, of 58, Upper Houghton-street, Southport, by hits I wife. Last week, it will be ,remembered;Richeo was before the Bench for neglecting to main- thin his wife, whereby .she became chargeable to the Union. Mr. T. S. Steel represented the complainant and Mr. E. Hatfield, of Southport, represented the defendant. The magistrates on the Bench were Alderman Smethurst (presiding), Mr. W. T. Williams and Mr. C. Jackson Holmes. Opening the proceedings, Mr. Steel said that the defendant was before the Court a week ago, and the case was then adjourned for a month with the view, to proceedings being taken by the wife. The parties- were married in December, 1902, and for some time kept a public-houst, in town, where the defendant stayed until 1904. He was then drinking very heavily, and in consequence of his conduct the brewery company required him to leave the premises. The licence was taken over by the complainant's father, who paid the defendant a sum about £2( or £3O by way Of compensation. The defendant removed his furniture from the house, and under his orders it was sold by public auction,. the proceeds of the sale being taken by the defendant. He stayed in Warrington for some, time, drinking and getting casual employment_ He was a good musician, and played at the Theatre occasionally. He also went travelling getting orders for sewing machines, and he had an insurance book. During the whole of that time he never paid anything to his wife. In 1908 the defendant went to Southport, where he still lived. The complainant had once called to see him, and had stayed with him two or three days. Twelve- months ago last August she called to sect defendant. and asked if he would do any- thing for her. He ordered•her -away from the house and said he never wanted to see her again. In May last she wrote to the defendant asking if he wopld come and see her, but to that letter he ne4r replied. The complainant had no regular employment, but the defendant was at Southport in the employ of, the Southport Corporation during" the summer, playing on the front. In addition to that he had a pension from the Army in which he held the rank of drum-major. With what he earned in the sum- mer he had suffiCient to last him throughout the winter. Mrs. Riches went into the witness box and gave evidence supporting this statement, and this completed the complainant's ease. Wife's Duty To Husband.

Addressing the Bench, Mr. Hatfield said that he had not heard a particle of evidence on the question of desertion. The defendant was not charged with neglecting to maintain his wife; neglecting to provide maintenance was not desertion. The defendant was three years in Warrington after leaving the public-house. He had been a bandmaster at Orford Barracks, and during the season he was employed by the outhport Corporation to play the clarinet in the band.

Again questioned, Mrs. Riches said that lately her father and mother had employed her work- ing in the house. Her sister had also em- ployed her lately. She was now living on the charity of her friends. She went to the Union three weeks ago, went into the hospital, and remained there until Saturday. Mr. Hatfield: Didn't you go to the Union for the purpose of being spiteful to your husband? Mrs. Riches: No, sir. . _

Because you could not get kindness froni him, you were glad to get rid of him?—l did not want to be abused. It is a wife's duty to stick to her husband.; why didn't you follow him?—l could not go and be knocked about. _

_ • Further cross-examined, the witness admitted that she did not want to live with her hus- band because he was not kind to her. If she had stayed with him she would not have been at' the *Court that day.

_ Re-cross-examined: She did not always want to live on her sister's generosity. She had re money in her pocket and felt it rather hard. Addressing the Bench further, Mr. Hatfield said that there had been a lot of outside re- marks in this case. They had heard evidence which might have been used In a charge of cruelty or in a charge of neglecting to provide reasonable maintenance, but the . charge, brought that day was of desertion. He sub- mitted that there was not a tittle of evideilie of desertion.. The defendant left the house with his wife's consent, and for the last eleven years they had lived apart by mutual consent. The defendant was not in good health and was deaf. There was an absolute " drug "on the labour market for musicians and the defendant was useless in other spheres. After the Magistrates' Clerk had stated that the Bench was satisfied that there had been desertion, evidence was given by the defendant. When asked if he was willing to take back his wife he replied: "What is the good when have no money? If she has plenty of money I will take her back."
He was ordered to pay ss. a week towards his wife's maintenance.
Even in charity one half the world doesn't know how the other half gives.
