div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY OCTOBER 30, 1915.
BOON IN RECRUITING.
As we foretold would be the case, the men
of Warrington are not the men to stand back when they know their services are really needed. Lord Derby's scheinc for canvassing

the 5,000 eligibles in the town who still re- main unenlisted was fully explained last week, and the result has been most satisfactory. in King's call to arms put the issue so plainly before the country that there could be no resisting its claims, and before the can- vassers got to work there was a rush to the recruiting office at the Police Station. Mon- day was an exceedingly busy day, and for the week something like a record for recent times was set up, though exact figures are not available. The system by which men have the option of being posted to a regiment at once, or of being transferred on enlistment to the Army Reserve without pay' until
wanted, promises to be a popular innovation. King George's appeal to his people, asking "men of all ,classes to come forward volun- tarily and take their share" in the struggle

against "a highly 'organised enemy who has transgressed the laws of nations," comes at a time when the soul of the nation is profoundly moved. It is profoundly Moved by the spec- tacle of Serbia's " superhuman effort "—to borrow the words of the Serbian Prime Minis- ter in his message to this country—" to de- fend her existence in response to the advice and desire of her gat Allies." And a great wave of pity and horror and burning indigna- tion has swept the country at the ruthless severity meted out by the military despotism of Germany to a noble woman who had spent her whole life in the alleviation of suffering, and had shown the same impartial devotion in her humane task whether the objects of it were German enemies or her fellow-country- men.

"In ancient days the darkest moment has ever produced,in men of our race the sternest resolve." That is a message which should make us compose all petty squabbles and jeal- ousies; urge each one of us to give the utmost service of which we are 'capable, and resolve
that, however faulty we may think the Gov- eminent or the system under which we are all working for a common end, we at least will not only "do our bit," but " do our best."

div.head: HAVE WE SAVED AND HOW?
div.p: HAVE WE SAVED AND HOW?

The Pudding Lady's mission to Warrington under the able management of Mr. Wilfrid Rowland and those who work with him proved a great success, and much real interest was taken by very large audiences in all she had to say about economical cooking and kindred subjects. There are, of course, other phases of saving which have been placed before the public by their special advocates. All this labour in the common good deals with a sub- ject that comes under the comprehensive head of " thfift," a word which is not very phpu- lar in some circles. It would be interesting and of practical use to social workers of all classes if those who have ventured upon war- time savings of, any kind would let the public know of the steps they have taken and the results that have followed their efforts to effect savings. Care is now needed more than ever in the husbanding of resources, and advice, founded upon actual experience, would have a first-class value. Will our readers supply us with this information? Names would not be mentioned where privacy was required.

div.head: IS CORPORAL TOMBS "A WARRINGTON V.C."?
div.p: IS CORPORAL TOMBS "A WARRING- TON V.C."?
We have received the following letter this week :
• Sir,—Just a line to thank you for the letter published in your paper I sent the other week on "Bands for Slackers."

Well, tlie boys have asked me where does Tombs, V.C., belong to at all. Here is a slip of paper out of the "Birmingham Weekly Post "—Corporal J. Tombs,Thrmingahm V.C., and not Warrington V.C. First he is that and then this. The boys of the First King's would be very pleased if Tombs, V.C., would answer this. I tell the boys he belongs to Warring- ton, but what are the lioys saying about me, when they see such a thing in a Birmingham paper? I tell them he lives. in Warrington. I would just like to talk to him myself. I was with him a couple of days before .the charge, and of course he "wet" his ribbons with me, but did not have much to Say. I thank you very much if you will publish the answer in the earliest paper to settle this argument.—Yours, Szc., PRIVATE WHITTLE, Ist King's Regiment.

div.head: [COPY.]
div.p: [COPY.]

left the local Aluminium Company's works to take up arms. His address when the war broke out was 17, Howley-lane, Warrington, and that was the address officially recognised, we believe, .by the War Office authorities.

Perhaps Corporal Tombs will oblige his inquiring comrades by saying authoritatively the place that has the greatest claim upon him. Of course, a man is a "native " of the place in which he was born, though he may have had very little to do with it.

Birmingham V.C. Wounded. Corporal Joseph Tombs, V.C., King's (Liverpool) Regi- ment (a native of Sparkbrook), was wounded last week, and he is now a patient in an Eng- lish military hospital. On Thursday he ,was visited by his father, Mr. F. Tombs, Vicarage- road, Chester, who learned that he had been badly wounded in the right arm. A shell burst quite close to him. Rather severe injury was also caused to the head, and Tombs is in a feeble state and suffering considerably from nervous shock.

We do not think it has ever been definitely stated where Corporal Tombs was born. Like many other noted men, he is claimed by various places, and, as we stated when the honour came to him, he has been of a roving disposition, so that many towns in many parts of the world are directly interested. All that Warrington can claim of Tornbs is that he had lived at Warrington for four years when .the war broke out, and that he
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 30, 1915.

div.head: WARRINGTON WAR FINANCE.
div.p: WARRINGTON WAR FINANCE.

judged by the half-yearly statement of Mr. W. H. Woodcock, the .Borough Collector and Assistant Overseer, the gentleman who sees •that we pay our rates and in return does his best to get us our votes, Warrington, aftcr a year of war-time experience, is well able to pay its way. As a matter of fact; the rate yielded a larger sum than in any preceding half-year, the £78,500 drawn into the muni- cipal net being nearly £lO,OOO more than in the previous half-year. That, it is true, was due largely to the considerablet increase in the rate' which the Council imposed upon the borough last spring. But the Council mig—ht add many one-and-fourpences in the .0 to the rates, and if the borough could not stand it, the addition would be a worse than useless act. However, the larger sum has been paid with less loss than ever, small thougl . that loss has generally been. There was not a single " excusal," Mr. Woodcock reporting thiat there were no cases calling for remission. Losses in collection constitute a record—on the small side—for only £8 Os. id. was so lost,

including £2 4s. Bd. in bankruptcy cases for water rates, which are not ranked as prefer- ential debts. On demolished, uninhabitable and rate-excused property, such as Belgian homes and the Red Cross Hospital, Mere were some, though insignificant, "allowances." The real loss under this head was for empty property, £9OO, about £5O more than in the preceding half-year, Fan increase chiefly accounted for by the increase in the rate and not by any hicrease in the number of houses empty. That amount in a town, of between 70,000 and 80,000 inhabitants shows. empty property, as actual experience proves, to be very scarce indeed. There are practiclilly no empty houses, the empty, property berng a few large shops, some, we regret to say, in the main streets.

The Borough Collector's staff, like the staffs in most of our places of business, has shrunk owing to the demand for men. The whole of the unmarried men of military age in the Treasurer's office eleven in all have enlisted. Certain duties relating to registra- tion were also undertaken by the heads of the staff. As we have seen, the work has increased, and the results have been most gratifying. Clearly, Mr. Woodcock and his colleagues May claim to run their department with an efficiency that is capable of rising superior to unaccustomed' and trying conditions.

div.head: PRESSURE FELT.
div.p: PRESSURE FELT.

The Borough Collector is not unmindful of the spirit i which his calls have been met by The ratepayers. "Present high rates," he says, "are pressing heavily upon many mem- bers of the community "—but they have paid. It would be strange if even in ordinary times an increase at one bound of is. 4d. in the £ did not make somebody wince. But besides this, costs have gone up for all classes of repairs, interest on mortgage has grown, up- keep generally is a more serious matter. He intimates that a new scale of assessment to give relief to cottage property owners, and to prevent rentstfrom being unduly raised is in contemplation. As against this we have heard it suggested that the rates will be increased again when the next Budget makes its appear- ance. We hope this will not prove to be true, for rates of 9s. 4d. in the are quite high enough, especially when food prices and all other kinds of prices' are boonng. All un- necessary expenditure has been stopped, and there would appear to be little reason for a further advance, but rates, like facts, are stubborn things, and, on occasion; run against reason.

div.head: RATE POWER.
div.p: RATE POWER.

People often want to know how much a certain rate will realise. Here are Mr. Wood- cock's actual figures for last half-year: On the poor rate every penny produced £1,185; and on the improvement rate every penny produced £1,09..

div.head: POSTPONED WORK-AND UNPOSTPONED.
div.p: POSTPONED WORK-AND UNPOST- PONED.

In view of what we have said respecting the apparent needlessness of an increase in the rates, because our spending departments have been warned off all new work, it is interesting to reflect upon some things that have recently been done and some that have been left un- done. At the Town Council last week Coun- cillor Locker asked Alderman Bolton, what most of his constituents are wanting to know —When is St. Elphin's Park going to be opened to the public? It is years since the Park was acquired, and now, at this late time of day, the Chairman of the Parks Committee says it is one of those things that must wait until the war is over—for the little asphalt the walks require to make them fit for use. But we did not wait till the war was over for the defacement of Reward. Place, -a deface- ment, which, moreover, has caused a perma- nent cost to the town of t 2 a week for ever, or as long as the " convenience " stands, for wages t 6 caretakers. Nor did the war pre- vent the erection of a shelter to obstruct the entrance to the Cemetery and to attract chil- dren in such numbers as to be a nuisance at what should be a sacred spot. Any fine Sun- day the 'shelter is like a magnified bee hive, so many are the children entering, leaving, and swarming all over the place. The war is a good plea, but it should be uniformly ap- plied. Perhaps the Council will now supply the shelter with a caretaker on the Howard Place plan.

div.head: OUR VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: OUR VOLUNTEERS.

As will be seen from our report of the meeting in the Town Hall, an effort is to be made to put life into the Warrington Volun- teer detachment. Those who escape from the nation's claim upon their services and are fit, may reasonably be expected to volunteer for home defence. Perhaps the appeal made to their patriotism, not only by the report of the meeting, but by the letter written on the subject by "Brassard," will have the desired effect. ,
How Lord Derby's Canvassing Scheme Progresses.
GOOD LOCAL RESPONSE.
The following Royal message was issued last week-end :
BUCKINGHAM PALACE,
TO MY PEOPLE.

At this grave moment in the struggle between my people and a highly organised enemy, who has transgressed the laws of nations and changed the ordinance that binds civilised Europe together, I appeal to you.

I rejoice in my Empire's effort, and I feel pride in the voluntary response from my subjects all over the world, who have sacrificed home, fortune, and life itself, in order that another may not inherit the free Empire which their ancestors and mine have built.
I ask you to make good these sacrifices.
The end is not in sight. More men and yet more men are wanted to keep my armies in the field, and through them to secure Victory and enduring Peace.
In ancient days the darkest moment has ever produced in men of our race the sternest resolve.
I ask you, men of ail classes, to come forward voluntarily and take your share in the fight.
In freely responding to my appeal, you will be giving your support to our brothers, who, for long months, have nobly upheld Britain's past traditions, and the glory of her arms.

strife, thinking that she would find the British Empire unready and , unprepared, and that, anyway, she would not join in. Britain and her Allies had just got to win, and Lord Kitch- ener said only a few clays ago that, if he had the men, he would be able to hold the situation in the hollow of his hand. There were only two ways of getting men for the Army—either by conscripting them, or by persuading them to come forward as volunteers. Hitherto, at least more modernly, English soldiers had al- ways given themselves to their country volun- tarily. England prided herself on her volun- tary system, and the Trade Union leaders had said that if the case were put before the work- ers of the country there would be no need for conscription, and the present effort to secure recruits was being made as the result of that advice. The men of Lancashire were known the country over for their independence, and he asked them to show it now and to demonstrate that they were not inclined to be dictated to by anyone. (Hear, hear.) - Mr. Plinston added his plea not only for men for the Army, but also for. Volunteers to under- take the duty of finding the men for that abso- lutely indispensable body.

div.head: RECTOR'S VIEWS.
div.p: THE RECTOR'S VIEWS.
Compulsion Legitimatey Voluntary
ItespOnse Fails.

The Rector of Warrington, (the Rev. Canon Willis), preaching at the .Parish Church on Sunday, said voluntaryism was on its trial. If this final effort to induce those who ought to come forward failed, to make them do their duty nothing 'remained but compulsion. Every one of military age in satisfactork health and not otherwise engaged in war work would then he compelled to serve.. That, in his opinion, would be perfectly fair. How very unfair it was that any should profit by the fact that other brave young men volunteered and died! It was only fair that all, including women, should play their part in the present effort. Compulsion entered into almost eVery phase of life—there was, for instance, compulsory educa- tion and there was the payment of rates and taxes. The State ought to apply compulsion to those who would not come forward to serve their country in such a crisis :as this.

The King's manly and straightforward appeal, which appealed to all hearts, and the murder of Miss Cavell by the Germans ought to stimu- late a voluntary response from the nation. The name of the German,Emperor, who 'could have ,preyented• this murder, mould be handed down to Posterity as that of the most infamous criminal who ever lived.

div.head: PICTOIHL APPEAL.
div.p: A PICTOIHL APPEAL.
The Murder Of An English Nurse By
A German Officer.

Much attention was aroused yesterday after- noon by a huge picture exhibited at Market Gate as an appeal to Warrington men to join the forces. It depicted NurSe Cavell lying on the ground and shielding her face from a Ger- man. officer, who had a revolver in his hand. A firing party were depicted in the background. In the right-hand corner of the picture were the words, : "Men of Warrington, will you still linger here While British women are foully murdered by the Huns?"
The picture was painted by Mr. Herbert Dell, of Church-street. - ,
WHERE ARE THE CANVASSERS?

There has been a niost unsatisfactory response to the appeal for canvassers to wait upon the 5,000 recruits that Warrington, has it in its power to provide. Those who have offered their services began operations last night, but they will have to be considerably augmented • in num- bers if the work is to be thoroughly done. If they would only come forward there are more than sufficient men and women in Warrington who are capable of and eligible for doing thi,; highly necessary work. Only 500 are wanted, but they are Wanted promptly: All willing to canvass are earnestly requested to attend at No. 3, Horsemarket-street, at 7 o'clock on Mon- day evening.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDING.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDING.
• HODGSON-BRACECAMP.
Vicar Of Si. Paul's Daughter Married
At Oxford:

At St. Giles' Church, Oxford, on Saturday, Mr. Grenville H. Hcagson, third son of the Rev. H. A. Hodgson, rector of Beddington, Surrey, was married to Miss Dorothea Brace- camp, only daughter of the Rev. W. Bracecamp, vicar of St. Paul's, Warrington. The wedding was a very quiet one, the briZe's father being on duty at the Front as a Chap- lain to • the Forces, and her brother, Second- Lieutenant Frank Bracecamp, being on active service with the Royal Field Artillery. The bridegroom, who will be well remembered as the resident engineer for, the pew Warrington Bridge, was 'himself in khaki in the uniform of a Lieutenant of the Royal Engineers. His brother, who acted as best man, Mr. Christopher M. Hodgson, is a Second-Lieutenant in the Royal Field Artillery. The bride, who was given away by her mother, wore a travelling costume of brown cloth, with velvet hat to match, and she and each bridesmaid, carried a Prayer Book in- stead of the usual bouquet. The bridesmaids were Miss Marjorie Bennett, Padgate, War- rington, and Miss. Freda Wilkinson, Liscard, who were attired in nary blue costumes. Each wore a pretty brooch, the gift Of the bride- groom. The ,Rev. H. A. Hodgson officiated. A, reception was held at the Mitre Hotel, and the couple subsequently left for North Wales, where: the honeymoon is being spent.

div.head: " -CALLING THEM UP ! "
div.p: " -CALLING THEM UP ! "
Latest Local Recruiting Effort.
ARE YOU COMING?

"Stop the War! The only way is for every eligible man to join the Colours now!" " England wants men to fight and women to work. Apply within from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m," " Men of military age, step insicle and join now. Your pals are calling."

• Are you coming? In bold type these three calls to the manhood and the womanhood of England stare out from the windows of the premises •at 3, Horsemarket-street, which this week have been opened as the headquarters of the local recruitini committee. There callers will find two energetic secretaries ready to give any information and assistance in their power, and they are Messrs. Ernest A. Sanders and Mr. Herbert Hayes—the agents of the rival political factions in the town who; for the nonce, have buried the figurative hatchet and are now work- ing in bon accord for the good of the country in her hour of 'need.

div.head: LORD DERBY'S "LITTLE REMINDER."
div.p: LORD DERBY'S "LITTLE REMINDER."

During the past few clays many a young man in Warrington has received "a little reminder" from Lord Derby, and facts go to show that in many cases the reminder has "got home," local recruiting having received a gratifying fillip. So far all the men' of military age have not been canvassed, but it will not be very long before they are; for many volunteers have come forward to undertake the work of canvassing, although—the task being a big one—the services of many more will still be welcomed. Of course, the job is one that ,can only be under- taken by men who themselves are over the mili- tary age, and, moreover, it is one that requires a great deal of tact, for many a promising young man might be deterred from doing what is, nowadays, almost unanimously considered his duty, by a word "out, of season,' as thQ phrase goes.

div.head: KING'S MESSAGE.
div.p: THE KING'S MESSAGE.

To back up Lord Derby's appeal comes the. ringing message of the King to his people; the heart to heart talk which greets the eyes of all who pass by the public hoardings. It is a poster ,that cannot very well be overlooked save by those wilfully blind. There are signs that the King's call has been heard, and hopes that it may be heard yet more. An English King never yet called in vain, and George the Fifth will be no exception to the rule. _ _

Following up the call of the posters came two open-air meetings at the Market Gate, the first being held on Monday and the second ~bn Tues- day. At the Monday meeting the band of the 2nd/4th (Territorial) South Lancs. Regiment— under Acting-Bandmaster R. E. Sadler—was in attendance, and played appropriate music.

div.head: IF THE GERMANS CAME TO-MORROW.
div.p: IF THE GERMANS CAME TO-MORROW.

Captain Mathams, who has charge of the recruiting at the Drill Hall, was present, and made a brief speech to the considerable crowd who had been standing listening to the melody. If, said the Captain, England was going to win the war; she . must fight her own battles; she must not place too much reliance upon the help of other nations. If the Germans came to War- rington to-Morrow, Warrington would be a heap of ruins, the mothers and the sisters of the men of Warrington would be outraged and dis- honoured, and little children would be slaughtered and spiked on bloody bayonets. That was the lesson that the, soldiers who had been out had learned from the experience of Belgium. That must never be permitted to happen in England, and the crucial question was: Are those who are not in khaki going to hang back; are those who are not working by night or ,by day—and by both if necessary—to supply the men in the fighting line with the munitions of war, going to hang back any longer?

div.head: DOUBTING NATION.
div.p: THE DOUBTING NATION.

Referring to the position in the Balkans, the speaker said: "Some of us reckoned On certain nations coming in, but the moment the Ger- mans started to march asainst Serbia, what happened? The Bulgarians came in with Ger- many. The Rumanians, whom we all expected to be with us, are hanging back. Then for the first time in history, the great British Empire condescendect,to say to a small nation, which was running away from its treaty obligations, 'Here is a rick territory. Here is a land which we have brought to prosperity. Take it as a present; only fight for us.' That little nation, one of the smallest in Europe, after getting an offer like that from the biggest nation in the world, said; 'No thank you. We will not take Cyprus.' I do not pretend to say what it means, but I ask you: Would not the man of common-sense say, 'Greece won't take Cyprus because she is not sure that we are going to see this business through, and that we :are coming out on top' ? I there any other infer- ence to he drawn?" When, added the Captain, they saw Greece for that, of course, was the nation he referred to—doubting their policy, did it not make their sense of manhood rise? Did it not make them want to say: "I'm an Englishman, and I'll show them"? All who stood listening to him were, of course, not able to join either the Army or the Navy, but they could all do something, and that "something" it was their duty to was up to every ohe to do something for England. (Hear, hear.) GERMANY'S GREAT MISTAKE.

A second meeting was held on Tuesday even- ing on the same spot and was addressed by Captain Eric Fairclough, and Mr. Charles Plinston, both of whom made earnest appeals to the men of the town to "join up," and do it soon.
Germany, said Captain Fairelough, was ready for war—she was prepared in all departments— 'and when she thought the moment opportune she took steps to start the present terrible

Rev. J. Carson's Will.
The Rev. James Carson, of the Rectory, War- grave, Newton-le-Willows, whose death was recently announced in "The Examiner," left £1,974.

div.head: " Cabiria."
div.p: " Cabiria."
The great film " Cabiria," has been booked exclusively for Warrington by the Grand Electric Theatre, Bridge Foot, where it will shortly be on view.

div.head: Thelwall Heys Military Home.
div.p: Thelwall Heys Military Home.
The monthly Pound Day in aid of Thelwall Heys Military Home was held on Thursday, and as a result goods to the value of about .210 were received.

div.head: Infectious Disease.
div.p: Infectious Disease.

During the week ended. October 23r11 the following new cases of infectious disease in the borough were reported :—Scarlet fever, 22; diphtheria, 3; tuberculous phthisis, 6; enteric fever, 4; erysipelas, 5. There were in hospital: Scarlet fever, 105; enteric fever, 12; diphtheria, 7; phthisis, 20; total, 144.
Religious History of the Turkish Capital. _ _

On Thursday next tie Rev. G. Parkin will pay a visit to the Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church, and at 3.30 in the afternoon will preach, and in the evening at 7.30 will lecture on "The Religious History of Con- stantinople." Mr. J. T. Rowland will preside.

div.head: To Help St. Peter's Church.
div.p: To Help St. Peter's Church.

On behalf of the parochial organisations con- nected with St. Peter's Church, a sale of work will be held in the John-street School on Mon- day and Tuesday, November Ist and 2nd. Mrs. Ireland Blackburne has kindly consented to open the sale on the Monday afternoon, and on the Tuesday the opening ceremony will be per- formed by Mrs. Peter Rylands.

div.head: Illuminating Power of Gas.
div.p: Illuminating Power of Gas.

The Corporation liave applied to the Local Government Board for a Provisional Order in order :that they may abolish the existing standard of illuminating power of gas supplied by the Corporation and substitute n calorific standard, and also that they may increase the pressure. An Inspector of the Local Govern- ment Board will hold an inquiry into this application at the Town Hall at 10 a.m. on Wednesday, November 10th.

To Old "Blue Coat" Boys. As we announced some weeks back, Mr. and Mrs. Rose, who for many years have been respectively the headmaster and the matron of the Warrington Blue Coat School, are on the eve of severing their connection with that insti- tution, and are goilag into well-deserved retire- ment after many years of faithful and un- grudging service. In order that "Old Blues" may have the opportunity of saying farewell to their old friends and preceptors, a special service is to be held in the School Chapel on Sunday evening, commencing at 6.30.

div.head: For Golborne-street Church.
div.p: For Golborne-street Church.

A sale of work in aid of the funds of the Gol- borne-street Baptist Church is to be held in the Church Schoolroom next Thursday, and will be opened at 3 o'clock in. the afternoon by the Rev. H. Ogden. The sale will differ from most other events of the kind in that admission will be free. An excellent assortment of goods from the young men's and young ladies' stalls was left over from the annual sale in July last, and the purpose of the forthcoming .effort is to clear off the remaining stock. The proceeds will be devoted to the building fund. The work of the church has been rendered all the more difficult by the absence of thirty-five young men who have 'joined the Colours.

div.head: Parish Church Sale of Work.
div.p: Parish Church Sale of Work.

The annual Parish Church sale of work will be held in the Fairfield Schools, Manche.ee- road, next Thursday, Friday and Saturday, opening each day at 3 p.m. The Vice-Chan- cellor of the,Duchy of Lancaster is announced to open the sale on the first day, and on .:the second and third days it will be reopened by the Rev. .Wilfrid Stanton (Thetwali) and the Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Peter. Pea- cock). respectively. Refreshments will be pro- vided, and each evening entertainments will be given.

div.head: Baptists' Missionary Sunday.
div.p: Baptists' Missionary Sunday.

To-morl7ow will be observ'ed as McSsionary Sunday in the Baptist Churches of the town and district. The deputation will be the Rey. C. E. Smythe, a veteran missionary from China, and a most acceptable speaker. In the morning he will conduct the service at the Hill Cliffe Church, and at 2.30 in the afternoon he will be present at a special gathering, in. the Golborne-street Church, of members of all the Baptist Sunday Schools of the district, and will give an address. In the evening he will take the service at the Latchford Baptist Church. The Rev. 11. Ogden will preach at the Golborne- stieet Church in the evening, and he will take as his subject "The World for Christ."

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyatts' Anniversary.
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyatts' Anniversary.

The sixty-fifth anniversary of the foundation of .the Bold-street Wesleyan Church will be celebrated, this week-end, commencing with a lantern lecture in the Schoolroom to-night. The title of the lecture will be "Love, Light and Death," and it will be given by the Rev. Percy Tucson. On Sunday the Rev. J. T. Wardle Stafford will preach, his sermon in the evening being specially addressed to young men and women, and being entitled "The Great Cam- paign." Miss Hylda Cragg-James will sing the solo and will also sing at a special service in the afternoon, when other musical items will be contributed by Mr. Bradford Barton (violinist) and Mr. W. H. Payton (solo- organist). Mr. John Taylor will preside and the speaker will be the Rev. W. Thompson Derry. On Monday the Rev. J. T. Wardle Stafford will, under the chairmanship of Alder- man Bennett,- lecture on "The Decline and Fall of the German Empire." Days of Sacrifice.

Preaching at the Golborne-street Baptist Church on Sunday evening, on the subject of "The Seriousness of the Present Moment," the Rev. H. Ogden (the pastor) said that steadily the nation was realising that it was in the fear- ful grip of war, but there were yet still many who treated the present serious times as Nero treated the burning city of Rome, fiddling whilst it burned. What was the result? Nero's name was covered with disgraceful infamy for all time. They had heard wild ribaldry in the highways even before the very dust created by the cars conveying the wounded to hospital had settled. Perhaps, the preacher went on, such a question as the American Exchange was as foreign to them as were Constantinople or Pekin, and yet the relentless building up of the Exchange against them was a very serious matter for the people of this country. These were days when sacrifices were required, yet how many there were who had not been pre- pared even to. reduce their normal amount of butter or• to sacrifice their rasher. of bacon. It. was the duty of the preacher to urge the strictest ectmomy•-arid to be an example to the ,loose- Minded and the frivolous.

div.head: Late Sir Peter Walker.
div.p: The Late Sir Peter Walker.

On Friday afternoon of last week the remains of the late Sir Peter Walker were laid to rest at Osmaston, Derbyshire, with military hon- ours, the deceased baronet having been a com- mander of the Derbyshire Yeomanry and Colonel of the. West Derbyshire Battalion of the Home Guards. There was a very large attendance of mourners and friends at the service, which was conducted by the Vicar of the parish and the Chaplain of the local Yeomanry. The coffin, covered by a Union ,Jack, on which were placed the late Sir Peter's 'sword and helmet, was conveyed' on a motor ambulance to the churchyard. Among those who attended from Warrington were Alderman Bennett and Mr. Herbert Hayes, representing the Conservative Association; Mr. R. H. Dain- tith, Conservative Club; Messrs. Robert Hutton, J. Fulton-Smith, E. Parry, C. Holland, J. Dunn, Fred Parsonage and George Johnson, representing the Warrington breweries. Floral tributes were received by the hundred, includ- ing those from the *Warrington Caledonian Association, the Warrington Conservative Asso- ciation, the Warrington Conservative Club, directors Burton and Warrington Breweries, and the several departments of the Warrington Breweries. Sir lan Peter Monro Walker, the new baronet, was prevented from being present by indisposition.

div.head: An sAbandoned Baby.
div.p: An sAbandoned Baby.

The police authorities at Warrington are desirous of obtaining information respecting the abandonment of a male child about ten weeks old. The child was found in the rear of a house in Pierpoint-street, Warrington, at 6.20 p.m. on Tuesday, the 19th inst. It was dressed in new clothes and appeared to have been well looked after. The child is now in the Workhouse.

div.head: For the Red Cross.
div.p: For the Red Cross.

In aid of the Raddon Court British Red Cross Society Hospital, a concert will he given by Mrs. W. B. Roberts's Orchestra in the Patten Hall Winmarleigh-street, next Thursday evening, commencing at 7.30. The fallawing rr,ted artistes have kindly promised to appear: Mrs. Mee, Mr. J. Rabbitt, Mr. R. Dickinson, Mrs. Haviour, Mr. Herbert Geary, Mr. Robert Smith, Mr. Jubb and Miss Gertrude Henshall.

div.head: Find Dead In Bed.
div.p: Find Dead In Bed.

- An inquest was held at the Police Station on Thursday morning on the body of Margaret Terrigan (58), a widow, who lived at 33. Dakin's-yard. The deceased was found dead in bed on Wednesday morning at eight o'clock. A post-mortem examination was performed by Dr. Peacocke, who testified that death was due to natural causes.—A verdict in accordance with this testimony was returned.

div.head: Warrington Market.
div.p: Warrington Market.
Wednesday.

The market was brisk and a fair quantity of oats and wheat offered. Wheat is still advanc- ing in price, 7s. to 7s. 6d. per bushel of 701 b. Oats are dearer, price per 451 b 4s. 31d. to as. 4d,.; samples offered slightly better than the pre- vious market. Oat straw, 445. to 455. per ton; wheat, 41s. 6d. to 425. 6d. per ton. Flour is dearer, 40s. per 2801 b., bakers' grade. Eggs 4 and 5 for is. "The Friends Thou Hast

Never cast aside your friends if by any possi- bility you can retain them. We are the weak- est of spendthrifts if we let one drop off through inattention, or let one push away another, or we hold aloof from one through petty jealousy or heedless slight. Would you throw away a diamond because it scratched you? One good friend is not to be weighed against the jewels of the earth.—St. Peter's Church Parish Maga- zine. • A Week's Deaths.

During the week ended October 23rd there were in Warrington 20 deaths, against 18 in the corresponding week last year. They arose from the following causes :—Enteric fever, 1; epidemic influenza, 1; enteritis, 1; phthisis, 1; other tuberculous diseases, 1; cancer, 1; pneu- monia 1; heart disease, 1; all other causes, 12. During the same period there were 39 births, against 41 last year. Motor Accident Near The Weir.

A motor car containing a Latchford gentle- man, his son and a young lady friend, was coming to town the other evening when it skidded right in front of a tramcar and made for the river wall. Tram Driver. Roe acted promptly, put on his emergency brake, and undoubtedly prevented a very bad accident. As it was, the resulting collision was very slight; but the car ran into the wall, wrecked itself, and only hurt the young lady slightly. Post Office Whist Drive and Dance.

Mr. Thomas Walsh, hon. treasurer of the recent Post Office whist drive and dance, held at the Crosfield Memorial Hall in aid of the Prisoners of, War Fund, has this week handed over £2l to the Borough Treasurer, who has placed the amount to the Mayor's Fund. The committee, without particularising, de- sire to thank all who contributed towards the success of the gathering by attending, by giv- ing prizes or refreshments, or in any other way.

St. John's Church Festival. Them, anniversary services will be held to- morrow, when the Rev. Sydney 0. Morgan, of Hoylake, will preach morning and evening. Mr. Morgan is a clerical member of the Cheshire and Flintshire Presbytery, and one of the coming young ministers of the Presbyterian IChurch of Wales. The soloist for Sunday even-- ling is Madame Sanders. On Monday the annual tea and concert will be held. Tea is to be on the tables at 6.30 p.m., the chair being taken at 8 o'clock by His Wor- ship the Mayor (Alderman P. Peacock). The John Yonge has also kindly promised, to "(2 present. div.head: SHALL SERBIA DIE?
div.p: SHALL SERBIA DIE?

"Serbia is making superhuman efforts to de- fend her existence, in response to the advice and the desire of her great Ally. For this she is condemned to death by the Austro-Germans and Bulgarians. For twenty days our common enemies have tried to annihilate us. In spite of the heroism of our soldiers our resistance cannot be expected to be maintained indefinitely. We beg you, the many friends of Serbia in Eng- land, to do all that you possibly• can to ensure your troops reaching us, that they may help our army and that we may defend together the com- mon-cause that is now so gravely menaced."— M. Pashitch, the Serbian Prime Minister. "The small British force sent out to Salonica —I think 13,000 in round numbers."—Lord Lansdowne.
And shall poor Serbia die? And shall poor Serbia die? Alone amid her mountains, with her proud face to the sky?
We send our little armies while her life-blood ebbs away; We dally and procrastinate while traitors swoop to slay, And our paltry driblets trickle to Salonica Bay.
But north and east and sotfth and west the banded armies come, While free men weakly hesitate and calculate at home, Secure behind the ramparts of the Fleet and of the foam.
They cry to us for succour; they held the pass alone; Their hearts and fields are burning, and their stoutest sons lie prone, And still they watch and wait for us—is Eng- land's heart of stone?
Must all men die for England while she alone delays, And, while her friends are failing-her, the sword of vengeance stays? If Serbia fall, like Belgium, indelible disgrace
Will brand the haggling statesmen who stood 60 feebly by. And watched her nobly struggle, and left her
there to die, iler hand upon her sword-hilt, her proud face to the sky.
A truce to hesitation, shame on these base delays; Shall we stand calculating with Europe in a blaze, While Greece turns feeble-hearted, and Ferdi- nand betrays,
And those who knew and trusted us begin t° turn away? The proud old heart of England shall surell answer " Nay!" We fight for right, our sword is bright, we will not wait a day!"
We ask for men to lead us-0 God, we ask for men! Give us a lead and trust us—our hearts are sound, and then The world shall turn to England with the ola faith again.

And shall poor Serbia die? And shall poor Serbia die? Our souls respond, impulsive, to the lit.tle nation's cry. She must not, no, she shall not—we swear you and I, Or a million marching Englishmen -sfrill know the reason why! •"*"TTNI-VIT 27th October, 1915.

ACCIDENT TO THE KING.
THROWN FROM HIS HORSE AT THE FRONT.
. The Press Bu it yesterday issued the following : October 28th.
While the King was inspecting his Army in the field this morning His Majesty's horse, excited by the cheers of the troops, reared up and fell. .

The King was severely bruised, and will be confined to bed for the present. (Signed) • ARTHUR SLOGGETT, ANTHONY BOWLDY, BERTRAND DAWSON, WILMOT HERRINGHAM, CUTHBERT WALLACE. .The King has had a fair night with some sleep. The temperature is now 99.2 and pulse 75. His Majesty's general condition has im- proved and no complications have arisen. (Signed) ANTHONY BOWLDY, BERTRAND DAWSON.

JOFFRE IN LONDON.

div.head: Visit To Lord Kitchener.
div.p: A Visit To Lord Kitchener.

General Joffre arrived in 'London yesterday morning, and in the course of the forenoon visited Lord Kitchener at the War Office. The presence of the distinguished General in Whitehall attracted great attention on the part of the public. Later in the day, General Joffre, Lord Kitch: ener, and other officers had lunch with the French Ambassador at the Embassy.

div.head: CONFERENCE
div.p: A CONFERENCE

General Jofire attended a conference at No. 10, Downing-street, in the afternoon. Among those present, in addition to the Prime Minister, were Lord Kitchener, Mr. Balfour, the Minister of Munitions, and one or two English and French military officers. General Joffre conferred with • the Minister of Munitions last evening. -
HEATH OF THE REV. 11. WILKINS

been reported, missing since the big advance took place. The last letter which he wrote home was dated September 20th, and the only news which Mrs. Armitage has since re- ceived concerning him was conveyed in the following letter, written by Private S. A. Cleaver—a comrade of Private Armitage's— under date September 30th Missed After Fierce Engagement.

"We have been in another fierce engagement, and I have some news, which, as a pal of Tom's, I feel it my duty to write and tell you. We were in the German trenches for a few hours together after making the Charge, and at that time he was all right. During a sharp counter-attack we got separated. Tom's party was Surrounded, and I think he was taken "prisoner. We ,went into action with another battalion for the attack. I made inquiries amongst the fellows, all of whom were strangers and who would scarcely remember Tom if they saw him. However, I give you the facts as they occurred, and I am' very sorry to have to write suCh bad news. Tom and I were always together, in and out of the trenches, and to lose him is to me like losing a brother. you ought in due course to have a line from Tom himself."

div.head: REES.
div.p: REES.
Former AX arrinuton Alinister.

The Rev. Richard Wilkins Rees, who some years .ago'was a prominent member of the War- rington Wesleyan Circuit, and who had many local friends and admirers—not only at Bewsey- road Church, where he ministered specially, but generallyd on Monday night at his resi- dence, Epworth Villas, Duffield-road, Derby, in which town he Was superintendent o; the King- street Wesleyan Circuit. lie hid been seriously ill for some days past, sufferhig trom pleurisy. Mr. Rees was in his second. year at. Derby, and had already made many frien.ls, not only as the result of his gifts as a preaciwr and pastor, but by the 'charm. of his personal Anraeter. A Welshman, as his name suggest, he was trained at. Didsbury, and was first .sent cn circuit in 1884. The towns in which he has !abound were Yarmouth, Southend, Grav-isend, l'tirt Leven, 'Viroolwich, Cardiff, Manchester, Warrington, Blackpool, Blackburn,' Barrow .in-Furness, and .lastly Derby. A man of Strong literary taste 3, he wrote fre, luent articles for the reviews, anti he was well- known in the world of lettefs, among many souvenirs which he cherished being a signed ,portrait of George Meredith. Mr. • Rees was only 55 years of age, and he leaves a widow and 4ine child—a son who interrupted .a promising University career. to serve in the Army, and who :now • holds lieutenant's rank in the 14th Battalion of the Sherwood Foresters. The loss -to Derby Wesleyanism is a severe one, and it is the second of the kind within a motth, the Rev. F. Lenton, of the Green Hill Circuit, having passed 'away within this .period. It is over 60 years since the King-street Circuit lost a minis- ter by death.

div.head: "WESLEYAN INTERCESSION DAY.
div.p: "WESLEYAN INTERCESSION DAY.
'War Services In The Local Churches
To-morrow.
Special war services will be held at the Wesleyan Churches to-morrow, and special sermons Will be preached at the morning and evening services. The list of preachers is as _follows :

_ Bewsey-road: Rev. P. meson (morning) and the Rev. W. • T. Derry (evening); Sankey _Bridges:. Mr. E. W. Evans and Mr. T. Upson; Latchford :Rev. E. May (morning and evening); Lymm: Rev. A. J. Morton and Mr: J. E. Pass- more; .Penketh: Rev. W. T. Derry and Rev. T. Dixon; Moore: Rev 11. P. Dixon and Mr. R. H. Sutton; Padgate:- Mr.. M. 11. Llewellyn and Rev. A. J. Morton; Stockton bath: Mr. T. Wright and Rev. P. meson. Special services were held at Bold-street •Sunday.
Lord Derby and Church's Loyalty and Patriotism.

Like all other Christian bodies, the Wesleyans have played an important .part in the war, as the following letter from Lord Derby to Sir Robert Perks indicates :—" I thank you for the information that, by the direction of the Wes- leyan Methodists services of thanksgiving and intercession in connection . with • the war Are being held next Sunday in all the Wesleyan Churches and Mission .Halls throughout Great Britain. Anybody who has had any connection with the Army knows well the work done by ,the Wesleyan Methodists for our soldiers and sailors, not only at. home, but at all the prin- cipal naval and military stations abroad; and am not the least surprised to learn that, at this crisis of our ,ntional history your Church, .and other great Nonconformist ,Churches, have responded so nobly to their country's call. The freedom to worship according to his own con- science is one of the Proudest possessions of the British race; and this freedom extends to every soldier and sailor serving in His . Majesty's Forces. The soldier, who may find that on entering the Army he has, by some mistake, been entered as a member of a Church to which he does not belong, has the right of receiving the ministrations of the Chaplain of the Church to which he belongs. I .feel confident that in discharging the duty r have undertaken of gathering to the Colours more. and still more of my fellow-countrymen. of all creeds, I can rely upon the sympathy and co-operation of the Christian Churches throughout the. United Kingdom; and not the least upon the Wesleyan Methodists, whose loyalty and patriotism have descended from the 'days of their: founder,. John Nesley, undiminished to the present date."

PRIVATE W. EMERY.
In Hospital

Emery, 82, Scott-street, is now in the Lord Derby War Hospital, Win.wick, suffering from heart and chest trouble, contratted while serv- ing on the Continent with his regiment. He hoped to get out for an hour or two on Monday afternoon and to visit his home, along with several comrades, but he was not then well enough to do so. Private Emery, who is nineteen years of age, was educated at Hamilton-street School. He was formerly, employed as a foreman fustian- cutter for the United Velvet Cutters' Associa- tion. He attended Silver-street Sunday school, and he joined the Territorials about /four months before the outbreak of war, and had been at the Front since June.

div.head: WOUNDED WARRIORS.
div.p: WOUNDED WARRIORS.
Concert At The Lord Derby War Hospital.

To show their sympathy with the wounded soldiers, the St. Helens Amateur Operatic Society again paid, at their own expense, a visit to the above hospital on Saturday evening and gave an excellent vocal concert, chiefly com- posed of selections from "Maritana " and the "Lily of Killarney." The so.lbists were MioLily Webster, Madam Ethel Parr, Miss G. Tither, Messrs. Cottom and Hughes, supported by a large and well-balanced chorus, under the baton of Mr: H. Addison, the accompanist being, as on previous occasions, Miss Bertha Smith. The humorous element was provided in the shape of recitations by Messrs. Milne and Cottom.
A large audience showed their appreciation in a most enthusiastic manner, two of the singers having to respond to shouts of encore. The party were afterwards entertained at supper.

div.head: EXCELLENT CONCERTS AT THE
div.p: EXCELLENT CONCERTS AT THE
WHITECROSS HOSPITAL.

A concert, organised by Mr. Percy Smith, for the benefit of the inmates of the Whitecross Military Hospital, took place at the Hospital on Wednesday evening. Some noted local artistes had offered their services, and the entertainment was a most excellent one, and was greatly appreciated. Miss E. Hewitt and Mr. Poole delighted all present with their rendition of the two duets " Watchman " and "Excelsior." Miss Hewitt followed with the songs "My Hero," and for an encore "The Call of the May-time." ,Miss Perdue rendered in fine style "Mien Schnieder" and "When Irish Eyes Are Smiling." Two cornet solos "Scottish Memories" and "Dear Little Shamrock" were given by Mr. Rutter, and Mr. Poole was loudly applauded for his contributions "Up From Zummerzet." "Glorious Devon" and "Friend of Mine" were the titles of the two songs effectively given by Mr. Fieldhouse. Professor Baxteau mystified with his conjuring tricks, and Mr. Scarisbrick proved an able entertainer in his monologues, Sze. At the close of the concert Mr. A. Bottomley proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the artistes, I to which Mr. Smith responded. The previous Saturday the Brooklyn Male Quartet, assisted by Mrs. Sophton and Mr. J. Blackburn (cornet soloist), gave a concert to the wounded soldiers at the hospital. The pro- gramme consisted of 'quartets, duets, solos and humorous items. Mr. W. Furness thanked the narty for 'their visit, and said that, judging from the " Tommies' " applause, the endeavours of the artistes to provide a pleasant evening had been successful.

div.head: RADDON COURT CONCERT.
div.p: RADDON COURT CONCERT.

A capital entertainment was given last Satur- day at the Haddon Court Military Hospital by Mr. W. Taylor's Warrington Concert Party. Miss Annie Taylor was heard to great advant- age in her two songs, as were also Miss Cissie Rigby and Mr. George Taylor, especiallyain the duet "Larboard Watch." for which they were loudly applauded. Mr. Robert Forster gave two items in an appreciative manner, while two violin Solos by Mr. Ronald Syprs were skilfully rendered. The humorous element was in the capable hands of Mr. R. Scarisbrick, who was loudly encored for his very funny items. Thq accompanist was Miss Eva Shaw, who played in a very skilful manner, a•first-class concert being brought to a close by the singing of ..he National Anthem.

div.head: DANCE AT DRILL HALL.
div.p: DANCE AT DRILL HALL.

A highly successful dance in iid c:f the Wounded Soldiers' Amusement Fund, was held, by permission of Captain Mathams and Captain E. Fairclough, at the Drill Hall last night. The hall was tastefully decorated, with coloured festoons and flags, a large Union Jack occupy- ing a prominent position at the entrance. The music was supplied by the band of the 2nd South Lancs. Regt., under the able conductor- ship of Acting-Bandmaster R. Sadler, and the officiating .M.C. was Mr. W. W. Whittle. The arrangements were , under the management of Company-Sergeant-Major Morris and Sergeant Goodwin, of the 4th South Lancs. There were three hundred present, including the Mayo T and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Peter Peacock). A number of patriotic speeches were given and the event concluded with the singing of the National Anthem.

div.head: PRISONER OF WAR.
div.p: PRISONER OF WAR.
PRIVATE F. FERNEHOUGH.
Veil At Present, But "Dving For Something To Eat."

News has this week been received by Mrs. F. Fernehough, of 29, Wilderspool-causeway, Warrington, that her husband, Private Frederick, Fernekough; of . the 2/4th 'South' Lancashire 'Regiment, is interned as a prisoner of war at Munster, Westphalia„ Germany. Writing to his wife on a postcard dated October 17th, he states : " You will see from the postcard that I am at present a Prisoner of war in Germany, so in future will You send all parcels clearly addressed to the place stated on the side of this card. I am well at present, but am dying for something substantial to eat and drink, in particular bread, sugar, tinned fruits, tea and coffee, and also syrup. Will you send some illustrated papers, tobacco and matches, as all of us are lonely and it would help cheer us up?"
Private Fernehough • joined the South Lan- cashires nearly twelve months ago and seven

div.head: TERRITORIAL MACHINE GUNS.
div.p: TERRITORIAL MACHINE GUNS.
Sergeant Widocks' Contempt
For Slackers.
CONCERT, WHIST, FOOTBALL.

Sergt. Widocks, of the machine-gun section of the Warrington Territorials, writing to Coun- cillor Henshall, says:— " I received your very kind letter on Saturday night last, on my arrival home from the trenches, where we had spent 14 days of mixed experiences. When I say 'we' I mean the machine gunners, as you doubtless know that the old 4th are not doing treAch fighting, but are doing work almost as important. You will be glad to know that the gunners came out this time quite unhurt—far different to our ex- periences of last time, when we had 11 casual- ties. We toddled home this time quite a jovial crowd, but were feeling rather tired, as we had a six or seven miles tramp before reaching our humble abode. You quite realise that there is no place like home though, however far you have to walk to get there. It is so nide to lie down and think Well, I can sleep to-night without 'whizz-bangs' and Krupps ' for companions,' and you sleep with a contented look on your face. Of course, I only surmise the kind of look we swear at these times. We had not many exciting times to chronicle this time, although on the last morning of our stay the Boches sent us souvenirs of the armouf-piercing variety as early as 4.45 a.m., and when a 6in. shell enters your dug-out without knocking—well, it is time to get up. This we did, and had a lively quarter of an hour, but glad to say no one was any the worse for the disturbance.

div.head: Bacon And Cheese. To Annoy The Enemy.
div.p: Bacon And Cheese. To Annoy The Enemy.

"Instead of going back to bed again we lit our braziers and fried our bacon and cheese, and as the wind was blowing towards the Huns' trenches no doubt they would get a smell of our good things and wish they had not so rudely awakened us! We had one very quiet day, and as there was nothing more exciting to do we sat down and played whist. -In fact we had a miniature whist drive, and I am pleased to say I won the fourth prize, which consisted of three Woodbines! It was hard lines winning cigarettes,, for I had only that day received my share of the Woodbines that our kind friends in Warrington periodically send us, so I tried to exchange my prize for a button that one of the boys had cut off a German's overcoat—but he declined. A few nights before we went to the trenches we held a concert in the gun room, and with the assistance of the signallers, it proved A great success. I had the honour of presiding and we had a merry time from 7 p na. until 9 p.m. It was like being at the 'Hip.,' as we have some exceptionally good talent amongst us—tenors, baritones and comics. Every one agreed that it was worth coming to, but they may have said that because we charged them nothing, the only stipulation being that they should bring their own candles! I think that is what caused us to be so light-hearted. Any way, we have been requested to repeat the

performance, but whether- we shall h-ave the assistance of the signallers or not I cannot say. I will tell you why. Yesterday they challenged the gunners to play them football, and not caring to bow the knee to them, we condescended to play them. Of course, We beat them-3 goals to 2—nut the score does not at all represent the game, but we let them down as lightly as possible. It was a very good game, played somewhere in Belgium, and we greatly enjoyed it—at least 11 of them did—l can't speak for the other 11. These little breaks in our work do us immense good, and help to make us forget things.

div.head: Let Them Stay At Home.
div.p: Let Them Stay At Home.

"I can't tell you anything about the war. I wish I could say it was finished. I wonder if it will end before conscription makes its appear- ance. I see you have had high jinks at War- rington to get recruits—music and sports to try and charm the doubtful starters. Really, Sir, it makes me feel bad to read about it. 3 f they won't come without music for goodness sake let them stay at home and go to the pictures. I know there are a great lot that are doing munition work, &c., but I also know there must be a lot who are not doing. anything—only slacking. Of course if they are afraid to come —well, we will do their share and our own as well. You know, haw I feel_regarding this most vital question. • Ido think • every young man that is able ought to feel it-his duty to join. T know every one has. not got an inclination for military life, but when his country's very ex- istence is at stake it is his bounden duty to come forward at this juncture. I know a man out herg who has two sons in the same regiment. He is 50 years of age, and like a certain brand of whisky 'still going strong.' (This is not meant for a free advertisement). I am not saying any more, as I might cause offence.
When We Come Marching Home!

"The winter is slowly creeping on us, and the mornings and nights now are quite nippy. I was hoping we should have been amongst you again this Christmas, but I now think other- wise. Never mind, one day we hope to .march through the familiar ; gates in 'Sankey-street. past the fountain, to the Town Hall steps-and you will see some smiling faces that day. I think I must end this somewhat uninteresting epistle now. I sincerely hope that you, Mrs. Henshall and son are quite well. Please give my kindest regards to all friends. With the best of wishes I will conclude and remain "Yours most -sincerely,
"E. J. WIDOCKS."

div.head: GRIM TERRITORIAL PARODY.
div.p: GRIM TERRITORIAL PARODY.

"Sing Me To Sleep " : The Version In The Trenches. Private J. W. Bentley, of the Warrington Territorials, writing from "Somewhere in ,France" to a friend in Warrington, encloses the following lines, which he says the Terri- torials sing to' the tune of "Sing me to sleep" Sing me to sleep where bullets fall, • Let me forget the war and all, Damp is my dug-out, cold my feet, Nothing but bully-beef and biscuits to eat.
Sing me to sleep where bombs explode And shrapnel shells are a-la-mode; Over the sandbags helmets you find, Corpses in front of you, corpses behind
Far, far from this place I long to be, Where German snipers can't snipe at me, Just see me crouching where the worms creep, Waiting for someone to sing me to sleep.
RIFLEMAN J. SIMISTER. Wonnded and Missing.

resided with his sister, Mrs. Wilkin, at 91, Willis-street, Warrington, has been missing since May 9th, when—it is presumed—he was wounded during the attack on Neuve Chapelle. Previous to September,l9l4, when he enlisted in the 2nd Battalion Rifle Brigade, Rifleman Simister was employed as a wiredrawer at the Longford Wire Works. Ile was a keen foot- baller, and had gained a reputation as a pro- fessional boxer in Warrington. Rifleman Simister was sent to France with his regiment in January and, as stated above, he was wounded in May. Since then all efforts to trace him have been fruitless. Through various agencies, the War Office have made inquiries in Germany, but so far as can be ascertained he has not been taken a 'prisoner. it comrade of Rifleman Simister, in a letter to Mrs. Wilkin, writes:—" You will Pardon me ;taking the liberty of writing to you, but as/ your brother Jim was my chum since he came out here, I think it is my duty to do so. lam very sorry to say that I cannot tell you where he is. I have asked all the ' chaps ' who knew him, and they say that he got wounded in the arm." •

div.head: ON HONOUR'S SCROLL.
div.p: ON HONOUR'S SCROLL.
KILLED.
DRIVER J. GANNON.
Killed By A Shell Along %I, ith Two
Officers.

Official notification has been received by Mrs. James Gannon, of 56, Plumpton-street, War- rington, that her son, Driver J. Gannon, driver in the Royal Field Artillery was killed in action on October 3rd. Second-Lieutenant Julian St. Clair Holbrook, in a• sympathetic and kindly letter to Private Gannon's parents, states that their son was killed instantly by a shell which also caused the death of two officers. Paying a fine tribute to the deceased, the officer states he was a clever signaller and soldier, and regrets having lost him. Two letters were found in
DRIVER GANNON. Killed.

div.head: DIED OF WOUNDS.
div.p: DIED OF WOUNDS.
PTE. JOSEPH THOIVIPSON.
Brother llissing Since Last May.

News has been received by Mr. and Mrs. Thompson, of 11, Norris-street, that their son, Private Joseph Thompson, of the Royal Scots Fusiliers,. has died of wounds received in the recent great advance. The injury which proved fatal took the form of a wound in the chest, and he passed away in a hospital at Boulogne on October 26th.
A letter was received from a nurse in the hospital—it being dated October 21st—stating that Private Thompson was progressing favour- ably, although still weak from the effects of his ordeal.
Later, however, came .a letter to the effect that the wounded man had passed away. Joined Up Last Year.

Private Thompson, who was twenty-three years of age, was educated at St. Ann's School,' and was employed by Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons. He was a regular attendant at the Gospel Hall Church. He enlisted in December of last year. • Mrs. Thompson has another son in the Army —Private John Thompson, who is a married man and a member of the 6th South Lanca- shire Regiment. He went out to the Dardan- elles in May last and has not been since heard of, having been officially reported as missing. The only letter which has been received from him was written before he left England. Private Thompson is a married man, resid- ing at 5, Dickenson-street, He, as a boy, attended the Wycliffe School and worked at the Corporation Gas Works. He is thirty years of age, and, like his brother, is a member of the congregation of the Gospel Hall Church.

div.head: MISSING.
div.p: MISSING.
RIFLEMAN J. SIMISTER.
Local Boxer Not heard Of Since Last May.
Rifleman James Simister, who, before the war,
while in the firing line again when he was re- ported as missing.
RIFLEMAN A. lIEESOM. Missing.

div.head: WOUNDED.
div.p: WOUNDED.
LANCE-CORPORAL J. J. CHAMBERS.
NVounded After Thirteen Months' Active Service.

Lance-Corporal John Joseph Chambers, of the Ist Battalion King's Liverpool Regiment, son of Mr. Michael Chambers, of 10,. Boives-street, off Forster-street, has been wounded in the back whilst serving at the Front with his regiment. • Lance-Corporal Chambers, who is thirty years of age, is an old soldier, having been in the Army for about ten years. lie served in India for a considerable time. Ile has been at the Front about thirteen months previous to re- ceiving his wound. He was educated at St. Benedict's School, Orford-lane, and worshipped at St. Alban's Church.
PRIVATE JOSEPH SPEAKMAN.
Irish Fusilier With Three Wounds And Broken Leg.

Private Joseph Speakman, Royal Irish Fusi- liers, an employe at Messrs. Hutchings' Tan- nery, Howley, and son of Mrs. Speakman, 1, Banner's-yard, Brick-street, was wounded in Gallipoli early in August, having .been shot in the leg in three places, one of the bones being fractured.
Private Speakman, who is 22 years of age, is now in hospital in Alexandria. He is an old Parochial School boy.
Lacashire Doctors and Nurses in Egypt.

Writing from hospital on the 13th inst., to his mother, he says: "When I got your letter I was overjoyed, for I have never had a letter since I left England's shores on July 11th. I am glad to tell you that I am going on as well as can be expected. My wound is healing, but the doctor cannot let it heal up until the bone has grown again. The only drawback is that I have an awful pain in my foot and my nerves are shattered. I am feeling sore through lying on my back for five weeks, but every care is taken by the sisters. They give us every atten- tion, and they look after us very well, but the climate here does not agree With wounds. Most of the sisters come from Lancashire, and the doctor is also a Lancashire man, and strange to say, almost all the patients are Lancashire fellows. I don't go short of any- thing in the way of cigarettes or chocolate, as our Adjutant and Captain are in the same hos- pital, and he sends me plenty of things. I only wish-that I could be sent back to England, to some hospital near V'arrington. But I shall keep up a good heart. Last week I received my gift from Princess Mary, and I will" bring it home with me. I have had nothing to eat, only chicken, since I came here. We are cheered up each afternoon by a talking Machine. I think my fighting days are over now. I have often thought what a queer chap I will be on crutches, and I have thanked God that I have not got my
Wounded.
PRIVATE JOSEPH SPEAKMAN.
leg off. . . I think the next five weeks will sce me in England."
" For His Mother's Sake."

A nurse also wrote to Mrs. Speakman as follows :—" I promised your son that I would write you a few lines to let you know how he was, going on. He will have told you that his leg is broken, but he is mending very nicely, and he is much brighter and stronger in him- self. . . Yon would have been cheered to have seen the look of relief on his face when he found that the leg would be spared 'for his mother's sake.'"

div.head: SAPPER T. PETIT.
div.p: SAPPER T. PETIT.
Carried By Comrade Half-a-Mile To
Safety.
News has been received by Mr. James Pevitt, of 37, Oldham-street, that his son, Sapper Thomas Pevitt, of the Royal Engineers, who at present is lying at the First Eastern General

Hospital, Cambridge, is progressing satis- factorily. Sapper Pevitt was wounded by shrapnel in the leg, as his regiment were taking the second line of German trenches in the great advance. When Sapper Pevitt was struck he swooned and a Lance-Corporal of his section, it now transpires, lifted him on his back and carried him half a mile to. safety. The rescuer left hiin after bandaging his wounds, so Sapper Pevitt crawled for two hours to the dressing station. After attention he was put on a stretcher and was conveyed to the Canadian General Hospital, "somewhere in France," and eventually was transferred to his present abode. On Thursday a letter was received by Sapper Pevitt' father from a chum of his son's, wherein he states:— " I am glad to hear Tom is progressing satis- factorily, which gives pleasure to all his pals out here. You will be surprised to hear that the chap that carried Tom to the dressing station was afterwards wounded in Lae wrist and is now in hospital at Dublin. I have written to Torn, giving him his address, so that he can Communicate with his rescuer. I may say that your son was a general favourite with the boys, and all in this section wish him a speedy recovery, so that he may return to his old friends." Sapper Pevitt was educated at St. James' School, and prior to enlisting in January last was employed at Messrs. Dolan's, joiners.

div.head: SOLDIER AND SAILOR.
div.p: SOLDIER AND SAILOR.
Fate ei Two Brothers In Fighting-
Line.

Mr. Charles Ainslie, of 2, Halifax-street, War- rington, had two sons serving their country, one as a soldier and the other as a sailor. The sailor son has been killed and the soldier son, after having been wounded and gassed, is now about to get his discharge from the Army. The sailor son—Sydney—was killed on Feb- ruary 23rd, whilst serving aboard H.M.S. Defence. Just where and how he was killed are details which the War Department have not yet revealed to the stricken family, but they have vouchsafed the information that his body was buried with full naval honours "' some- where in Scotland," five hundred sailors follow- ing him to his grave. Sydney was 26 years of age and he had -been in the Navy over ten years, joining in Liverpool as quite a youth; in fact he was some months short of sixteen when he first put His Majesty's uniform on. The other son—Frank—is a baker attached to the Army Service Corps. He was home on leave in Septelhber, having been badly gassed. At Easter he was' wounded and he also came home , then. Prior to joining up in August last year, 'he worked at Mr. Toft's bakery. He is nine- teen years of age.

div.head: SIBERIAN VICTORY!
div.p: SIBERIAN VICTORY!

The other evening a newsboy of the loud- voiced variety was calling in Sankey-street: "Siberian Victory." It was thought that the youngster had been following the late Lord Salisbury's advice and had been study- ing a big map, but had, unfortunately, blun- dered upon the wrong end of it. That we may have been wrong in our surmise appears probable after reading the following in " Punch " this week : " According to Press reports German troops and artillery are being transferred from Galicia to the Siberian front."—" Liverpool Evening Express." "The Russians, we understand, are giving them every facility in the way of railway trains and escorts."—" Punch."

div.p: LIYMM

„ . Red Cross Hospital.—lt has been arranged that from last Tuesday, all in-patients at the local Red Cross Hospital will in future be received from Lord Derby War Hospital, Winwick, in- stead of from the Manchester base.

Tradesmen's Association.—The annual general meeting of the Lymm Tradesmen's Association will be held on Tuesday evening next at eight, in the Hirst Pavilion, for the purpose of electing officers for the forthcoming yeat and to re- ceive the treasurer's and secretary's report. District Nurses Fund.—At the Council meet- ing on Monday night a letter addressed to the Clerk was read from Mrs. F. Muriel Palmer, .Holly Bank, Lymm, in which she acknowledged a cheque. for £2 2s. for the District Nurses Fund. She asked the Clerk to convey her thanks to the Council.

Registrar. For Lymm Transferred.—At a Church meeting held in the Zion Independent Methodist Church, Cherry-lane, on Tuesday night, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. H. T. Mercer, organist and treasurer for the above church, for his services in the past. The Registrar for the village is leaving to take up a position at Sale. Several members of the Church spoke eulogistically of the services Mr. Mercer had performed for the church.

Co-operative Concert.—A select and enjoyable -intertainment took place on Thursday at the Drill Hall, in the presence of a large audience. it being the annual "Co-operative Concert." Vhe Brooklyn Concert Party from Warrington, endered several pledSing individual and com- ined items, all of which were accorded hearty cipplause. The accompanist was Mr. E. Trow, who also gave a descriptive pianoforte solo.

New Registrar For Lymm.—Mr. Thomas Peters, of Heatley, has been appointed registrar for births, deaths and marriages for Lymm, in succession to Mr. H. T. Mercer, .who is leaving to take up a position at Sale. The new regis- trar is well known in the village, so is assured of a hearty welcome. Mr. Peters has for the past thirty-five years acted in the capacity of a clerk in the Manchester County Court Offices.

Lieutenant K. de Jong.—Lieutenant Kenneth de Jong. son of Dr. Edward Meyer de Jong, is at present home on leave from the firing line for a few days. On Tuesday he visited his father, who is at present acting as medical officer in charge at Weeton, near Blackpool. He looks the picture of health, and none the worse for his experiences in the field. Lieutenant K. de Jong joined the Army as a Private last winter, and is now Adjutant to his battalion, the Sussex Pioneers,, at present "somewhere in France."

Present at the Council Meeting.—The mem- bers present at the Urban District Council meet- ing on Monday evening were: Messrs. R. H. Gotobed (presiding), W. G. Groves, C. E. Cowper, T. H. Warburton, F. Ingham, S. Critchley, G. H. Parker, J. Hardy Holt, and F. Lockyer. Also present were Messrs. William MuHard (clerk and collector), J. Cecil Mort <assistant), D. Mort (surveyor, sanitary and canal boat inspector), T. H. West (gas manager), and C. J. Barnes (water engineer), and Dr. Leonard Thorpe (temporary medical officer). Zion independent Methodist Church.—The annual harvest festival was held at the' above church on Sunday, the preacher 'for the day being Mr. G. Hunter, of Leigh. A crowded con- gregation listened attentively?, to the sermon, chosen from Romans xii. 21, "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." There was a fine show of fruit and flowers, the latter eventually being sent to several hospitals to help cheer the wounded British soldiers. Miss Blanche Rathbone rendered effectively a solo in the evening entitled "Bringing in the sheaves." The collections and sale of fruits fully realised expectations, and were in advance of last year's amount.

A Question of Administraticn.—At Monday night's Council meeting it was reported that a letter had been received from the clerk to the County Council inquiring if the local Council were willing for the County Council to be the authority for the administration of the Births Notification for, and Midwivea. Act, and if the Council were desirous of carrying out, or con- tinuing such, on their own behalf.—lt was de- eided that before anything is done in the matter the Clerk be instructed to write to the County Medical Officer and suggest a conference of representatives of District Councils in accord- ance with the suggestion of the Macclesfield Rural District Council.

Death Of Mr. J. 6011.—We regret to record the death of Mr. J. Bell, who resided at Sandy- lane, Lymin, and who passed away on the 16th inst. The deceased gentleman, who had been -ailing for some time, contracted pneumonia Ond underwent an, operation for cancer at the Man- chester Royal Infirmary. The late Mr. J. Bell, whose age was about 45 years, was well-known and highly respected in the village, where his geniality and unobtrusive manner earned him many friends. He was employed at the Lino- type Co.'s works at Broadheath, and was much respected by his fellow workmen. He wor- shipped at St. Peter's Church, Oughtrington, and was interred at the Parish Church on Wed- nesday of last week. Many lovely floral tributes from his relatives and friends were received. He leaves a wife and one child to mourn their loss.

Death Of Mr. Alec Struthers.—The death occurred on Saturday last, from influenza, followed by pneumonia, of Mr. Alec Struthers. who resided at Star-lane, Statham, Lymm. The -deceased was a prominent Methodist worker, and was for many years connected with the school and church, where his efforts secured him the gratitude of a host of friends and admirers, who mourn his loss. The late Mr. Struthers was employed as a tool-maker by Messrs. Moss and Sons, of Lymm, and he was greatly respected and esteemed by his fellow workmen. He was interred on Wednesday in St. MaTy's Churchyard, in the presence of a large and sorrowful gathering of relatives and friends. Many handsome floral tributes WPIP received. The late Mr. Alec Struthers leave.: a wife and three children, one of whom, the cmly boy, was removed last Thursday to the Isolatian Hospital suffering from diphtheria.

Resignation of the Fire Brigade Captain.— Mr. W. Kirkpatrick, the captain of the Lymm Fire Brigade, has resigned that position owing to illness.—At Tuesday night's Council meeting Councillor Parker, the chairman of the Build- ing and Fire Engine Committee, said that Mr. Kirkpatrick had been ill for some time, and he (the speaker) would like it to be put on record that his resignation was received with regret, and that the Council thanked him for his past services. Mr. Kirkpatrick had been connected with the brigade for a matter of 40 odd years. He hoped Mr. Kirkpatrick's successor would be as successful as his predecessor.—Councillor Gotobed, who was in the chair, said that he would like to supplement what had been said by Mr. Parker. It was a matter of regret that they lost an old friend, especially when sickness was the cause. They all hoped that Mr. Kirk- patrick's illness would be of short duration, and that he would„be speedily restored to health and strength.
