div.head: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
div.p: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
SERGEANT-MAJOR CLARE.
Crashing Shells Into The German Lines.

Mr. F. E. Evans, chemist, The Cross, Lymm, has this week received a communication dated October 23rd, from Sergeant-Major Clare of the Lymm Territorials, at present in the firing line. In,a letter he states:—

"I am pleaseil to inform you that there are no casualties amongst the boys, which is good nem s. All are in good health and spirits. 'I here is nothing startling to report, only that we are gradually pushing back the Germans toward Berlin, and the men are thoroughly determined that the enemy shall not break our lines. We are continually crashing shells into the enemy's lines, so it is up to those at home to keep us well supplied. We shall in all probability be relieved from the trenches for a few days shortly, so the rest will do us good."

div.head: PRIVATE JAMES GILBERT.
div.p: PRIVATE JAMES GILBERT.
Home On Leave From The Firing-Line.

Private James Gilbert, of 16, Newfields, Booth' d Hill, Lymm, is at Present home on fur- lough from the Front. He left the trenches on Sunday, arriving in the village early on Wednes- day morning. He is not feeling well at present, suffering from a slight -nervous breakdown in consequence of hardships which he has endured at the Front and of the news of the death of his brother, Edwin Gilbert, who was killed in action on August 25th. Private J. Gilbert is in the sth Cheshires (Lymm Territorials), and he re- turns to the Front on Tuesday next.

div.head: CORPORAL BEN ELLIOTT.
div.p: CORPORAL BEN ELLIOTT.
Progressing Satisfactorily In A West Of England Hospital.

,Corporal B. Elliott, of the 2nd Scots Guards, whose photograph we reproduced last week, writing home to his parents—who live at Canterbury Cottage—from the 2nd Southern Hospital, Southmead, Bristol, says:— " I.am glad to inform you that I am getting on very nicely, except that I have, at times, severe pains in the head and spine. I am very comfortable here and have everything I want. All of us are well looked after, so you need not worry. I expect I shall be all right soon. I may be moved shortly." Corporal Elliott has a sister serving as a waitress to a Withington lady, whose sister re- sides near the hospital at Bristol, and upon receipt of the news of Corporal Elliott's in- juries the mistress's sister made inquiries respecting the Lymin soldier's. progress. In a letter to Miss Elliott's mistress, the lady in question states: "I went this afternoon— October 26th—to see Corporal Elliott at South- mead. He is such a nice man and he is getting on quite well. His injuries consist of a bullet wound through the head near the ear. There is a good deal of pain in the spine at times, and he has not had much good sleep. He is very pleased with the gifts of pears; flowers, "&c., took him, and he wanted to write to his sister, but he ought to keep very quiet, and writing is such an effort, so I.told him I would let her know. Ile has a nice Scot from his own regi- ment on one side of him, and some Australians close by. I asked Chaplain Canon Wood to look him up, and I will go again to see him myself soon."

div.head: WHAT IS WAR?
div.p: WHAT IS WAR?
Sergeant T. W. Field Discusses Sei.geral Vital Questions.

Sergeant T. W. Field, Newfields, Lymm, invalided home wounded in the Dardanelles, where he was serving in the Lancashire Fuei- Hers, writes : War is a very great evil, not always unavoid- able in National fulfilment of various obliga- tions. But it is nearly always undesirable. If the man who first reduced art and the destruc- tion of his fellow-creatures had no• other motive than of selfish, avaricious feelings of gain, then it would probably have been much better had he not been born at all. Yet, on the other hand, if his inventive intentions were solely for the punishment of persecuted virtue and helplessness, then there is possibly as much to be said for as against this grue- some business. War, then, in this latter sense is most necessary, to stem the unjust claims' of one Power against the other, a thing we have witnessed in the case of Belgium, very clear- sightedly. War has come to not a few of us English-speaking people as a science with emphasis. The various forms of knowledge looked for in the brain' of a soldier are not placed there without difficulty and patient trainin, and one of the many outstanding fea- tures at the present moment in our country is the supposition that as soon as we join a man up and adorn him in a suit of khaki he is a soldier. Collectively speaking, the man is; but we do not speak or even dare to express his state of efficiency. I notice in the many ap- peals for men statements such as "We are against a well-organised force." I know per- fectly well from what has fallen to be my experience that the statements are only too true, and the sooner those men who are so anxiously appealed to come forward, the easier the task will be for this country to shake off the fetters that are ever increasing. The Value of Joining Quickly.

The man who joins up quickly is a man who becomes efficient quickly, and it is men, and efficient men, that are so earnestly needed in this struggle. As I have said previously, war is a, science. Of most other sciences the principles are fixed, or, to speak plainly, they may be ascertained by the assistance of experience. There needs nothing bu.t diligence to learn that philosophy, mathematics, architecture, and so on, are all founded upon invariable combinations and con- clusions. Every man, even of narrow under- standing, may remember rules, apply them properly, and sometimes draw just consequences from them. But the science of war branches out into so many ways, and so many parts; there are so many reflections to be made, so many circumstances and cases to be brought together, that it is only by a continual appli- cation, grounded upon the love of his duty, and an inclination to his profession, that any man can attain this science. It is commonly thought it is only sufficient for a soldier to know how to obey. as he is only part of a great machine, and is there to be ordered about. I know this is a general impression to- day among our civil populace, and was actually given out to me in answer to a query. that I, pushed at a recruit. The Recruiting Sergeant.

Turning over my diary, I notice something that should have found the- pages. of "The Examiner" sooner. Here it is: The drill instructor, standing on• the square, was shout- ing out the words of command to a company, suell as "Left !" "Right !" "Left!" "Hold your heads up!" "About turn !" "On the right form company!" and so on, in quick succession, when he noticed one of his recruits standing alone well in the rear. Halting his men with the customary "Stand easy !" he walked over to the recruit, and the dialogue that followed was :
"Look here, my man, are you with us, or what's the matter with you?"
The lad.blurted out :

" Wel, it's like this, Instructor; I thowt I wud stop here and listen to thee, for tha seems to be a chap has dunna knows thee own mind two minutes together!" The Army is not without its humorous side of things. But I must push on. War is a business, which, like all others, must be learned. Although bravery and courage are two of the essential qualifications of a soldier, he must not be ignorant of the duties of his senior comrade, the N.C.0.; and while some of the

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY OCTOBER 30, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY OCTOBER 30, 1915.

qualities are born with us, the other qualities demand to be acquired before, a man is thor- oughly and truthfully §peaking a soldier, in genius as well as name. I will not attempt now to lay down any rules "upon the subject, as the most courageous and experienced soldiers have to act abcording to the contingent cir- cumstances that crop up from time to. time, in some very 'queer places. It was in. Egypt, fn 1914, during a little manceuvring by our Territorial troops, that our state of efficiency was duly brought home forcibly to me. I Can well remember some Egyptian cavalry who had Stood • near, our boundary wall laughing at the slow and slug-. gard movements of clur men. When I asked a friend of mine who could speak Arabic fluently, he told me they had been making comparisons and were disgusted at what they saw. Truly enough,. the Egyptian cavalryman is a particularly fine soldier, called the feller, and, a' curious thing, is the result, or was the result, of conscription. It is true that this item was one of the many things that com- pelled me, when writing from Egypt in Feb- ruary, 1914, to mention that the. most valuable part of a soldier is his, state of efficiency; and, as Bacon is credited with saying, • "When a warlike nation grows soft and effeminate, they may be sure of a war." Conscription.

Conscription is a much-used word, and I am afraid so much has been said on the subject that little remains to be Said by anyone. It would be all -right in one way, if I am allowed to express an opinion,, and all wrong in an- other way. • ,We should very likely, if it became law, take the very man we should leave, !and leave the man we should take. It sounds -rather funny, but I have made some very quiet ob- servations on the matter; and the convalescent grade of trade that exists, no‘v would not im- probably collapse altogether. No; I think we have the best system in our much-cherished Voluntaryism. So- to those men who are i•en- sidering the joining policy I say: Step ;n at once and make" a bid for a high state of elli- ciency, and help to bring things to a speedy conclusion.
THOS. W. FIELD.

considered that she should be relieved of doing the washing and ironing and have assistance in the washing up. At present he desired to refrain from commenting upon the plan of the hospital and desirable alterations in structure, but he must mention that there was no suitable place for keeping the patients' food—such as milk—handy for the nurses. Dr. Thorp then Proceeded to read a list of further requirements for the hospital. Where Does The Disease Come From?

At the conclusion, Councillor Cowper said that the list seemed alarming, and asked the doctor if he had any theory as to where the outbreak of diphtheria originated. Many times he (the speaker) had mentioned the refuse which col- lected at the Dam Head corner. Diphtheria and all the other terrible illnesses must come from somewhere. Councillor Cowper also stated that dead dogs and cats had been seen in the Dam Heard. The Chairman: I don't think that statement ought to go out. • Councillor Cowper: There have been dead dogs lying there a week or two. Councillor Holt expressed the opinion that the first diphtheria case was that of a child who went to Warrington, where diphtheria was very prevalent. Doctor Thorp: There were only two cases of diphtheria at Warrington last week. Continuing, Councillor Holt stated that the Dam Head ought to be cleared out. The ooun- cil ought to remedy all the defects they had in their own neighbourhood, .but at the same time he wanted it to be understood that so far as they could tell, the outbreak had not originated at Lymm.

div.head: INFECTIOUS DISEASE.
div.p: INFECTIOUS DISEASE.
Diphtheria, Scarlet Fever And Chicken Pox Break Out.
HOSPITAL REQUIREMENTS.

A serious outbreak of infectious disease in the Lymm neighbourhood was reported at the Urban District Council meeting on Monday evening by Dr. Leonard Thorp, the temporary medical officer. Dr. Thorp also made a series of comments on the state of the tymm Hos- pital. An Outbreak of Unknown Origin. ,

Dr. Thorp, in his report, stated that chicken- pox had widely spread in the district. The cases numbered 27, of which 13 had been reported during the -week ended Saturday, October 23rd. Another case was notified on Sunday and two more on Monday. There had been an outbreak of scarlet fever, but no case had been notified since September 29th. All the cases were doing satisfactorily. The hos- pital would be required for at least anotter three weeks. One child had ,been discharged that day. In respect to the outbreak of diph- theria, he reported that there were ten cases, six in the infant school, two in. the adult school, and two in the Statham school. The cases Were spread, over a wide area in the district and careful inquiries had failed to elicit the source of origin. The first case was taken to the Isolation Hospital on the 19th of the month; the second and third cases on the 20th; three more cases on the 21st; two more on the 22nd, and two more on the 25th. All the cases are doing satisfactorily. The Infants' School, from which six cases were taken, was disinfected on Saturday morning. One ward of the Isolation Hospital was now full of diphtheria cases, and it 'would be neces- sary to remove the scarlet ,fever cases to an- other building in order to provide room for further cases of diphtheria: Wherq Improvements are Required.

Complains from the nurses and personal ob- servation had compelled him to go thoroughly through the hospital, Accompanied by Mr. Mort (the inspector). They spent some time there on Sunday morning, and he felt compelled to bring before the Council's notice certain points to ensure satisfactory nursing Arrangements. They probably mainly arose through wear and tear and through parts- Of the equipment not having .been replaced as occasion necessitated. In the wards, four beds were useless from constant " stoving." Two heating stoves smoked so much that they could only be used occasionally. It was consequently difficult to get the wards warm, especially at nights, through one fire- grate being insufficient. The fireguards re- quired alteration, as at. present they did not prevent cinders falling on to the linoleum, which might be disastrous if the nurses were out of the ward for a 'few minutes. Mackintosh sheets were required for each bed, there being none. The blankets were too small for the beds, and seemed as if they had been cut instead of being repaired. More Requirements.

The nurses, stated that they required larger stocks of sheets and towels. Bedside cupboards Fere also required, and bed tables, so that the infants might manage their food better and not spill it over the beds. Small chairs for the use of infants would be an advantage, even 'if they were not areal necessity. A supply of medicine cups, of which there were norie, and of feeding cups, of which there was only one, was re- quired for the serious cases Of 'diphtheria. The hot-water supply was entirely unsatisfactory: The nurses never had any hot water except that boiled on the ward fire, which only held a small kettle. In addition to kettles, there was only a kitchen boiler, as in an ordinary house, and it was a considerable distance from each ward bathroom. Bathrooms were placed at the end of each ward, and were too cold to bath the

children in, even if there was the necessary water. Large sinks were required in each ward for the washing out of the bed-pans and other utensils, which At present had to be done in the bath, a procedure which was most unsatisfac- tory. There were only two bed-pans in the hos- pital. He had only mentioned the most obvious requirements, but had made a more complete list of the things Which he trusted 'the Conncil would see their way to provide for the proper treatment and comfort of their patients. The nurses complained of the lack of lavatories. There appeared to be some variety of opinion on the food question; not as to the quantity,, but as to the want of variety—a difficulty which would be easily. overeoM9 by, the drawing up of a weekly diet sheet. The caretaker stated that at present she had more to do than she could manage; the 'cleaning of the hospital and the necessary cooking for three maids and twelve children occupied the whole of her time. He

div.head: Wide Of The Point.
div.p: Wide Of The Point.
Cpuncillor Parker said that the Council were getting rather wide of the point, and thought they had better discuss the necessary require- ments.

Councillor Holt said that he would support the doctor in getting thee things required. He believed that the hospital was badly equipped for dealing with infectious disease. Councillor Cowper gave it as his opinion that everything that was possible should be done to support the doctor. Councillor Lockyer asked if the doctor could throw any light on the cost of the requirements he had mentioned.

Dr. Thorp replied that he could not, owing to the varying prices. Councillor Parker moved that the doctor's report be accepted, and that the necessary re- quirements be procured. This was seconded by Councillor Ingham and carried.
A committee consisting of the Chairman, Councillors Holt, Parker, Mclntyre and Groves. with the Clerk, was appointed to assist the doctor.

The ouestion of ,finding accommodation else- where for the scarlet fever cases in order to make room for further diphtheria cases, was also discussed. and Mr. Mort (the surveyor), was instructed to call on the Altrincham authorities early the following morning to see if the scarlet fever cases could be removed there, a special meeting of the sub-committee being called for 10.30 a.m. on Tuesday morning to take such action in the matter as may then be deemed necessau.

div.head: DARK STREETS.
div.p: THE DARK STREETS.
Reason For Subdued Light And Other
Economies-.

Letters which have appeared recently in the local Press were the subject-matter of comment at the monthly meeting of the Urban District Council on Monday evening. Councillor Gotobed, who, was presiding, said that lately they had had one or two letters in the newspapers complaining of the darkness of the streets and some comments on the increase of the rates. Others wanted the Council to spend more. When the Council did him the honour of appointing him to the chair, he advocated a year of stringent economy. Economy was strictly necessary, and it was thought that by restricting their lights, the Council were only following the example of the remainder of the country. But in order to allay the feeling of insecurity and danger which some people seemed to have, the Council had decided to fix up a number of automatic lighters at what they considered the dangerous points. He hoped that when this was done they would hear no more complaints. It was a time when every one had to make sacrifices, and he thought that the Council were -entitled to ask the public to bear with them and to put up with a little inconvenience in the matter of lighting.

div.head: " Pestered To Death " With Questions.
div.p: " Pestered To Death " With Questions.

Councillor Cowper said that he got pestered to death by people asking about the lights. With regard to public lighting he thought that the Council had done all that they could. It be- hoved every one to do what he possibly could. The Council had done their best and the Public ought to be satisfied. Councillor Holt said that there were some people who wanted the Council to, spend money on the lights, and there were others who were always complaining about the lights going out. He was very pleased to see the letters in the local papers. for it showed that the people were beginning to be interested in what the local Council was doing. He hoped that there was. generally going to be an increase of this inter- est, 'and that when the next Council elections , came round, there would not be positions on the Council going a-begging. Lymm People So Well Off That -

Councillor Warburton said that the Lymm people were so well off that they really did not know where they were, and when the Council was trying to economise a little in this excep- tional time, the people ought to support the Council. What the Council was doing was more for the benefit of the people than of the Council. Councillor Holt pointed out that people did not know what the Council had to contend with. They were forced to provide classes which no- body attended, and lectures which nobody went to hear; and ,the Council had to provide the money.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

Joined Up.—Thv good-example shown by our many recent recruits is being eagerly followed by another batch of eligibles, namely Fred Bates and, George Bates, Royal Garrison Artii= lery ; Harry Woods and Josiah Long, Royal Field Artillery; Stanley Woods, Army Service Corps; Thomas Ireland, Royal Army Medical Corps; making the number who have voluntered from Renketh and district to over seventy. But still there's more to follow! . Leonard Moss, a former Penkethite, but whose home now is at Eaton-avenue, Litherland, Liver- pool, has returned home from the Front in France for rest. and repairs. Attached to the Liverpool Rifles, he was in the recent advance.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL.
THE LATE MR. EDWARD HOWARD.
"Memorial Of A Fragrant Life" Unveiled At The LM. Church.

A touching tribute to the late Mr. Edward Howard, of Thornville, Latchford, was paid after the evening service on Sunday at the Independent Methodist Church, Grappenhall, by Councillor R. Henshall, of " Sunnyside," Knutsford-road, Latchford. In the presence of a large congregation a tablet was unveiled as a lasting reminder of the deceased's noble and generous work at the above place of worship. The tablet, beautifully executed, was of Sicilian marble, with a black edge, upon which was inscribed:—
"In loving memory of the late Edward Howard, who died February 18th, 1915, age 43 years, for many years the faithful and diligent servant of this church. Erected as a memorial of a fragrant life."

Councillor Henshall paid an eloquent tribute to the late gentleman, whose loss has been keenly felt by a wide circle of friends con- nected with the Indepeildent Methodist Church. Mr. Howard, as a youth, became attached to the Brick-street Independent Methodist Suii- cray School, where he quickly secured a host of friends. As the years passed on, he was able to give valuable service to the Sunday School, and eventually became teacher and secretary. When the new church at Grappenhall was erected he found a fresh sphere for his fruitful and noble work, which was highly prized by his colleagues. Towards the building wherein is now- erected this fitting memorial his best endeavours were directed and long and earnest effort given.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Wesley Guild.—The usual meeting of - the Wesley Guild was held on Monday evening, when a very interesting paper was given by Mr. W. E. Plinston on "The drink traffic in our town." He said Warrington was often called a dirty town, but when compared with other manufacturing towns it compared very favour- ably. It, however, occupied a prominent place among the borough towns of Lancashire for drunkenness. He gave statistics to prove this. He also gave illustrations showing the large number of public-houses in certain areas, though from the figures quoted there has been a large reduction of licences during the past 20 years. The new buildings erected to take the place of some of the old ones were very com- modious, and in some respects the drinking facilities were increased rather than diminished by this action. The Rev. A. J. Morton presided, and Miss E. A. Bennett was the accompanist.

Very Good Reasons.
Upton Sinclair, the well-known writer, told the other day about a school address that he once made.

"It was a school of little boys," said Mr. Sin. clair. "The Jungle was selling at the rate of 100,000. copies a day at the time and feeling fiueh I opened my address by laying a $5 bill on the table before me.

" T am going to *PA t yi.n boys,' I said, 'about Socialism. I hope to convert you all to Socialism. When I finish my remarks the boy who gives me the best reason for turning Socialist will get this $5 bill.' "Then I spoke for some 20 minutes. The boys were all converted at the end. I began to question them. "You are a Socialist, are you?' I said to the boy nearest me. " ' Yes, sir,' he replied. " ' And why are you a Socialist?' I asked. "431 e pointed to the crisp $5 bill. "'1 am a Socialist,' he said, 'because I need the money.'"

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

A Charge Dismissed.—At the Chester Assizes on Monday, before Lord Coleridge, George Frederick Mitchell (25), munition worker. was charged with having assaulted Ellen Pinion at Stockton Heath on September 13th. He pleaded "Not guilty."— Mr. Artemns Jones prosecuted and Mr. Trevor Lloyd defended.—The jury found prisoner not guilty and be was discharged.

Volunteers At Church.—The members of the local platoon of the Voluntary Training Corps attended matins at Daresbury Parish Church on Sunday. The Rev. T. T. Lee-Jones preached the sernion. After the service the Volunteers marched to Preston Brook, lunch being taken at the Red Lion Inn. They then proceeded to Grimsditch, via. Dutton, and arrived•home at about 4.20 p.m., after marching 12 miles. Platoon-Commander F. Warburton was in charge of the platoon.

Parochial Committee's Short Meeting.—The meeting of the Parochial Committee, which was held at the Council Schools on Tuesday evening, was not of long -duration. Mr- George Pilling was in the chair, and also present were Messrs. J. H. Clarke, J. McDermid, F. Pearson, N. Mclntyre, A. Bottomley, 11. J. Westbrook, W. E. Hough (clerk to the Runcorn Rural District Council), S. Wright (surveyor), and E. Brad- shaw (clerk to the Parish Counoil).—lt was de- cided, on the recommendation of a Alb-com- mittee, to come to an agreement with Mr. Yar- wood, of Cobb's Farm, Appleton, for the use of a nightsoil tip on his farm at a rental-of .240 a year, the agreement to be spread over a period of five years.—The Sanitary Inspector reported that several houses had been disinfected.

British Women's Temperance Association.—A meeting of the Stockton Heath branch of the British Women's Temperance Association was held at the Providence Schools on Tuesday afternoon. Mrs. Griffiths was in the chair, and there was a good number 'of ladies present. A short address was given by Mrs. Henry Roberts, who, at the outset, expressed her delight at finding the women of Stockton Heath banded together for the purpose of doing good work. Referring to the drink question., she said that- science had told them—and they knew perfectly well that it • was true—that alcohol was not, goodjor.them.. In these times,, when they could never meet together without feeling the dark cloud of war which hung over them and when they were fighting the great enemy over the seas, they had to fight a very big enemy at home. Our Allies, the Russians, had done a very wise thing by completely striking out from their country the use of alcohol, and if the English Government had only done the same thing twelve months ago when the feeling in the country was strong against drink, the country would have been helped considerably. But the time passed and nothing was done. The brewers were still in arms and the drink bill was stated to be larger than usual. The question arose—What became of the beer? The men were out of the country. Was it possible that the women were taking more than was good for them in lone- liness and distress? There was still much temperance work to be done amongst the women of England.—Recitations were said by Mrs. Worrall and Mrs. Mounfield.

div.head: FOR THE ADULT SCHOOLS.
div.p: FOR THE ADULT SCHOOLS.
Successful Sale Of Work To Help Funds.

The members of the Stockton Heath Adult Schools held a sale of work on Thursday at their rooms iu Greenbank-street, Wilderspocd. The sale, which was very successful, was opened by Mrs. T. Pemberton, of Warrington, Mr. W. H. Sherburn being in the chair. After the opening hymn had been sung, Mr. Sherburn gave a cordial welcome to those pres- ent. As many of-them were aware, he said, the Adult School movement in Stockton' Heath was very young, and it was not at Present very large from the point of view of numbers. It was started a year or two ago in a studio, but soon this was found to be too small, and a larger room had to be engaged. The finding of such a room was a difficult task, but at last the pres- ent room was discovered.

Mrs. Pemberton expressed her pleasure at being able to be present that afternoon. Refer- ring to the piano which the members had recently a&luired, she said that it was a good thing to ;have musical evenings, especially in such a sad time. She then declared the sale open. _
A vote of tha-nks was accorded Mrs. Pember- ton, on the motion of Miss Sherburn, seconded by Mr. Mann. Mrs. Pemberton was also presented with "a bouquet of carnations by Mrs. Sherburn.

div.head: willsT DRIVE AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: willsT DRIVE AT LATCHFORD.

The Parish Room, Latchford, was on Monday night the scene of a successful whist drive and dance, organised in aid of the funds of tho British Red Cross Society and the St. John Ambulance Brigade, the event forming part of the "Our Day " effort. Over, two hundred tickets were sold, and the large company spent a most enjoyable time, cards being played from 7.30 to 10, and dancing following, and being' continued until' one, flan. .. The Latchford Orchestral Society supplied the requisite music. The arrangements were carried out by a com- Mittee, over which Mrs. Geo. Dakin presided, and Mr. Jowett acted as M.C. for the whist tourney. At the commencement the Rev. G. C. Briggs (the vicar of Latchford) looked in and made a brief speech explanatory of the obiec,t7 for which the drive and dance were being lil e."• objects Which, he thought, were most deservirlg of all the support that could be accorded "t 0 them, both organisations having rendered Mag- nificent service to the men who had been wounded at the Front. During the evening buttonhole flags, bearing the Red Cross. and flowers Were sold to swell 910 proceeds, and a raffle for a black satin cushion cover helped still further towards the £2O. odd realised.

div.head: CHRISTMAS PRESENTS.
div.p: CHRISTMAS PRESENTS.
Messrs. Richmond's 330 Soldier. Workmen Remembered.

The workmen employed by the Richmond this Stove Co. have always taken a deep interest in their comrades who have joined the Colour6, and n war relief fund they organised in their behalf ha's been the means of doing a great deal of good. A month ago it was decided to send a Christ- mas preStnt to every workmate who had enlisted, and as the number was 330, they 'sot themselves a somewhat stiff pThblem. However, in three weeks the necessary £45 was collected, and the presents are being arranged for in good time.

Mr. J. Fairclough, the hon. secretary war relief fund, Richmond's Works, C4rappenhall, would be much obliged if the relatives of Richmond's men in the Army or Navy would send him their present addresses, so that no one will be missed when the presents are for- warded.

div.head: PLUM PUDDINGS.
div.p: PLUM PUDDINGS.
Orford Barracks Will Forward Them
To Friends For You.

Last Christmas a number of Christmas pud- dings were sent to the Front from Orford Barracks, being supplied by Orford parish and others. They were duly received and acknow- ledged by the Indian Contingent. The gifts are to be sent again, but this year they may be addressed to individual friends and rela- tives. The scheme is explained int a circular which has been addressed to his parishioners by the Rev. G. Vale Owen, vicar of Orford. The reverend. gentleman says:— " Last year nearly 200 puddings were sent from Orford Barracks to the troops at the Front, and of these more than 130 were given by our own congregation and their friends. Can we surpass this number this year? There is an additional inducement this time. Last Christmas we had, to scud them to the troops to be distributed as it was found possible. This year you may address each pudding to the particular soldier to whom you wish to send it, and as transport arrangements have now been much improved we have good hope' that the pudding will be duly delivered tis addressed.
Points To Be Observed.
"But the following items should be carefully noted:—
"Write the address clearly and in full, with regimental number, company, battalion and regiment, both on tag and on label pasted 00 basin.

"Write name of sender on label pasted (In basin; and a message to the soldier mdY added al.so. "Metal enamelled basins are better than crock. "Puddings must be delivered at Orford Vestry on Monday, December 6th, between 7.30 and 8.30. "These points being observed, Captain Crana has once again kindly promised to undertake the forwarding of the puddings to their destination free of charge."

A SOLDIER BIGAMIST.

div.head: Married Man With Ten Children
div.p: Married Man With Ten Children

Poses As Bachelor. At the Chester Assizes on Monday, before Lord Coleridge, Henry Searle, 33, a cycle worker, who belongs to the King's (Liverpool) Regiment, and ap- peared in the dock in khaki, pleaded guilty to bigamy at Birkenhead on May 13th. Mr. A. M. Latham, for the prosecution, said it was not until some time after marriage that the woman discovered that prisoner had a wife living. Prisoner was first married on November sth, 1904, and had ten children by his wife, one of whom died. Prisoner's home was at War- rington, but he was stationed at West Kirby with a regiment in which he enlisted after the outbreak of .war, and here lie met the woman with • whom he went through the form of marriage.
It was stated, that prisoner nlisted as a cor- poral, and became a sergeant, 'Jut was reduced to a private, and his military character was described as indifferent.

prisoner said the girl paid all expenses, even buying the wedding ring, and the wedding cost him nothing. The girl: Because you told me you had £ll in the Army, which you could not get. Prisoner: When was the last time I saw you? —When I saw you off at the station at London, about a month after we were "married."

div.head: WAR-TIME HOUSEKEEPING.
div.p: WAR-TIME HOUSEKEEPING.
'The Pudding Lady' Discourses
And Demonstrates.
THE NEED FOR THRIFT.

With the object of howing Warrington house- wives how it is. possible to make a little money go a long way, Miss Florence Petty, who by poster and advertisement has been introduced to the town as "the Pudilinc, Lady," on Tues- day gave two of her lecture-demonstrations in the economical culinary art. It is gratifying to, record that both were largely attended, and were, in the main, composed of just that class whom it was desired to reach, her visit having been arranged in furtherance of the National Thrift Campaign, which just now is looming largely, and appears to be likely to loom even larger. Mrs. Henry Greenall was in the chair in the afternoon, and she told, the audience that She thought a Thrift Campaign was the sort of thing that ought to appeal to everybody in these days of war, for .one way in which all could assist was by exercising wise economy.
PRAISE FOR THE POOR.

div.head: Plucky Manner in Which They Cope With
div.p: Plucky Manner in Which They Cope With
Poverty.

Miss Petty is an ideal demonstrator and lec- turer; she knows just what the menfolk and the, kiddies like, and she knows just how to buy and cook it in the cheapest and tastiest maimer. In the afternoon she talked of herself, in ad- dition to the oven, the gas stove, the saucepan —and the other necessary impedimenta of the kitchen. She told the audience of her experi- ences as a social worker, and mixed her remarks with many a blithesome story, the best, per- haps, being the story of the youthful Mile End essayist, who, having been told how food left over from one meal might best be presented at another, wrote: "The husband's supper can be made out of his wife's remains:" Miss Petty bestowed praise on the plucky manner in which poor women face their poverty—face all the difficulties that confront them not only in the kitchen, but also at the front door, where so often.calls the met' who comes for "the money." There were idle, shiftless women, she said, among every class, and the proportion was only greater among the 'lower 'strata of -society, because, generally speaking, the poorer women had but scanty education and had more difficul- ties to contend with. The children of the future would be healthier, both. physically and morally, if only social workers could get hold of the young mothers, or of the girls on the eve of marriage, and could have a proper opportunity of instructing them. Precept, ut No Practice.

Miss Petty-went on to speak chattily of work she had undertaken_ in the St. Pancras district of London=a district simply teeming with the many-faced phases of the social problem—and regretted that many of those who had been per- suaded regularly to attend the School for Mothers, when they got home made no attempt to put into practice what had been taught them or demonstrated for their benefit. So lament- able was the disregard of advice and instruction that she (Miss Petty) had- arrived at the con- clusion that the women bad not the power of reasoning, nor the initiative, to apply what they learned at the Mothers' School to their own honies. Often, of course, the fault was not theirs, as in cases where one more. or less ser- viceable saucepan .and an open grate repre- sented all the cooking appliances that tlio wife and mother could turn to in Order to prepare her culinary efforts. Miss Petty went on to urge the -need for tactfulness and sympathy on the part of social workers, asking them to re- member that nothing was to be gained, whilst much might be lost, by violating the privacy of even the poorest home. .social work was, per- haps, in some respects,- both the most encourag- ing, and at the same time the most discouraging, work that could be undertaken, but the social worker who meant to "make good" must learn the lesson of perseverance, not minding if there ,seemed to be no result- from their efforts, but always believing in the people amongst whom they worked and 'always hoping for the best for them and from them. The Value of "The Word in Season." ,

There was much power in a chat between woman and woman, and it had frequently,. in her experience, led to great improvements in rather dubious homes; for women, who, perhaps, had been somewhat careless beforehand, had developed fresh interest in their homes, and took a pride in having the place "extra nice" when her visits were due. Her work, Miss Petty added, had brought home to her very agreeably the fact that the only charity that was really worth anything to the poor was that spirit of true friendliness which helped them to help themselves. Miss Petty went on to' detail at length social work in Essex which she had, at the request of Lady Meyer, undertaken, and expressed the hope that in the future, when people really understood about food and the best way of cook- ing it, their teeth would be so strong, that dentists might as well take down their name- plates, for they would not be required.

Miss Petty's lecture-demonstration in the evening was of a most practical character, and it was listened to and watched by an audience which made a strain upon the holding capacity of the large hall in which it was held. START WITH THE SCHOOL-GIRL !

Miss Bessie Dutton, of Moore, was in the dhair, and in the course of a few preliminary remarks paid a high tribute to Miss Petty's work among the poorer mothers of the greatest city in the world, and pointed out how im- portant, as a practical matter, it was that the women with but small amounts on which to do .their housekeeping should learn something of the principles of true economy and should get to know how to buy, prepare and cook nourishing dishes with the least possible trouble and at the lowest possible cost. At the present moment thrift was a most important thing, and Miss Petty, by showing housewives how to be thrifty in the matter of foodstuffs, was doing a real service to the country—was, in fact, acting as a great benefactor. Miss Dutton went on •to 9xpre6s the wish that the lessons of thrift were taught more fully and more regularly in the schools, adding that girls might learn a good deal that in after-life would be of inestimable advantage to them in their housekeeping, for, after all, looking at it from the point of view of housekeeping, a knowledge of cooking was of greater value than a know- ledge of sewing. THOSE WHO COULD NOT ATTEND.

Miss C. Broadbent announced that letters regretting inability to be present had been re- ceived from the Mayoress (Mrs. Peacock), Lady Crosfield, Mrs. John Crosfield, Mrs. Harold Smith, Mrs. Willis, Mrs. C. B. Parker, Mrs. Ziba Armitage, Mrs. W. Peter Eylands and Miss Ferriman.
Miss Petty then gavo her lecture-demonstra- tion, preparing a large variety of appetising, but economical, dishes, and cooking them in a Richmond gas oven.

utmost to save Miss CaN;ell. They were trickea and lied to by the butchers wearing the Kaiser's uniform, who were determined to slay their victim, before publicity and the bursting storm of world-wide indignation could save her. The war has produced many heroines, hut none braver than Edith Cavell, who with her last breath said "she was happy to die for her country." Her death, with its unspeakable cruelty, is yet another monstrous crime, which makes the very name of Germany stink as a pestilence, and cries aloud to Heaven for vengeance. Queen Mary's Hostel.

The new King's College for Women is a proof that the Domestic Arts are receiving attention. The students lately took up their quarters in the new and -handsome buildings in Campden Hill-road, W., comprising the Household and Social Science Service Departments and Queen Mary's Hostel. The latter, the gift of Sir Richard Garton, is a model of comfort and daintiness, and every student has a charming bed-sitting-room and dressing-room. The hostel cost twenty thousand pounds to build and equip, and contains a wonderful series of laboratories, kitchens, sculleries and laundries. Bacteriology, hygiene, physics. psychology and chemistry are included in the college curri- culum, whilst research work is carried wit in the kitchen- laboratory with natural awl pre- pared food. Here during the process of eo..Jk- ing, all kinds of food are subjected to the most minute scientific examination. The student • , course lasts three years. The Latest Skirts.

Skirts may be tersely described as broad and brief. They are certainly narrower, but the width is not exaggerated by good dressmakers. Nor is any sign of swing permissibl6. Short- skirted frocks in one piece, when made of soft or thin fabrics, are slightly full at the waist, but when velvet or a thick woollen material is chosen, the skirt is gored; and fits the waist closely. At the hem it springs out in flutes. Soft woollen fabrics, with a slight weaving of silk, are much in request for this type of frock, which is worn under a winter Oat. The names of these materials are, as varied as the goods themselves, but one of the pest is known as

crepe cloth. Voile Closely woven, and therefore' warmer than the summer material, is still very popular, for,. being soft and limp, it falls in graceful folds, and is warm, enough for autumn indoor wear. Graduated tucks or bands .on the skirt form a very suitable mode of 'trimming. These may be of taffetas, velvet or satin. • Combination Of Materials.

Quite a novel way of using two materials has been devised, whereby - a striped effect is obtained. Alternate narrow widths of a trans- parent fabric, and velvet, satin or silk are joined together to make a skirt, Which when arranged thus, falls in flute-like folds that are not unpleasing in effect. • Such arrangements for producing change seem to be preferred to trim- mings of .011 elaborate nature. Sometimes the corners of a coatee bodice are handsomely orna- mented with handworked bead embroidery in bright colours, if the colour of the dress should be dark; otherwise this winter a little soutaehe or braiding, the latter in the military style, corn- poses the trimmings on suits made '•by the ,best tailors. Mantles and wrap coats also depend for novelty on the combination of materials, and these are often very cleverly combined. Fur And Feather Plaits. -

Plaits, an old-world aform _of decoration, are in. vogue again. In a soft .make of silk, very pliable, a narrow braid is very effective when plaited. On tulle bleus'es, and flresses, plaited ribbons and ribbon velvets are novelties that will probably survive the winter. Milliners also are using this form Of decoration, and such unlikely things as furs and feathers are quite successfully plaited and used as trimmings for hats. Usually these take the place of a band, and surround the base of the crown. Feathers and flowers were until quite recently considered to be in bad taste when used together on a hat, but this winter one is rarely seen without the other. Thus two large chrysanthemums appeared above a plaited feather band, on one of the newest models, a feather mount rising to a • ridiculous height from between the .very beautiful blooms. Flowers and velvet are a much happier combination, and a more pleasing model composed of rich black panne, had a brim of white violets, each blossom being separately and thickly sewn on a white silk ground. -

By MARJORIE.

The War Empress. If these were ordinary times the German Empress would be commencing her prepara- tions for Christmas. As it is, she is said to be teaching little children the Hymm of Hate. Politically the Empress is without influence, but she shares the opinion of her War Lord that all " the inferior nations " should be subject to Germany's will. In her household she finds much to do, but a good deal of her time is taken up with petty squabbles and intrigues at Court, and the matrimonial scandals, is which the Crown Prince is the leading figure, are a source of trouble to her. The Empress prides herself on her strict adherence to the Protestant faith, and she views with unconcern the wanton destruction of Rheims Cathedral, and of • in- numerable churches in Belgium. From the first it has been the Kaiser's policy to send German Protestant regiments to fight against Catholic Belgium and France, whilst Catholic troops have been sent against Orthodox Russians in the East. It is largely due to this settled policy, that there has been so little respect for the sacred buildings in France and Belgium. Murder Most' Foul.

We can only wonder what the wife of the Imperial Murderer can think of the killing of the nurse—Edith Cavell—by the German mili- tary authorities at Brussels. Here was an educated English lady, who, for eight or nine years had been in charge of a well-known nurs- ing institution in the Belgian capital, in which capacity she had trained a, large number of German nurses. She had herself nursed many wounded Germans during the war, and because she had befriended and. helped to save some refugees from German savagery, she was secretly tried and done to death in the middle of the night. Turn the dough out on the floured board, knead it slightly, roll out, cut into shapes according to taste, -place on a floured baking-tray, and bake in a quick oven for ten or twenty minutes. To Use Up Cold Meat. Heat loz. of butter or good dripping in a saucepan, and fry in it one tablespoonful of finely-chopped onion till a golden brown. Draw the pan from the fire and add half a breakfast- cupful of fine breadcrumbs, a cupful of meat chopped very finely, half a teaspoonful of salt, a little pepper and nutmeg, half a breakfast- cupful of white sauce, and a teaspoonful of lemon juice. Heat over the fire, and take up
just before it boils, and serve on croutons of bread. These are rounds of bread- fried till
3risp in butter or dripping. Garnish ,with parsley, and serve. Baked tomatoes served with this are a great improvement.
Cheese Ramekins.

Pour a cupful of boiling milk over a cupful of stale, dry breadcrumbs; when they are thoroughly soft, pour off the milk not absorbed stir in two tablespoonfuls of butter, 4oz. of grated cheese, half a teaspoonful of mixed mustard and salt, with the merest pinch of cayenne and the yolks of three eggs. Mix thoroughly, and just before using adl the beaten whites whiped to a stiff froth. Bake in little patty-pans in a rich paste in a very hot oven. • • Breakfast Rolls.

. Heat half a pint of milk to about blood heat, and then dissolve in it Oz. of German yeast. Rub 2oz. of butter or clarified beef dripping into I.ilb. of- flour, also a little salt. 'When this is mixed, make a hole in the centre, and pour in the yeast; with a wooden spoon stir in the flour till tho yeast has enough flour worked into it to form a thick batter, scatter some flour over, cover with a cloth, and set tho whole in a warm place to rise for an hour. When the flour i 4

cracked through by the action of the yeast, work the whole of the flour into the dough, adding more milk. Cover it up again, and leave to rise for half an hour more. Place the dough on a pastry board, add more flour if required,

divide it into small pieces, and make into rolls of different shapes. Lay these on a floured baking sheet, and place in front -of the fire to rise for quarter of an hour. Brush over with a little milk, and bake in a quick oven for 10 Minutes or so. These rolls Will be equally good when heated again.. Carrots.

To boil carrots in their own juice, wash clean and scrape them, cutting out discoloured spots; cut them into rather thick slices, and throw them into as much boiling salted water as will barely cover them. Boil gently until they are tolerably tender, then boil quickly to evaporate the water, of which only a spoonful or so should be left in the saucepan. Sprinkle pepper on the carrots, put in a small piece of butter rolled in flour, turn and toss them gently 'until the juice is thickened and adheres to them, and serve immediately. They are improved by adding n dessertspoonful of minced parsley and cream mixed with a little flour to prevent curdling

Permit me to make my bow and to introduce myself, Uncle Ned, finding that he was not so old as he had began to think he was, has gone off to the wars—or, to be more strictly accurate; he has for the time being deserted his chair in the " Examiner " Office, and is now somewhere " in the South of England get- ting ready to put into practice some of that patriotic spirit about which he has so often written. He has asked me, in his absence, to conduct this Corner for him, and I do so with great pleasure, and trust that you will show your admiration for his pluck and gallantry in offering his services to his country by continuing to take an interest in the competitions which he started, and in which he took so much inter- est, and also by persuading all your friends to send along their names and be enrolled among Uncle Nod's many nephews and nieces. All put your shoulders to the wheel and let him find his already numerous family of nephews and nieces twice as large when he comes back as q was when he went away. _ _ _
UNCLE JACK
LAST WEEK'S COMPETITION.
"My Favourite Animal" was the subject set by Uncle Ned for last week's essay, and it has produced a fair crop of entries, some of which I am going to print.,
Niece Gladys Taylor, of 25, Fitzherbert-street, and who attends the Beamont Council School, writes : •
" Aly favourite animal is the horse. I need
not _641 you what _a fine, noble animal the
_ English horse is. There are many kinds of horses, such as the racehorse, the hunter, the

carriage horse, and the strong, heavy horse that draws our great drays and waggons. How sad - a' fact it is that so beautiful and useful, and so intelligent an animal should be often much abused. Few animals suffer more than the poor patient horse." Nephew Joseph Higgins, who lives in Bewsey- street, chose the St. Bernard dog as his favourite animal "because dogs of this breed have saved many a person's life; especially the lives of people who dlimb the Alps in Switzerland and Italy." Eva U. 3lorrall, of 47, Priee-street, writes

asking to be enrolled among I7nclel•Ted's nieces. I have much pleasure in enrolling her and in informing her that her number will be 524. ,She tells me that she is eleven years old and that she means to enter as many competitions as she possibly can, and in proof of that statement she gets to work straightaway and forwards me the following brief essay on her favourite animal : "'The dog, especially if he be a big black retriever, is my favourite animal. Such a dog is most faithful and intelligent. One can make it a great companion. We all know from tales told us that black retriever dogs have proved great lovers of little children, and many times have saved their young com- panions from drowning and fire."
Bravo, Eva, a very promising start! Niece Lilian llimsworth, who lives at 15, Fitzherbert-street, and attends the Beamont Council School, writes :

"•I have chosen as my favourite animal a little kitten. They are very playful little things. Sometimes they are treated very cruelly by their masters. I saw a man thrash- ing a lovely little kitten, and it was mewing so pitifully that it made me feel so sorry. If kittens see a bobbin of cotton they will scam- per after it and they do enjoy the frolic."

Nephew Horace Himsworth, Niece Lilian's brother, also has a try for the prize, and selects the pony as his favourite animal. "I should very much like a pony of my own to ride on," he says. So should I, Horace. You say that you ,have made your essay short, • because you know that Uncle Ned does not like long letters. But, at the same time, he does not like them too short, and neither do I either—not quite so short as yours! Nephew J. Kitchen, of 41, Bewsey-street, writes :

"I think I like all animals, but my favourite is the dog. .Dogs are put to all kinds of uses. The first, of course, is the way in which they are helping our gallant ally, Belgium, on the field of battle as Red Cross dogs. Then we have them for transport work on expeditions such as Capt. Scott's. We also have them for hunting and for watching. There are many different breeds. The dog is called the friend of man."

Another new member! Won't Uncle Ned be pleased! Nellie Boote, of 8, Reynolds-street, Latchford, writes:— " I wish to become a niece of yours—to be iucluded in your family, which I am glad to see is growing into such a large one. I am eleven years of age, and am in the sixth standard." Yottr number, Nellie, will be 525, and you should, in future, always quote it when enter- ing for the competitions. • "My favourite animal," Nellie writes, "is the dog, because it is so faithful and is such a good companion. There are several instances oi dogs saving the lives of children from drowning and also from fire." -
ITaiold Brown, of 40, Wakefield-street, writes that the horse is his favourite animal, adtling "It works for its own living by pulling carts along." 6am 13rown, Harold's brother, mid an ex-prize

winner, selects the cat as his favourite:— "Itis a playful animal. . .. Some cats that are old come upstairs in the morning and waken the people who are in bed. .. . Cats can live fourteen or fifteen years." Sam adds a postscript to his short missive. "I am," he says, "very glad that I won the prize- and I hope to keep on." That's right, Sam. "It's dogged as does _it!" • Jeanuie Wright, of 10, Church-street, writes: "My favourite animal is the dog. I think that dogs are so lovable and faithful, if you are kind to them! If anyone is ill in the house a dog who is very Affectionate will, in its own way, try to cheer the invalid. A dog can also be a very nice play-friend." Florence Crompton, of 4, Factory-lane, sends quite a long essay:— "My favourite animal," she says, "is a good and faithful dog. Faithful dogs are very useful, both in town and country houses. -1 remember a short story about a dog named Fido, who followed his master everywhere he went. It happened one day that his master, was sent to the bank with two bags of silver. He-started off on his journey with Fido at the horse's heels. On the way the man dis- mounted and sat by the roadside to have lunch. The faithful Fido lay on the bags of money. His master re- mounted his horse and rode away, leaving poor Fido and the money. [My! wasn't be a careless sort of chap, Florence But the dog got up and ran after the horse, biting and nipping at its heels. His Plaster, thinking the dog was mad, shot at him and left him in the road to die. But Fido dragged himself back to the money bags and rested on theta as be- fore. - Later, his 'master, Missing the bags, went back for them and found them by the roadside with poor Fido, bleeding from his wounds, on top of them. He doctored up poor Fide and made him_well again." A very good story, Florrie! Sarah Stephens, of 15, Hoyle-street, is another of Uncle Ned's numerous family who favours the horse, as also does Hilda Smith, of 124; Bostock-street. Hilda -writes :—" Horses are doing very good work at the Front, by drawing our artillery. And they are risking their lives as well as our brave soldiers . . 1" Another Hilda—Hilda Hassan, Of 36, Factory-lane—also gives her vote for, the horse, and like the other Hilda, she makes reference to the part which the " friend of man " is playing in the war, adding " It goes to battle with, perhaps, as much feeling of danger as any human being." Maud Higham, of 35, Gladstone-street, prefers a black cat to any other animal, and Mona Archer, Of 11, Heathside, votes solid for -a St, Bernard dog. Cicely Northall, of 116, Cartwright-streef, is an energetic member of the Corner, for not only.does she send me a creditable essay on her favourite animal—though it is not quite good enough for a prize—but she also forwards me the names of three new members whom she has got. They are:— Doris Hitchen (12), 122, Cartwright-street; . Dolly Shipley (14), 109, Cartwright-street.

Gladys Williamson (If 2 108, Cartwright- street; and You're a good girl, Cicely! Doris' number will be 526; Gladys' 527, and Dolly's 528. I hope soon to see them taking 'part in the competi- tions. Morrie Burrow, of 30, Wellington-street, is also desirous of joining, and her number will be 529. We shall soon have the noble six hundred at this rate. I have to welcome yet another niece=-Dorothy Lingard, of 3, Walker-street, who informs me that she attends the ArnleY-street School-,-and a very nice school tto, Dorothy !--and thirteen years of age ! Dorothy's number will be 523. My word! the "My Favourite " Com- petition did fetch in the entries for in addition to those I have mentioned, there were essays from Morrie Burrow, Louie Minshull (29, Wake- field-street), Marian Barton (42 Wakefield- street), Jack Barton (42, Wakefield-street), llettie Ditehfield (57, Tanners-lane), Kathleen Boscow (1, LongshOw-street), Violetta Crighton (" Scenic Gallopers," Flag-lane), Florrie Stan- way (18, Edgeworth-street), Margaret Massey (80, Bostock-street), May Williams (26, Gari- baldi-street), Minnie Farmer (15, Kean-street), Lily Booth (47, Green-street), Ethel Gibbons (82, Catharine-street), Maud Hiokey. (35, King- street), and a host of others. , I award this week's Prize to Florence Crompton. THE WOODPECKER. We have been talking of animal; now let us turn to birds. I wonder how many of you know that there- are five different woodpeckers known in England, all of them being shy birds, fre- quenting silent woods, Where they not only rear their young, but find their subsistence among the stems and branches of forest trees. They have received their name from their habit of pecking among the decayed timber in search Of the insects upon which they feed. They also chip away the wood for the purpose of making a convenient hole wherein to deposit tfieir eggs. It might be supposed that much injury in this manner would be done to the trees which are thus operated upon, but it is not so; the instinct of the bird leads it to attack only such trees as are already in a decaying condition, and by the chipping away of dead portions of the trunk the tree is rather improved than otherwise.

A brewer's dray had collided with a heavily laden milk cart and sent can after can splash- ing into the street. Of course, the world assembled to watch the great event. A small man, coming up late, had to stand on tip-toe and keep dodging his head from side to side in order to see past an enormously stout woman who was just in front of him. "What is it? What is it?" he kept asking. • • - At last he caught a glimpse of the shattered cart and the fresh white milk streaming through the street. "Goodness!" he exclaimed. "What an awful waste!"

div.head: HINTS ON . HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON . HEALTH.
Useful Information In Popular
Language.

Flies And Typhoid. The curve for typhoid or enteric mortality reaches its highest point in this kingdom in. October and now is the time to beware of flies: and all other means of contamination. Owing largely. to the magnificent sanitation and hygiene and other measures that have been taken by our efficient Royal Army Medical Corp S there has been comparatively little enteric among the soldiers at home or abroad Nevertheless, typhoid carriers are doubtless in- creasing in number and there is a very consider- able chance that typhoid fever may be brought home by the soldiers on sick leave or furlough and readily disseminated amongst the popula- tion. The common house fly is now known to be capable of disseininating the germs of typhoid and the .. most rigid precautions as regards cleanliness are necessary in order to pre- vent an epidemic. It is always dangerous to have flies about and they must never be toler- ated in the kitchen or larder or elining-room, or, ' indeed anywhere where- they can come in con- tact with food. Prevention, always the best cure, is particularly important in dealing with typhoid and other infectious diseases spread, by flies.—" Good Health." , Sweets And The Teeth.

A few words ought to be said with regard to the selection of food. Soft, pappy foods appear to be most' conducive to decay because of the ease with which they stick to the teeth and thus encourage fermentation. Sugar and sugary foods are also objectionable because of their strong tendency to set up fermentation and decay. Another objection to such fpods is that they do not give sufficient exercise to the teeth. Many people seem to forget that the teeth are formed of the hardest tissue in the body, .and are evidently intended by nature for the purpose of crushing and grinding the food. such exercise of the teeth is essential in order to keep them in a healthy, sound state. Stale bread, toasted bread or zwieback, baked macaroni, and similar dishes, nuts, and .especially fruits, are all admir- able foods not only for the sustenance of the body but equally for the preservation of the teeth. Apples and pears are particu:arly useful be- cause of their cleansing effect upon the teeth mechanically and through the influence of the mild acids which they contain. The same is true of pineapples, and .to a large extent of 'almost all fruits, small or large. Eating, a raw apple at the close of the meal is a good practice to encourage in children a-s well as adults. Many drugs, and especially draughts con- taining iron and acids, have a particularly harmful effect upon the teeth, and should be avoided if for no other _reason. Itundreds of men and women have ruined their teeth by taking iron preparations or acids.-:—Dr. Olsen.

div.head: (BY KATHLEEN BROWN; Form V.; Age 16.)
div.p: (BY KATHLEEN BROWN; Form V.; Age 16.)

When we compare the state of England at the present .time with its state in 1815 we see two periods in history which are most similar, and our universal hope is that the results may also be similar. In 1815 we were at war with Napoleon, the greatest of the French Emperors. He had a great desire to be ruler of the world, but his ambitious nature preyed his downfall. England was at that time engaged in the greatest struggle for freedom which she had ever experienced. She was fighting • for her liberty against fearful odds, but "right proved to be might," and she emerged from it with the renowned honours of Waterloo fresh upon her. Napoleon was not 'satisfied with his usurped kingdom; he wanted more, and deter- mined to obtain Europe. England was at times without a single ally and had to fight very fiercely and bravely for her position as "Master of the Seas." Napoleon was an aggressor; so is the German Emperor. Germany wishes to conquer the -world as did Napoleon. In both periods the British Navy has proved its worth. In the Napoleonic Wars the year 1797 was termed "England's Darkest Hour." She was destitute of allies and only saved the situation by the gallantry and fortitude of her Navy. " England saved Europe"; may she do the same in the present strife. Napoleon was always oppressed by England during the struggle. If England had been submissive he would have had little difficulty in conquering the rest of Europe. In 1797, that fateful year, Napoleon was master of the Continent, and it only remained for him to crush England, to be Lord Of Europe. 'England, however, stood firm. - There has been a recurrence of these events in the present year. The German Emperor wished to conquer Europe; he could easily. crush Belgium, France and Russia, but he had not thought of England. The resolute little island 'strove to save the weak, and the aggressor's plans were .frustrated. That 'strip of water between us and the Continent had again saved Europe. England saved herself in the previous struggle by dogged watchful- ness And- perseverance; we are adopting the same plan at present.. We are blockading Ger- many and preventing her ships from crossing the ocean. We did the same in 1815. In this year (1815) the Emperor's Navies were block- aded in the Baltic, the Texel, and other safe harbours, and were so carefully watched that all plans were useless and the intended invasion of our island was again prevented. When Napoleon meditated invading Asia and taking Europe in the rear he was attacked by the British Navy, and the Battle of the Nile and Sir Sidney Smith are said to have spoiled Napoleon's destiny. Has not our Navy done the same this year? Have we not again spoiled an Empire-seeker's destiny? We are fighting now as then for our liberty, against a ruthless, ambitious tyrant. Both Napoleon- and the Emperor Wilhelm have shown themselves to be devoid of humane feelings or to have con- sidered in any way their followers or victims. Recollect the retreat from -Moscow, the suffer- ing and untimely deaths of so many, faithful followers of the- Emperor and then remember the devastation of Belgium, the atrocities which were committed in those Belgian towns and the 'destruction of a beautiful country. The internal conditions of England at both times are somewhat similar. In 1815 there was much distress in England owing to various famines and the pressure of taxes. We also are feeling the effects of the war, and in some' towns there is real distress. But at the pre- sent time as a hundred years ago we being on an island have many more of the neces- saries of life - than those living on the Continent. We have in this war many competent men both in the Army and the Navy. Wellington, Sir Sidney Smith, .Nelson and Jervis saved the situation for us in 1815, surely French, Jellicoe, Kitchener and others will do the same in 1915. The Napoleonic stpuggle has shown that even in the face of fearful odds the just cause triumphed and the ambitious Empire builder fell to the ground. It is the earnest ,desire of most of the civilised world ,at the present time that right will again be victorious and that once more a Waterloo will be heralded far and wide, announcing the fall of Germany and the ever- lasting establishment of justice over tyranny.

The aged lady, next door had been quite ill. so one morning Willie's mother said to her small son "Willie, mil over and see. how old Mrs. Smith is this morning." Willie departed but in a few moments he came running back and said:"She says it's none of your business." "Why, Willie," exclaimed his mother, "what did you ask her?" div.head: Well-Paid Posts That Are Open
div.p: Well-Paid Posts That Are Open
To The Fair Sex.
HELP WANTED IN
HOSPITALS.

A meeting, convened by the British Red Cross Society, was held at the Cairo-street School, Warrington, on Wednesday evening, in order to discuss various ways in which women may work in hospitals, in addition to nursing. Miss Sylvia Broadbent was in the chair, and on the plat- form were Mrs. Mocatta, Miss M. Broadbent, Miss D. Monks and Miss Knowles, the senior organising officer for women's work in Warring- ton.

div.head: NURSES AND OTHERS WANTED.
div.p: NURSES AND OTHERS WANTED.

Opening the meeting, Miss Broadbent ex- plained that the Special Service Section of the Voluntary Aid Detachments was a new de- parture, and they had been asked by the War Office to obtain candidates for work in hos- pitals, other than nursing work. They still wanted more nurses, but there were a great number of other positions in the hospitals that they hoped to fill. The first special reason why they were asked to take up this work was in order to release men for active service. Within the last two days she had visited two large general hospitals, and she was very much struck by the number of young strong men who were working as orderlies or clerks, work which could well be done by strong, energetic and sensible women. The opportunity was now given to women to do work not only voluntarily, but to do work for which they would be well paid. Miss Knowles said that more and more the country was dependent on the women. Women Must Come Forward If Men Are To Go. The men could ,not go to the Front if the women did not come forward and qualify them- selves to carry on the work of the country. There had been a great deal of criticism on the sub- ject of the late appeal for women for war ser- vice; they were told that women had effered themselves, and had4not been used, but t ew that employers had been convinced that women could do the work, there was a great demerel for omen. Referring to the work at present being performed by women, Miss Knowle; said that women were employed on the railwas.s, es.pestal servants, on Corporation undertaki gs at agri- cultural work, and, in the wire works, munition works, textile factories, banks, insurance offices, 8:c. Miss Knowles went on to give a learning to her audience, saying that in the past there had. been a good deal of want of seriousness in the offers for war service. People had meant to do the work, but when it came to the roint they had been absolutely unreliable, which was fatal. The women must be able to show tint they had the same amount of energy and entluranee as men had, otherwise their work to replace leen would be most unsatisfactory.

div.head: Not Child's Work, But Men's Work.
div.p: Not Child's Work, But Men's Work.

People must first count the cost • before they volunteered; it was not child's work, it was men's work, and called for a great deal of endurance. It often meant long hours and pos- sibly harder work than that to which they had been accustomed. The War Office felt that a great deal of the work now being performed by men in the hospitals could be done by women if they could get hold of the right women, who were qualified and willing to put their backs ' into it. , Many of these _posts were quite well paid, and there vas no question of women being put in at a cheap rate. The scales of payments were:—Dispensers, £1 10s. a week; store- keepers, V Gs.; head clerks, £1 155.; clerks, £1 55.; head cooks, £1 15s. (with three meals); and cooks, £1 (with three meals). Miss Knowles pointed out that the candi- dates must be thoroughly qualified. A good , deal of the work was heavy, especially that of the storekeepers and cooks. Candidates must be prepared to be inoculated and vaccinated. Above all, they must have physical and moral strength in order that they might be enabled to carry on the work. They would be asked to agree to serve either for six months or for the period of the war. She concluded with an appeal to the members of the audience to offer themselves. VOLUNTARY HELPERS WANTED.

Moving a vote of thanks to Miss Knowles, Miss Broadbent pointed out that there were also vacancies for girls (between 18 and 23) in hostels in France. No salary was given for this, but all expenses w.ere paid. Voluntary part-time helpers were also required in the local hospitals.
The vo-te of thanks was seconded by Mrs. Mocatta, and was carried unanimously. A vote of thanks was also accorded Miss Broadbent for her services in the chair.

div.head: TO WHOM TO APPLY.
div.p: TO WHOM TO APPLY.

Ladies who desire to offer their service should apply to the following:—Miss M. Broadbent, The bollies,_Latchford; Miss D. Monks, Stone- croft, Appletitn; Mrs. Mocatta, hon. command- ant of the Warrington Voluntary Aid Detach- ment; or to Miss Knowles, senior organising officer for women's work, 3, Museum-street, Warrington.

div.head: Quay Accident.
div.p: Quay Accident.

At a sitting of the Warrington County Court, held before his Honour Judge J. Scott Fox, K,C., last week, Messrs. Maginn Bros., livery and stable proprietors, Arpley-street, sued the L. and N.-W. Railway Company for 28 9s. 9d., the cost of damage done to a taxi- cab, it was alleged, owing to fault on the part of the company's servants. Mr. A. Owen, of Manchester was for the plain- tiffs, and Mr. Arthur Browne, of Warrington, ' for the defendant company. How It Happened.

The ease for the plaintiffs was to the effect that on July 15th the driver of a railway van pulled up outside Bank Quay Station in such a man- ner, as, having regard to other circumstances which arose, caused the driver of the taxi-cab, Mr. Patrick Maginn, needlessly to damage his vehicle in an effort to prevent what might have been very serious injury to one of the company's servants—a young van boy. The ran, it was contended, was drawn up at right angles to the kerb, the back of it standing at such a distance from the gutter" as would have permitted the driver of the motor vehicle tdopass behind it. Just RR Mr. Maginn was, about to so Pass a lad in the company's employ jumped off the rear of the van—or came from behind the vehicle—right into the track of the oncoming car. Mr. Maginn saw the lad in the nick of time and at once turned his car on to the kerb, thereby damaging it to the amount claimed. Even then he was not able entirely to avoid the boy, for he was knocked down, though fortunately, he was not much injured. Having heard evidence bearing out Mr. Owen's statement, his Honour remarked that the case was a very unusual one; in fact, he (lid not recollect one anything like it before.

div.head: His Honour's Suggestion.
div.p: His Honour's Suggestion.

After some considerable time had been devoted to the case his Honour interpolated with a sug- gestion which, he thought, would meet with the approval of both parties. He was inclined to think, he said, that the railway company should be made to pay for the damage done to the taxi, but without costs. He did not find that they were legally liable to do so—he might, or might not, so find after hearing the evidence in full—but he took into account the fact that the plaintiffs had certainly suffered damage and loss in consequence of their driver's commend- able efforts to avoid serious injury to a fellow creature. -

_ . Mr. Browne, on behalf of his clients, gave an undertaking that the £8 9s. 9d. claimed would be paid, and it was agreed to divide the Court fees between the parties; each to pay 14s. Thereupon his Honour marked his list "Case wittidrawn on terms agreed."

div.head: GERMANY AND THE DANISH BUTTER MARKET.
div.p: GERMANY AND THE DANISH BUTTER MARKET.
Scheme To Inflate Prices Foiled.

During the past two days news has reached this country that prices in the Danish butter market have dropped by „t 2 to ,k 3 a hundred- weight. Three weeks or so ago the price of Danish butter ruled firm at some 2205. per cwt. Now, according to the latest news from Copen- hagen, the exporters in Denmark are willing to accept 1705., or even less, which represents a fall of more than sd. a lb. Buyers from Germany and Austria had been willing to pay anything up to 50s. above the riling market rate, which at times rose as _high as 300 s. a cwt. It was this panic-buying by the Central Empires that so upset the Danish trade with England that recently there has been no official weekly quotation for Danish liutter here. The panic purchases from the Central Em- pires, where butter is scarce almost to the point of famine, encouraged the Danish ex- porters to raise Prices to a pitch at which English buyers refused to deal. This country, as was explained yesterday by prominent men in the trade, is not so dependent on Danish butter- supplies as some other countries, and about three weeks ago buyers who in the. North of England and elsewhere have been numerous, cancelled their regular orders—in fact the German-enhanced Danish product was practi- cally boycotted. It is understood that the Danish exporters have now decided to ship half of their exports for sale here at the best rates obtainable. the other half going to Germany and Austria- Hungary. The German hope—some provision traders describe it as actually, a plan—to secure for themselves all or nearly all the Danish supply has thus, been foiled.—" The Times."

div.head: HEATII SENTENCE AT CHESTER.
div.p: HEATII SENTENCE AT CHESTER.

At Chester Assizes on Wednesday, before Lord Coleridge, John James - Thornley, 26, a lamp man, was indicted for the wilful murder of Frances Johnson, aged 24, at Macclesfield, on September 18th. Johnson, it was stated, Was employed at a cotton mill, and for two and a half years had been walking out with the prisoner. They quarrelled, and Johnson gave her ring back to Thornley, who was afterwards heard to say that if he could not have the young woman he would take care that no one else should. On the night of September 18th Johnson was found dead in her bedroom with her throat cut and other injuries. The prisoner was shortly afterwards seen to jump into a canal. He left in the girl's bedroom a note addressed to her father and step-mother as follows : "Dear Pa and Ma,—l told you I would kill or cure Frances, and I. have done it. I hope you will forgive me for breaking God's holy law."
It was urged that the prisoner at the time of committing the act was insane, but he was found guilty and sentence of death was passed.
Kicks.

Harry Payne Whitney, the day his own and other noted horsemen's racers were shipped for London on the Minnehaha, said of the death of racing in New York : A good many jockeys have been hard hit. A jockey told me last week a very sad tale of misfortune. I listened sympathetically. " `Ah, Joe,' said I, 'when a man is down, few hands are extended to him.' "The jockey, qs he chewed a straw, smiled bitterly. " Few bands—yes—that's right,' he said; ' but think of the feet.' "
