div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST. '
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST. '

Veteran Baptist at LatchfortL The Rev. Henry Briggs, who preached at the Baptist Church, Latchford, on Sunday last, was described as of Todmorden. I under- stood that to mean not that he actually lives there now, but that he laboured there for so long a period that it has become customary if not necessary so to describe him for the purpose of ready identification. As the Rev. H. Ogden well knows as a native of that town, , ,Mr. Briggs was the pastor of n Baptist Church in Todmorden for between 30 and 40 years, during which a handsome and Substantial pile of buildings, including manse as well as church and Sunday school premises, was erected. Thanks to the minister's admirable leadership ,and untiring efforts, the whole was paid for, before-ill-health and other circumstances con- strained him to resign his charge. Once a good friend sent Mr. Briggs to America on a recuperative holiday. As editor of a local paper in those days, I had the pleasure of reviewing a work of his on the Book of Ruth. On leaving Todmordcn Mr. Briggs went into retirement at Nelson, where one of his sons resides, but after jt while he recovered suffi- cient strength to take another charge, and accepted a..call to Littleborough. After serv- ing there a„few years, he finally withdrew from the regulai ministry, and I believe his home is again at Nelson. When I went to Todmor- den he was a member of what was then the School Board, and he subsequently became a prominent and most determined and consist- ent passive resister. Having known him in- timately for some years, I could set down much to the credit of this very sincere min- ister, who freely sacrificed himself for the good of others, and, as it was impossible in the circumstances that he could be other than a poor man' must have been surprised and dis- appointed by the ingratitude (to use the mildest possible word) displayed by some who ought to have stood by him.- I thought his - friends at Latchford might be interested in a personal testimony to the merits of last Sunday's preacher, who, although by no means a "great ". preacher, is certainly one of the most genuine and simple-hearted and least self-seeking 'men I ever met. It is worthy of note ,as a coincidence that his brother, the Rev. R. Briggs, filled a York- shire pastorate for more than 30 years.
Uncommon Names. Two or three Christian names which I came

across in last week's edition (for instance, Nami, which occurred in the list of indict- ments for this week's Assizes at Liverpool) reminded me of an experience at the West Riding Police Court at Halifax considerably over 30 years ago. At the Petty Sessions one Saturday, at which I happened to be present, a witness gave the name "Kelita." "Kelita," exclaimed the Chairman (an old and devoted Churchman, by-the-bye), " Kelita! Wher- ever does that name come from ?" And the scandalised owner of it, making no attemiat to hide his disgust, immediately retorted, " Th'. tent chapter o' th' Neemiah, an' th' tent voss !" Told that story before, have I? If so—and it's not unlikely in a contributor of a weekly column consisting largely of reminis- cences—the impatient reader may well for- bear for the sake of others who have not met with it previously. Not Fit for a Dog.

An accused person last week complained before a local tribunal that language had been used to him which was " not fit Tor a dog to hear." I was somehow reminded of the young hopefid who, asked to go on a short errand one stormy night, pleaded " It's not fit to turn a dog out; send father-!" Soot as Manure.

Last week's paragraph at the head of the "Farm and Garden " column sent my mind back to a period when, in a district in whicli I then lived, the chimney sweeps had thq utmost difficulty in disposing of soot. The neighbouring farmers would not have it given, and, when the only available tip was closed against them, the alternative that suggested itself was, to surreptitiously empty the bags into the already Sickening trough of creeping industrial slime called by courtesy " the river." Eventually, however, a profitable market for the troublesome refuse was dis- covered at a distant agricultural centre, and _thenceforward the soot which had caused such perplexity and become such a nuisance was regularly sent off by train at quite re- munerative rates.

Plucky P.C. Bennett. I see that this constable, who stopped a runaway horse at Bridge Foot, has been "commended" by the Watch Committee. The officer in question is quite unknown to me personally, and I have not exchanged a syl- lable On the subject with anyone nor heard any comment upon it. Having given that assurance by way of preface, I will be frank even to bluntness, and state that I have never before known such an act passed over, as ap- parently is the case in this instance, with a mere complimentary word. In my experi- ence of different towns in Lancashire and Yorkshire it has been the invariable rule either forthwith to reward such bravery with an appreciable gift Or to encourage emulation by conferring a merit stripe, which entails increased pay. After all, it were perhaps un- just to assure that the authorities regard as closed the incident to which I now particu- larly refer. Constables in the local force may no doubt be assured that all such acts - and deeds are duly noted with a view to promo- tions as vacancies occur in the higher ranks.

Temperance Teaching in Schools. The local paragraph headed " Temperance Lecturer for Schools " recalled for me a little encounter I had many years ago with some such representative of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope Union as the Church of England Temperance Society commend to the Warrington Education Committee. It was in the days of the old School Board._ At the instance of the organisation just men- tioned and with the consent of the local authorities, an expert had been sent from headquarters to give a_ course of temperance lessons in the elementary day schools of the district. The scholars were asked to send in short essays on the subject of the lectures. That suggested to-me the publication of some amusing " howlers " obtained under similar conditions elsewhere. The explanation called for in the circumstances was properly given in the introduction; nevertheless, the union agent, who must have been wofully deficient •in the saving quality of humour,. waxed very wroth on the inference that my poor little " howlers " had somehow come from the papers for which he was responsible, or that it might be supposed they had been derived from that source, and that he would be sus- pected of having 'disclosed them. He was only to be aPpeased by the insertion of a personal disclaimer: Perhaps I was incapable of reviewing the situation from his standpoint, but it, struck me as rather funny—nay, de- cidedly so, aggravated as it was by the serious and solemn demeanour of the important' per- sonage who made the complaint. Tree-planting.

Readers may once more be reminded that Sir Walter. Scott was wont to say that when Ono has nothing else to do he should plant trees. Said Alderman Bolton last week, "II any committee recommends that -trees be planted, we:do it." He was referring to the Parks Committee's ready compliance. with the wish of-the Stieet Imprdvement CoMmittee that trees • should be planted in further justi- fication of the. title " Lovely "-lane. The cultivation of beauty spots is altogether ad- mirable, and I could tell of wonders that have been worked by tho like simple means in

div.head: MOTHER AND CHILD.
div.p: MOTHER AND CHILD.
Huddersfield Experiment Con- cerning Infant Mortality.
REMARKABLE RECORD.

Ten years ago Mr. Benjamin Broadbent, who was then Mayor of Huddersfield, tried to save the lives of the babies born during his tcrm of office by certain measures of care and supervision. He records the result of the experiment in an artido published in " The Times " this week. Of the 112 babies at least 97 are healthy boys and girls to-day; whereas, according to the average rate of mortality, of 112 babies born in 1905 only 84 are now alive. The article states :

In 1905 tho output of new human life in the United Kingdom was approximately 1,100,000 babies. Tho survivors of those are 10 years old this year,(they have reached what may be called the half-way house to manhood and womanhood, and they are out of the danger zone._ We know roughly what has happened to them in the mass. We know very well that there are nothing like 1,100,000 of them alive 'to-day. About 140,000 died before they were a Year old, and as many more died before. the survivors were five years old. Out of the 1,100,000 that were launched on the sea of life there were not many more than 820,000 that reached, the comparatively safe water of five .years old; nearly 300,000 wrecked— decimated thrice over. What should we think of . 280,000 'casualties—all fatal—out of 1,100,000? And what of the uncounted

wounded? Between five years and ten years the numbers are probably not materially diminished. But of the 820,000 that remain a sad number are maimed and deteriorated, they will never make sound and healthy men and women; some are blind, some are crippled, some mentally defective. Out of the baby crop of 1905 we are pretty certain that 280,000 are lost and probably at least 30,000 more are deteriorated. The question inevitably forces itself, Was all this waste of human life and health really inevitable? Could not some- thing have been done to preserve in life and health some of the 300.000? By a combina- tion of circumstances it seems to be possible to answer these questions with some confi- dence.

div.head: An Experiment in Saving.
div.p: An Experiment in Saving.

Ten years ago the whole of the babies born from November 9, 1904, to November 9, 1905, in the district of Longwood in the borough of Huddersfield, were brought within the range of personal observation. There was, no selec- tion, no exclusion; every baby born in the district was noted and kept in view. The first baby in the group was born on Novem- ber .10, 1904, and the last on November 8. 1905. As each baby duly reached its first birthday a special visit was paid to the home to ascertain the actual existence of the baby; the tale of babies was completed when the last born was a year old—that is, on Novem- ber .8, 1906. It was then possible to note what had. happened in the first year of life to the whole group. There were 112 horn; there were 107 known to have lived through their first year; four were known to have died, one had removed, and could not be traced. To anyone who is at all familiar with infantile mortality statistics the result thus ascertained will be surprising; to those immediately in- terested it was intensely gratifying and en- couraging. During the whole of the first year there had been maintained in connection with this group Of babies a constant, regular over- sight. kindly, wise, tactful, and, in a measure, skilful, though not professional. The result so far was that of 112 babies born there were 107 one-year-olds. The survivors of these are now 10 years old, or will be 10 on November 8 this year. What are the 10-year-olds like? And how many are there of them? How will they compare with those hundreds of thousands their contemporaries?

div.head: Ten Years After.
div.p: Ten Years After.

From the time that the babies were a year old there has been what can only be called a loose and rather casual connection kept up with them. But the kindly oversight and thought of the first year was never quite for- gotten, and the bond established was never quite broken; it asserted itself in many unex- pected ways which cannot here be detailed. Still it had always been a purpose when the 10-year period arrived that there should, if practicable be some attempt made to get together this group of babies, and perhaps have some kind of celebration. This purpose has recently been carried out, thanks to the help .of school teachers and of those who had been in touch with the children from the time of their birth. The list of the 1904-5 babies was gone through, and all those who could be got at were invited to meet each other. Some of the replies to the invitation are quaint, but must not be quoted. On the day of meeting . each child was asked to sign his or her name in a visitors' book. The gathering was an interesting one in itself; but that again is beside the present purpose. The names regis- tered numbered 89, but one was a " supple- mentary " baby who was born a few hours too late to be included in the 112; she has, however, always been accorded the same privi- leges as the others. So that of the 'lO7 one- year-olds there were present 88 10-year-olds. The number was so remarkable that it was considered worth while to try to ascertain what had become of the remaining 19. Of these nine are now known to be living, four are dead, and the other six are not yet traced; one at least has emigrated, and the others have removed and left no trace. The inter- esting fact is, however, established that there are 97 known to be living. A point of Con- siderable importance is also quite clear; every one of these 10-year-olds is healthy and fit for life. There is not one defective; there is not one of whom it could possibly be said that the child were " better dead."

The group is a small one, but so far as this is concelned it is surely a very striking fact that out of the 112 bibles there should be 97 healthy boys and girls at 10 years of age. Refer to the general figures•and draw out two sums in proportion. If this group had fared

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.--
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.--

various parts of Lancashire in 'which I have lived. But why stop here? Behind these highly commendable little schemes is the great. question of afforestation with its enormous possibilities. When 1 was in the Rossendale Valley, not very many year ti ago, the Bury and District Joint Water Board initiated what proved to be a completely successful experi- ment in afforestation, planting a portion of the area comprising their watershed with fir, spruce, poplar, birch, alder, ash, and larch, according to vary- ing conditions. As their engineer explained at the time, this was done partly for ornamental purposes, but especially because trees are an unmistakable advantage in help- ing to attract water to the reservoirs. More- over, only a few months ago, the Professor of Forestry at Oxford wrote of the need there is for other. reasons to grow more timber in this country. He says the war has placed us in a very serious position as regards pitwood, not to speak of telegraph poles, building timber, and even firewood, and there is plenty bf sur- plus land available now yielding a revenue Of perhaps a shilling an acre all round, if so much. There are large stretches of land un- fit for cultivation and yet qUite fit to produce forest 'crops. For the rest, is it not written in the chronicles of the Royal Commission that has elaborately reported in favour or sys- tematic afforestation on a gigantic scale? What need have we of further witness ? If we cannot at present have a national scheme, local authorities might at negligible cost copy the Bury example in a modest

as the whole output of babies in 1905 there would have been 83 or 84 alive and some of these would probably have been defective. As it is there are alive in this group 13 or 14 more than would have been alive if the general rate of mortality had been applied to them. Or putting the proportion sum the other way about, if there had been as many survivors, in the same proportion as is the case with the Longwood babies, out of the 1,100,000 born throughout the United Kingdom, there would have been 950,000 10-year-olds to-day in place of the 820,000 or thereabouts that are actually , in being; there would have been something 1:e 130,000 more boys and girls of 10 years of age in the United Kingdom to-day than there are. To revert to the crop metaphor, wo are something like 130,000 short of what would have been, if the same results had been attained with this group of 112, born in the same year. There will probably be the same shortage on the babies born in 1905; but since that year the shortage has been very con- siderably reduced and for the last few years it has probably been not more than 70,000 or 80,000 a year. Still in 10 years the short- age cannot be less than 1,000,000 human lives.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 30, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 30, 1915.
Needless Waste.

It is impossible to repair the wastage of past years; but it is not impossible to prevent the wastage in the years to come. It is piti- able to think of the loss that never need have been, but surely at this time there . should come a determination that such a terrible and needless leakage of life shall be stanched. It is our national life blood that is ebbing away, not only in Gallipoli and on the fields of Flanders and of France and in the wide wastes of the world, but also in our own homes safe- guarded from outside foes, but not protected from the ignorance and neglect within that kills as surely as the poison gas and shells. It is no longer possible to say that this loss of life cannot be prevented. There are places where no babies die, there are places in our own country where few babies die. They will to live—these helpless ones—and it is a matter of making the conditions fit for them to live. Where the conditions are right they do live. Nor is there any doubt as to what the con- ditions are that make the difference between life and death to them.

Nor can it be said that the killing off of the babies is in any "sense a eugenic process; the exact reverse is true and should be sufficiently obvious. The conditions that preserve life also preserve health. Where pains are taken to keep the babies alive for one year the result seems to be to establish a resisting power that wards off diseases that maim and kill from one to five. To see the 97 who ought statistically to have been only 83 or 84, and to see them strong and healthy, full of vitality and intel- ligence, is a sufficient object-lesson.

div.head: NEW BOOKS.
div.p: NEW BOOKS.
The Research Magnificent. By H. G. Wells
Londop : Macmillan and Co., Ltd

This latest book of Mr. Wells demands, and is worthy of, careful consideration. It is a story with a prelude, in both of which a new idea of life is set forth, embodying the latest philosophy of the author. The story is of a youth whose whole life was shaped by an idea which seemed to possess him from his earliest days, and when on leaving the University he found himself with ample means he resolved to devote himself to the development of this idea. It was a noble aim. He realised that life in the main is a failure— " Let us eat and drink for to-morrow we die." Even those whom the world calls successful and who make for themselves a name, seemed to Benham to fall short of the splendour of the ideal life.. He had an innate belief that he had to live life nobly and thoroughly. He thought all men might do this, and when in early life he was disillusioned and found that in most cases men have Other conceptions of .existence, in which ease, pleasure or ambi- tion is the determining consideration,. he re- solved that he at any rate would lead the noble life, and he set himself to search through the world for the means of developing the nobility which he believed to be innate in man.

It was truly a research magnificent, and though it was foredoomed to failure, the failure never. changed Benham's resolve as to his own course of life. He had many strange adventures and mot with many disappoint- ments, for in all his wanderings he never found anyone willing to accept his creed and join him in his efforts to renovate the world. One hardly knows whether Mr. Wells has written on this subject in a sympathetic or cynical spirit. In one of his .earlier books he told how the new heaven on earth would be the outcome of • a great world war. In another, he predicted it as the result of chemical action following the contact of the earth with a comet. But however that may be, the new and nobler life which has been the dream of poets and idealists will be brought about by the individual efforts of men such as the hero of this story, men who, undaunted • by the absolute selfishness and blindness of the world in which they live, resolve that they themselves will live the life of nobility with sublime faith that it will not. be lived in vain. There is much in 'this book that will lead to grave thought in the reader's mind. It is an attractive book, but it will not be fair to the author to follow only the story and lightly to pass over the philosophy which it is intended to illustrate and which is Worth very careful study.

div.head: CYNTHIA. (cm.)
div.p: CYNTHIA. (cm.)

I would if I could e'er bring unto thee Of flowers the sweetest and fairest; First would be love in the heart of a rose, The love that is honest and rarest. Affection born in Friendship's name Becomes akin to love divine, No.mother gives to babe at breast. Such love as my heart gives to thine.

I would if I mild e'er bring unto thee The virtue the daisy possesses, Enrich thy brow with a bright pansy crown And ivy entwine with thy tresses. Devotion born in gratitude Men seldom place on woman's shrine, Itsiionour is the offering. In which my heart goes forth to thine.

I would if I could enrobe thee for aye With blossoms fumed in Bible story, Thou would'st—like this arrayed—far grander be Than " Solomon in all his glory." Reverence born in purity Creates within this heart of mine The pray'r that God will smile on thee-- With Everlasting Love Divine. R. OSSULS'I'ON-RICIIE.

div.head: "OLD FOX."
div.p: THE "OLD FOX."
Some Curious And Interesting Facts About Ancient Houses.

div.head: HOW OUR ANCESTORS BUILT.
div.p: HOW OUR ANCESTORS BUILT.
BY ARTHUR

The Old Fox Inn, for the first time in living memory, may now be seen in its ancient aspect and studied as a piece of architecture. The result is much happier than could have been expected. It no longer appears a squat and crushed house of two storeys. Standing alone, it shows itself a proportioned, shapely building, a typical Elizabethan homestead, with a grainstoro among the rafters and not seriously spoiled by the hands of restorers. Such houses were springing up throughout England in the years. when Shakespeare, • like his own schoolboy, was "creeping unwillingly to school." Our countrymen had just learned the value of light, and for the first time in history windows had become a feature in architecture. Very soon they were to become a craze, and the builders woulkt place them (as in the case of the Barley Mow, which is of a later date) from end to end of their buildings. But before we are able to appreciate either the "Fox" or the "Barley Mow" it will be necessary to make a preliminary study of English domestic architecture. To this we will devote the present chapter, coming to a study of the "Fox" in a later issue of the " Examiner."

The earliest hqmes, of course, were cave- dwellings and 'holes in the earth. These did not involve architecture, and need not detain us, though the subject is interesting enough. The earliest fragments of houses which re- main in Great Britain are round in shape and of beehive pattern. An opening gave a vent for smoke, and the door admitted light and air. They were formed of wood and thatched with reeds, or perhaps daubed over with mud and clay.

div.head: HOW THE HOUSE EVOLVED.
div.p: HOW THE HOUSE EVOLVED.

From the beehive house the rectangular house was evolved, and, it is at this stage that the subject becomes interesting. The earliest homes which in any way resembled the modern house were made upon the model of a shepherd's hut. • Two pieces of timber were pinned together and then reared. Curved timbers were chosen, so that when raised they gave the shape of a' Gothic arch. Two other timbers were placed .11 few feet away, and a ridge-tree, that is a connecting beam, was placed from the apex of one to the apex of the other. Two tie-beams were added, and some braces, the whole being fas- tened by wooden pegs. The exterior Nva, thatched or wattled over with whatever material lay nearest to band. The pairs of bent timbers were called " gavels," which comes from the Saxon word for " forks," and which survives in our word " gable."

div.head: CURIOUS FACT.
div.p: A CURIOUS FACT.

It is a curious and very interesting fact that the forks were -always placed about six- teen feet apart, and the space thus formed was called a " bay." Remains of such houses are scattered from the East Coast of Britain to the West Coast of Ireland, and the " bays " are always sixteen feet in length. A building was either sixteen feet or thirty-two or forty- eight feet long. It seems quite probable that the space was fixed by the accommodation re- quired by two pairs of oxen. Eight feet was the width of a stall for two oxen, and sixteen feet would give space for two pairs. This was the measurement allowed by the Romans, as a passage by Vitruvius, who wrote about 10 8.C., shows.- In all probability, the stan- 'dard size of house, as well as the standard of land measure, was borrowed from the Romans. LAND AND HOUSE- MEASURE.

The matter may be put in simple form. They ploughed with four oxen standing abreast. The space occupied by four oxen was sixteen feet, and this space came to be called a rod, or rood, of land. The acre was composed of four roods, each sixteen feet broad and 640 ft. long. The ox-house was built in -bays of sixteen feet, and the other bays, whether for barn or human -habitation, came to be built of similar size. It was so among the Romans, and. whether we explore ancient homes in Norway, Germany, Britain, or Scot- land, they are almost .uniform in the size of the "bay."
HOUSES LIKE AN INVERTED SHIP. s

In shape, too, the Sold houses are the same among Teutonic. peoples. The timbers are always curved and the shape of the building is that of a ship turned bottom upwards. The comparison must have impressed the ancients, for the Latin word " navis," 'which means a ship, was applied to the roof. We still use the word when we speak of the " nave " of a church. The Germans describe an arched nave of a church as a "•schiff," which nieans Sill!). Our ancestors in the tenth century called their houses " hulks,'' which is also an- other word for ship, and the Norsemen called them " hearth-ships," which adds quite a touch of poetry.

div.head: EARLIEST KIND OF WALLS.
div.p: THE EARLIEST KIND OF WALLS.

There came a period when someone thought that the domestic building could be improved. The curving sides of the dwelling did not give the space and the freedom which vertical sides would give, and some genius devised a plan for introducing straight walls. . The ordin- ary plan of building by gavels (or " crucks," as they are popularly called) was retained, but the tie beams were made longer and pro- jected past the curved upright beams. A long beam called a pan was placed upon these and formed what modern builders would call a wall plate. Rafters were placed from the roof tree to the pan and formed a roof. This was the origin of the domestic roof, as we now know it. A wall of wattle or mud was then built from the ground ,to the pan. It did not support anything, being a mere filling in; the timber framework formed the house.

Such buildings may be found plentifully sprinkled over Lancashire and Cheshire. Pairs of " crucks " may be seen which must have been standing for seven or eight cen- turies, and which have been variously "built in," first with wattle, then with bricks, and in these later days covered with slates. Cot- tages which appear most mbdern from with- out prove most interesting to the antiquarian when viewed from within the " crucks," " pans," and " tie beams," being often in their original form. It is very interesting to note how universal is The sixteen-foot meas- urement. For centuries it was the standard of a building, and no one seems to have thought of deviating from it. It was indeed the standard by which rents were fixed. Shakespeare has a passage, "I'll rent the fairest house in it after threepence a bay." It was a convenient standard for renting and taxing, and the farmer sold hay by the " bay " and " gulf," a gulf being as much as would lie between two bays.

div.head: OUTSHOTS AND CHAMBERS.
div.p: OUTSHOTS AND CHAMBERS.

Such dwellings would offer warmth and shelter, but little comfort. A single chamber sixteen feet by about twelve feet would offer little privacy, and the need for additional rooms Would be felt. To meet this need pur ancestors began to plan small rooms, which were placed at the sides of the dwelling. These were called "outshuts" or "outshots" —a name which lingers in some parts of Eng- land as a name for an outside kitchen. The outshot was generally only four or five feet wide, just large enough to hold a couch, and seldom six feet high. These came to be called " chambers," and the eetitral portion, came tc• have the , distinguishing' name pf

div.head: OUNFIELD.
div.p: OUNFIELD.

" house-part." Even yet among old country folk the kitchen is called the " house " and the parlour the " chamber." The need for privacy would be the more felt when it is remembered that in the home of a farmer his helpers, as well as his cows and sheep, would all sleep in one building. There would be more bays than one, but the building would be open from end to end. He himself, to have bettor oversight, would per- haps sleep upon a raised platform. There is a passage in Harrison's " England," which describes the primitive farmer, " the good man long in his bed may lightlio hear() what is dome in each place with case, and call quickly unto his meinie (his household) if any danger should attack him."

TWELFTH CENTURY "COMFORTS." AA'e have not yet reached the period Of chim- neys, and a discussion of them will cow more conveniently in another chapter. Smoke from the peat fire would find its way through an outlet in the roof, after successfully black- ening the .whole interior and leaving bangers of soot to float down in every incOnvenient way at its own leisure. The smuttiness of the " house part " in Chaucer's day (we think it was Chaucer) gave the poet the figure of speech " as sooty as his halle." Nor had our ancestors learned the value of windows in that day. But they had dis- covered that there is usually a draught be- tween a door and a fire, and to lessen this in- convenience they erected a " speer," or screen. This screen, projecting from the wall, formed the cosiest corner in the house, and it survived in various adaptations from the eleventh to the eighteenth century:

A typical dwelling --o-f the fourteenth cen- tury contained a hall, an offshot called a " bower," and another offshot called a " buttery," or food store. The men slept in the hall and the women in the bower.

Country dwellings of the period suggest anything but comfort as we study their ar- rangements. Lofts were made by placing boards across the tie beams. The cattle occu- pied the ground floor and the farm men slept on boards above the horses and the women in the loft above the cows. A special offshot was made at the end, in which the master of the house and his family slept, the arrange- ment being so made as to enable him to see the entire interior from his couch.

div.head: WARRINGTON'S OLDEST HOUSE.
div.p: WARRINGTON'S OLDEST HOUSE.

Until recently Warrington possessed an ad- mirable example of an early cruck built house, and it is unfortunate from many points of view that it should have been demolished. This old homestead, which stood at the corner of Brick-street .and Cockhedge, was one of the oldest houses in the North of England. Its crucks were fine old timbers, twelve to four- teen inches in diameter, and such parts as have been preserved are sound to the present hour. It bad offshots which served as •bed- rooms, and an open fireplace, which, though not so old as the .building, offered a fine ex- ample of the earliest kind of chimney. This venerable homestead had doubtless sheltered a dozen generations of Britons and weathered four centuries of British weather before the " Fox " or " Barley Mow " reared their heads.
Tn another chapter we will discuss the be- ginnings of chimneys and windows, and describe some further stages in the evolution of the English house.

div.head: GRAND FLEET.
div.p: THE GRAND FLEET.
(With acknowledgments to the American author of the artic.es, " With the Grand Fleet," written for "The Times" of London, Eng.) The sea!

Salamis looked on it, William the Conqueror crossed it, Lipton and Dewey have sailed it, Brighton is situated on it, Jonah was thrown into it, and I myself have been sick of it on my way to Europe to write articles.

There are different sections of the sea, and it is not to be inferred that this part of it is identi- cal with anything scheduled above. On the con- trary, it is another section. But it is the same sea—breezy, wet, briny, with little waves that splash • and big waves that do rather more, and undulations that bring the throbbing heart of a journalist nearer to his palpitating mouth. And on this sea—this well-known, time- honoured, immemorial sea—what do I behold? A Fleet!

For some reason, unfathomable as the waters. I ani permitted to go round this Fleet. And 'T will tell you all about it. As a Dry Goods Store is directed by, a Wanamaker, so is this Fleet directed by an Admiral. Jellieoe is his name, but Jellieoe is not his nature.

An American might well expect to find in him some physical resemblance to Nelson's column in Trafalgar-square, but he would be disappointed. The column would hurt you if it fell on you; Jellicoe is not like that. The Commander-in-Chief walks the deck of the Unsinkable. Like his great predecessor of the Pinafore, he carries a telescope under his arm. When he wishes to see anything distant he • applies the telescope to his eye—not to a blind eye, as did Lord Nelson, but to a seeing, hear- ing, watching eye. He paces the deck, and as he paces a tense air of attention seems to spread galvanically amongst his men. They stand alert and upright; they do not slouch; their hands are not in their pockets; their backs are not turned carelessly on their Admiral. Yet Jellicoe is not a harsh or brutal tyrant; he is a good and kindly man. He is strong and yet gentle; clean-shaven and yet devout; and capable, so they say. His men love him, and his country will learn to appreciate him now that I have told it of his real worth. And always remember that he bears gladly with neutral journalists. • From the contemplation of Jellicoe I pass on to other ships and other men. And here let me tell you that the Captains and Admirals are chiefly remarkable for this, that they are not senile; and that life for them is ono ceaseless round of duties. Would you have thought it if I had not told you? And the ships! Here lie the giant Hyena and the massive Gnu, with their glossy guns and shining Midshipmen. Young men too,. these latter, with not a grey hair amongst them. Here is the Lady Squadron—the good Queen Anne, the saucy Bloody Mary, the Susie that does not sew shirts. Here rises' the Insoluble, hard hit in the Balkan Peninsula. The shell made one hole as it came in and another as it went out, but both apertures are now closed up—such is• the wonderful thoroughness of naval organisa- tion. Here roll the tiny Destroyers, grey as their own sea, black as their own coal, white as—no, not white as. And, mind you, every ship hes its complement of well-trained men— not a German amongst them—and every gun its adjunct of shot and shell!

At moments I feel that I must be on my own North American Fleet, and there came like a flash to me that memorable phrase of one of my countrymen—" Blood is thicker than water." I see it all; not as in a dream, but in a waking reality—great vessels melting into horizons and looming out: of distanees; gaunt guns and slumbering torpedoes; winking yard-arias of wireless; decks a-s(-rub and spars a-shine; can- vas that passes in the night. It is all there. And through the haze, and the sea, mid the sun-rise and the sun-set, and all my bag Of journalistic tricks—above and below all this, what is the inner meaning of this Mighty semi and this storm-tossed Fleet? To me it is clear. Its message—its meaning—is this: that over the bosom of this selfsame sea, and under the guns of this selfsame Fleet, a neutral country may render its invoices and ship its goods and haul in its dollars in perfect safety and happiness— yea, even trade its Christmas purchases with Germany! Some Fleet !--" Punch."

div.head: STUDY OF PATRIOTISM,
div.p: STUDY OF PATRIOTISM,
Is Love Of Country Sufficiently Taught?
BRITAIN'S GREAT MEN.
By W.J.L.

Speaking on Trafalgar Day when his prizes to scloor children were being distributed, Alderman Bennett expressed the opinion that patriotism is not taught sufficiently nowadays, and lovers of England and all that England means cannot but agree with him. A patriot is one who loves his country and zealously supports it and its interests. When Alder- man Bennett requests that patriotism shall be taught to a greater degree, it is only because he desires that the youth of the coun- try may love their country and be prepared to support its 'interests. Thousands of young men to-day are not supporting the interests of their country for the simple reason that they do not know what is at stake. In other words they have become so familiar with the liberties of the country that they do not love them. Patriotism is one of those lessons that cannot be taught directly, but it is easy to teach it indirectly. It can be taught in geography lessons and in history lessons, but there is one way I favour, which, though it is not adopted in the elementary schools, I think would meet with Alderman Bennett's ap- proval, and that is through the history of the lives of some of England's great Men. For, as„Longfellow puts it, Lives of great men all remind us, • We can make our lives Sublime, And, departing, leave behind us, Footprints on the sands of time.

It is remarkable bow little the English people know of their great men. In this con- nection, a little story told by Alderman Ben- nett will bear repetition. On Trafalgar Day he asked a young lady of about 20 years with what great man was Trafalgar Day associated. He was astounded to receive the reply " Napoleon !" DARK DAYS AND STERN RESOLVE. England's great men are as numerous as the leaves that fall in. the autumn, but in this article I want chiefly to mention some who lived during the sixty years' reign of George 111., that is, from 1760 to 1820. Dur- ing this period many events of great import- ance occurred. Early in the new reign war was declared against Spain. Later, America declared its independence. Other events in those forty years included the siege and relief of Gibraltar, war with Holland, the impeach- ment of Warren Hastings, -war with France, rebellion in Ireland, the taking of the Cape of Good Hope, the naval battles of Cape St. Vin- cent, the Nile, Copenhagen and Trafalgar, the battle of Cormana, the Peninsular Wars, the battle of Vittoria, and Waterloo addition to these event's, there was great political strife in the country; the Continent was up in arms, and the outlook of England was black indeed. Therefore it is no wonder that this period .produced great men. To quote the _King's Appeal: " In ancient days the darkest moment has ever produced in men of our race the sternest resolve."
For the purpose of this article it is impos- sible to classify the names of the men who have left a place in England's history, so I give them not in the order of importance, but as they occur to me.

Some of the statesmen rvho lived during the reign. of George 111. were William Pitt (Earl of Chatham), Right Honourable Charles Townshend, Thomas Pelham (Duke of. New- castle), William Pitt, Charles James Fox, Lord North, - George Canning, John Stuart (Earl of Bute), and Warren Hastings. The following aro divines and great writers : John Wesley, Charles Wesley, George White- field, Samuel Johnson, David Hume, Lawrence Sterne, Wm. Shenstone, Thomas Gray; Horace Walpole, Tobias Smollett, Edmund Burke, Oliver Goldsmith, Wm. Cowper, James Beattie, James Boswell, Richard B. Sheridan, George Crabbe, Robert Burns, Wm. Words- worth, Sir Walter Scott, Samuel Taylor Coler- idge, Robert Southey, Jane Austen, Thomas Campbell, Thomas Moore, Bishop Heber, Lord Byron, Percy Bysshe Shelley, John Keats, and Thomas Hood. Some great painters in- cluded Sir Joshua Reynolds, Thomas Gains- borough, George Romney, John Opie, John S. Copley, and Sir Henry Raeburn. Other famous men were John Flaxman (sculptor), Sir Wm. Herschell (astronomer), John Smeaton (engineer), James Watt (inventor of the steam engine), Sir Humphry Davy (of safety lamp fame), Mungo Park, Sir John Franklin, Rear-Admiral Sir Win. Parry, Capt. James Cook (explorers), Sir John Moore (who fell at -Corunna), Lord Clive (a great general and statesman), Admiral Lord John Anson, Sir Ralph Abercroinby, Viscount Horatio Nelson Sir Arthur Wellesley (Duke of Wel- lington), Lord Howe, and Baron George Rod- ney (who won the battle of Cape St. Vincent).

div.head: GREAT DEEDS.
div.p: GREAT DEEDS.

This list of the great men who lived in one reign alone, makes one feel a pride in our nation, but why -do we not hear more About them in our elementary schools? The lives of these men abound with interest. Which schoolboy does not love to read of the deeds of Nelson' at Copenhagen, at the Nile, and at Trafalgar? Is there a boy who does not care to hear of the work of Clive and Warren Hast- ings in India, or of Cook in his great voyages in the Pacific and his attempt to find the North-west passage? The story of Welling- ton is a chapter of romance. First he fought the Mahrattas in Mysore, then he conquered the French in the Peninsula, and to crown his military career he crushed the political life out of Napoleon at Waterloo a hundred years ago. I need not here enlarge on Nelson's fame, which, locally, Trafalgar Day is striv- ing to perpetuate.

Of otir great writers not half enough is known, and the same is true .of our great statesmen. Who knows intimately of the work Of the two Pitts? The Earl of Chat- ham (the elder Pitt) was one. of the greatest statesmen that ever advised an English king. He helped Wolfe and Clive to win Canada and India, and Frederick of Prussia to subdue France, and perhaps if his advice had been followed, the country now known as the United States of America, might have been a part of the British Empire. It is not for lack of great men that the lessons of patriotism aro not taught. There is ample scope for these lessons, and perhaps if they had been thoroughly taught in the past, there would to-day be no suggestion of compulsory military service.

div.head: LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES STEAMSHIP COMPANY.
div.p: LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES STEAMSHIP COMPANY.
The report of the directors of the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Co., Ltd., of the twenty-fifth year's working of the company's steamers, states :

Early in March the Government requisitioned the St. Elvies, La Marguerite, and the new geared turbine steamer St. Seiriol, and these three vessels have been continuously employed since that date in the Government service. Owing to the requisitioning of these steam6rs by the Government, it was impossible for the company to conduct the usual passenger ser- vice to and from Liverpool, Llandudno, and the Menai Straits, and consequently this service had to be abandoned.

The company's steamers Snowdon .and St. Teilio were placed upon the North Wales Station, and were employed during the season sailing to and from - Colwyn Bay, Llandudno _ and the Menai Straits. After deducting the sum of 6e6,254 18s. 7d. for depreciation on steamers, the amount available for dividend and other pur- poses, including the balance brought forward from last year, is £5,485 Os. 7d., out of which the directors recommend a payment of B per cent. dividend (less income tax), carrying for- ward a balance of X 13663 Os. 7d.

Avowni ITS WEIGHT IN GOLD. Zam-Itnl, In Every Soldier's Kit. A London reporter has been haring a chat with 3360, Lance-Corporal Owen, A.S.C., who has had some experience of the heavy work of the A.S.C. Transport at the Front. Lance- Corporal Owen is now attached to the 2nd Mid- dlesex Hussars.

Asked at Ranelagh Camp, Barnes, for a few hints that would help ‘to make campaigning easier, Lance-Corporal Owen said, without hesitation, "Zam-Buk should be just as much a part of a soldier's kit as his boots. Zam-Buk is recognised and advised by officers to recruits on joining. No 6ne who has not experienced it can tell the awful soreness after first learning to ride. Zam-Buk is almost the only thing that takes away that soreness and enables the young rider to continue his training with any degree of comfort.

"Then in handling horses, harness, the heavy bales and boxes from train to cart, &c., one is sure to get scratches, kicks from horses, and bruises which would develop into dangerous Poisoned wounds if it were not for the ever- ready Zam'-Buk. On the battlefield itself time and again the Medical Officers have spoken of the wonderful antiseptic properties of Zam-Bnk. "If you want to please your soldier friend, send him Zatu-Buk," says Owen. "There is not a day in the life of a Kitchener's Army man when Zam-Buk is not worth its weight in gold." _ .
Not only at the Front, but particularly at home and in the munition factories Zam-Buk is a daily need. Keep a box always handy.

div.head: amß k u
div.p: amß k u
HARVEST FESTIVALS,
ELAM 00D-AVENUE CONGREGA- TIONAL CHURCH.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held at the Elmwood-avenue Congregational Church on Sunday when the building was tastefully decorated with choice fruit and flowers. The congregations in the afternoon and evening were particularly large. The Bewsey-road Wes- leyan Choir enriched the afternoon's service with their assistance rendering a cantata "Two Harvests" in a most creditable manner, under the able leadership of Mr... John Hannan. They also sang the anthem "Abide .with me" very sweetly. .Miss Winstanley and Mr. Baker gave the duet " Love divine " feelingly. Messrs. White and R. Wallington were the accom- panists. The Rev. 11. Ogden presided, and gave an address.

In the evening the Rev. C. P. Pitt preached from the. text "God left not Himself witness, in that He did good, and gave us rain from heaven, and fruitful seasons, filling our hearts with food and gladness." These words, he said, were spoken by St. Paul at Lystra. The people would have worshipped him and Barnabas as gods. St. Paul, however, wished the people to turn their minds towards God, who was the God of Nature. The things of Nature such as rain and sunshine could bAar witness to Him. Christians must train their minds to find God in everything.. The highest work of God was to be found in the fruitful life of a man. The life which was rich in the beauty of character, rich in true Christian personality was one which serves, as a mirror, to reflect the image of Gotl to others. The man who hoped the longest is the man who lived the longest. He could have the most fruitful life. Christian life is the power which would give them an undying hope. A Glimpse Of The Divine!

With such a power they could see more of God's plan of life than the immediate circle of their experiences.' In history, the man of hope, who had seen the witness of God in everything —even when the clouds were darkest—had pre- vailed. Such were the prophets of Israel. A bunch of flower,-; might be valued by one man at .sixpence a bunch. Another might find their value in the fact that they gave to him a revelation of God—a glimpse of the Divine! The great thing was to find the true values in life. The most important thing was not what pro- gress the world had made—what work man hath done, but rather they must train themselves to find in those things a witness of the Divine. and give thanks for the work, which God had permitted them to do, for the harvest which He had permitted them to reap. The choir rendered the anthem "Thou visiteth the earth."

div.head: Successful Social Gathering.
div.p: Successful Social Gathering.

The festival was continued. on Monday even- ing by a successful social gathering. The at- tendance was good, and the gathering was pre- sided over by the Rev. C. I'. Pitt. All excel- lent musical programme was provided by the Misses Ilipkiss and M. Jones, and Messrs. .1. Hannan and T. Attwell, whose singing was greatly appreciated, many encores being requested. Mr. A. Dutton proved himself an elocutionist of no mean order. The accom- panist was Mr. B. Hannan. The members of the Brotherhood were responsible for the pro- gramme, and the Ladies' Sewing Class provided the refreshments. Thanks were expresse4 to those organisations. The fruit and f!owers used in decorating the church were subsequently dis- tributed amongst the sick.

div.head: ALL SAINTS' MISSION CHURCH.
div.p: ALL SAINTS' MISSION CHURCH.

The harvest thanksgiving services were held in the above church on Thursday, October 20th, and last Sunday afternoon and evening. The church was tastefully decorated by the lady workers. The preacher on Thursday was the Rev. F. W. Lloyd, of, St. Matthew's, Bolton. The anthem "The eyes of all wait upon Thee" was rendered by the choir, the soloist being Mr. Charles Bennett. The preacher on the Sunday afternoon was the Rev. John Martin, curate of St. Peter's, and in the evening the Rev. Edward Downham. At the evening service the choir gave the anthem "Ye shall dwell in the land." The soloists were Miss L. Bennett and Mr. Walter Wright. The congregations were .ex- ceedingly good and the collections above the average. The gifts of fruit, flowers and vege- tables were distributed amongst the sick and poor of the district.

div.head: "NI THE COURT
div.p: "NI THE COURT
AL FRESCO SLUAIBERER.
Says He Came To Town To Enlist.

- - - At the Borough Police Court on Saturday morning, before Mr. E. T. Fairclough (pre- siding), Alderman Alderman Tinnion and Messrs. A. J. Jolley and T. Pemberton, Michael Gallagher, of no fixed abode, was charged with sleeping out without visible means of subsistence. His defence was that he was coming to Warrington to join the Army. When hsked why he had not enlisted, he replied "I have never been caught sleeping out before." The Chief Constable said that the learned Clerk believed that they had a capture is a recruit, • but, the man had had an awful long while to think it over. The Chairman (to the prisoner); How long is it since you tried to enlist before? Prisoner: I think it was last Spring.
He was committed for seven days, the Clerk observing that Ile could enlist when he came out?
"A LESSON TO HER."
Another Chance For Forgetful Mother.

At Tuesday's Borough Police Court a youngish Af_oman, dressed. in mourning, appeared .further to answer a charge of having been drunk whilst in • charge of a child, to which Charge she had pleaded guilty at a previous sitting of the Court.

Mr. Laws, the police court missioner and, pro- bation officer, told the Bench—which consistEd of Councillor H. Roberts (in the chair), and Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes, J. Rymer Young and T. Locker—that the woman had kept off the drink ever since the case was adjourned, and her home was now in a much better state than It was before. The prosecution had been a les- son to her. _ _ _
The Chief Constable asked. under the circum- stances, to be • allowed to withdraw the prose- cution,' or for a further adjournment until the last Tuesday in December. The adjournment was granted.

div.head: UNDESIRABLE CUSTOMER.
div.p: UNDESIRABLE CUSTOMER.
Woman Who Got Drunk And Smacked Constable.

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, Mary • Jones, of no settled abode, was charged with having been drunk and refusing to quit the Baths Hotel when .requested to .do .so, and further with having assaulted Acting-Sergeant Thomas Clark whilst in the execution of his .cluty.—The prisoner pleaded guilty to the charge of drunkenness, but denied the assault. Miss Gittens, the licensee of the. hotel, stated that the prisoner on Saturday entered the bar ' .of the hotel in a drunken condition. Witness's sister, who was in charge of the bar at the time, sent for witness, who refused to serve the woman and requested her to leave the premises. Prisoner declined to do so. She used foul lan- guage and witness had to send for a policeman, who, with: the greatest difficulty, put her out- side. Her conduct was disorderly in the ex- treme. _ _

div.head: Scene in the Bar
div.p: The Scene in the Bar

Acting-Sergeant Clark said be was called to the hotel at 7.30 in the evening .and there saw the prisoner in a drunken condition. Several times he asked her to leave the premises quietly, but she rekused to do so. Witness walked to- wards the door for the purpose of opening it to vut her out and she came_ at him like a mad- woman, striking him in the face, throwing her- self on the floor and kicking him about the legs. Eventually lie got her into the street, and she continued her disorderly conduct all the way down to the Police Station. Tie had to obtain the assistance of a civilian. Prisoner's lan- guage was most disgraceful. Miss Gittens, re-called, said she saw prisoner strike the officer and struggle with him. Prisoner had nothing to say "except that she did not strike the officer at all." Not the First Time.

The Chief Constable said that the prisoner Was a comparative stranger to'Warrington. On April 11th last she was sent to prison for four- teen days' hard labour, without the option of a fine, for being drunk and disorderly, and she was also before that Court the previ6u,i year Apparently she got into trouble every time she came to Warrington. When she was in the Police Station the row she "kicked up" and the language she used were simply shocking. Prisoner was ordered three months' hard labour, and, as she left the dock. She shook her fist at the police • witnesses and shouted out,. "Curse the liars !"

div.head: "ONLY SNEEZE!) ! "
div.p: "ONLY SNEEZE!) ! "
Charge Against _Hippodrome Attendant
Dismissed.
At •Tuesday's Borough Police Court Arthur Caterall, of 21, Canterbury-street, Warrington, was summoned for assault by Fun. Lightfoot, of Dudley-street. -

Mr. Arthur Browne, who appeared for the complainant, said that his client was an insur- ance agent and -that the defendant was an at- tendant in the circle at the Hippodrome. On the night of Tuesday of last week complainant, with two friends, attended the "second house" at the Hippodrome. Just as the "star" turn had finished complainant and two friends were on the point of coming ofit when defendant said to him, "I have told you chaps before !" What he meant Complainant did not know, for he and his friends had no idea, for they. had been guilty of no disorderly conduct whatever. Lightfoot asked him what was the matter, and he replied "Well, you - are sneezing !" to which Lightfoot replied "I can't help that; I have a cold." Without further ado the defendant got hold of

Lightfoot and pushed him down the stairs, fol- lowing him up. When complainant got round the bend of the stairs defendant twisted his collar and said, "I will choke you," adding some bad words. Lightfoot had given no cause what- ever for such treatment; in fact, the attendant was mistaking the conduct of some other man for that of the prosecutor. Apology Asked For.

Complainant spoke to defendant, saying, "You ought to apologise for what you have done to me !" Defendant retorted, "Oh, you get on; I hear that tale every night." There- upon defendant put himself into a fighting atti- tude, and the complainant ran towards the stage door at the back of the Hippo- drome. Defendant ran after him and deliber- ately gave him a blow in the region of the heart,. knocking him down and rendering him uncon- scious for five or six minutes. He was lifted up and had to be taken home in a Gorsey-lane 'bus. Subsequently Dr. McKee saw him and ordered him complete rest; indeed, Dr. McKee would certify that the assault was a most brutal one. In fact, complainant was suffering that day from a bad heart attack , and was hardly fit to be out. .

Lightfoot, giving evidence, bore out his soli- citor's statement, adding that he and his friends were perfectly sober. and gave the defendant no cause for complaint. Answering Mr. Steel, who was for the defence, he denied that defendant -complained to him. "Do you not admit," asked Mr. Steel, "that you were asked to leave the theatre in conse- quence of your abominable conduct?" "That's a perfect lie !" replied the witness. "I put it to you that he only did his duty in putting you out?"—" Ridiculous !"
- And that you were under the influence of drink?—Ridiculous. "Is It Bother You Want?"

Edward Smith, a hairdresser, • carrying on business in Orford-lane, denied that the com- plainant was guilty of any disorderly behaviour in the theatre, and added that "after the show,'" when complainant spoke to defendant, the latter said, "Is it bother you want?" to which the complainant replied, "No; I want satisfaction and not bother !"

A witness named Garnett, who is employed by the Whitecross Company, and who was with the complainant on the evening in question, gave corroborative evidence. For the defence, Mr. Steel contended that the defendant was only doing his duty in putting complainant out of the place—he was only studying the comfort of the other patrons of the house. . Lightfoot was in an argumentative mood, and he gaid, `f I'll wait for you !" And he did so! He wanted to create a bother. He •got hold of 'defendant by the 'mackintosh twice, and defendant said, "Leave me alone! I won't argue with you! I simply did my duty !" It was all a fable to say that the complainant was struck in the mouth, or was knocked down; the defendant committed no assault at all. •

div.head: Defendant's Version.
div.p: The Defendant's Version.

Defendant, who said he had worked at the Hippodrome for six and a half years, stated that complainant and his two friends were standing at the barrier behind the circle bar. Witness heard a noise and received complaints from members of the audience, as a result of which he went to complainant and his two com- panions and spoke to them All he said was, "Just be quiet in the corner, please!" About ten minutes afterwards witness heard another noise, and again went to defendants, remarking, "If this occurs again you will have to go out- side !" When the lights were turned down, in order that the pictures might be shown, witness thought that the trouble might happen again, and so he walked up to the defendant and his companions for the purpose of ascertaining which was the actual offender. Just then Light- foot gave vent to a.yell, which could be heard throughout the whole house. As witness was about to speak to him and his companions, Smith kicked complainant's foot. Witness said, "You have created enough disturbance to-night. I shall watch you when you come in here again —in fact, I shall stop you, especially you," meaning Lightfoot Complainant said he only ,sneezed, and used objectionable language to witness. He replied, "We Cannot have this con- duct; you had better go outside." Lightfoot refused to leave, and witness had to force him down the first flight Of steps. . He struggled and shouted, ' " Smithy ! Smithy !" and his friend followed. Complainant refused to go out, and witness took him to the street, where Light- foot said he would wait for him (defendant).
"I Will Show You!"

Smith came back to the theatre after defend- ant had been put out and said, "I am sorry that this has occurred. I apologise for myself." He (defendant) told Smith that he was not con- cerned, and Smith remarked, "Well, I apolo- gise for my friend if he is not man enough to do so." The three men were waiting for witness when he left the theatre-. Lightfoot wanted to argue with him, but witness said he was not there to argue, but simply to do his duty, and commenced to walk away. Lightfoot more than once attempted to pull him back by the coat remarking, s" You have had a drop too much; I will show you!" He assumed a fighting atti- tude, and witness prepared himself for trouble. Complainant, however, ran up an entry, and Garnett ran up Bridge-street. Complainant fell down and Smith helued him up. Mr. Percy C. Dendy and Acting-Selgeant Whitby then came on the scene.

div.head: Left Because of the Noise.
div.p: Left Because of the Noise.

Elizabeth Monaghan, of 35, Sharp-street, one of the survivors of the ill-fated 'Ss. Hesperian, torpedoed by the Germans, stated that she heard Lightfoot make objectionable noises to- wards the end of the performance, and in conse- quence of the noise she was not able to enjoy the entertainment, and came out before it was over.

Samuel Crawford, of 19, Chester-road, also declared he heard an objectionable noise, evi- dently coming from either the complainant or his friends, and added that it took the atten- tion of the audience off the turn that was then proceeding. Percy Charles Dendy, of Knutsford-road, bore out Mr. Steel's statement as to what took place in the street, and said he took Lightfodt to be rather intoxicated.
The Bench, without retiring, dismissed the case.

div.head: "AN OLD TRICK."
div.p: "AN OLD TRICK."
How Railway Company Have Been
Defrauded Fr Years.

When charged at the Borough Police Court 1 on Thursday with travelling on the railway without a ticket with the intention of defraud- ing the London and North-Western Railway Company, Charles Ainslie, photographer, 2,. lialifax-street, .Warrington, pleacted not guilty. Mr. Arthur Browne, who prosecuted on be- half of the Railway Company, said that the' offence was what he might call an old trick. On Wednesday, September 15th, the defendant took a return ticket from Arpley Station to Latchford and travelled by the 2.55 train. He went on to Heatley, gave up his ticket and paid fivepence excess fare. The ticket collector had noticed him do this many times and be- came suspicious. He was watched by a porter from Heatley, and when he arrived at Arpley. he gave up the return half from Latchford. Similar tricks, added Mr. Browne, had been going on for 36 years.. .
- Miss Mary Tim'perley, a clerk at Heatley Station, gave evidence supporting this state- ment.
Watched the Defendant.

S. J. Rutter, porter at Heatley Station, stated that on receiving instructions he watched the defendant, who left Heatley by the 6.37 train for Warrington. At Arpley Station the de- fendant gave up the return half from Latch- ford. The witness questioned the defendant, who said that he had intended to pay the excess.

Evidence was also given by Miss Mason, clerk at Arpley Station, and by Sergeant Hewitt, of the London and North-Western Railway Company's police. For his defence, defendant pleaded that he had been worried lately. He had lost a son in the Navy and another had been badly"gassed" in France. He had been greatly upset by these deaths and his nerves became, unstrung. That afternoon he drank some brandy, and as he had been a teetotaler for some years, he was greatly upset. He had never been in a Police Court before. The defendant maintained that he had not the slightest .intention of de- frauding the railway company. The Chairman Said that the Bench greatly
sympathised with the defendant, but it was clear that he had no excuse for any form of fraud. He would be fined 20s. •

div.head: BRUTAL ASSAULT.
div.p: A BRUTAL ASSAULT.
Man Sent To Gaol For Ferocious
Attack On NAToman.

When Patrick Murray, a labourer, of 55, 'Oliver-street, appeared before the Borough magistrates on Tuesday in:Er:ling further to answer a charge of unlawfully wounding Harriet Senior, of 3, Six Houses, Dallam-lane, on Sun- day, October 17th. Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for him and asked that the charge be 'reduced to one of aggravated assault, announcing that if that were done his client would plead guilty. • The Bench acquiesced, and the charge , was accordingly reduced. The case for the prosecution, as detailed at the previous hearing, was that prisoner went to the house where the woman lives with her father—who is blind—and her mother. She resented a remark he made and he assaulted her, pulling her about by the hair and kicking her in the face. She shouted and screamed, but found that he had locked the downstairs door, with the result that her relatives were unable to come to her assistance. Prisoner subse- quently went away and the woman was assisted to the Infirmary by a number of young men. Drink Again.

On behalf of the prisoner, Mr. Steel said that the man and woman concerned had been living together on and off for twO years and the man had always treated her kindly until she trans- ferred her affections to a soldier who came over on leave. Prisoner was, not unnaturally, very jealous, and whilst under the influence of drink he went to the house and asked the woman about the soldier. She would not answer him, but, instead, laughed at him and, unfortun- ately, he did assault her. He 'Would admit that he dragged her off the sofa and hit her several times, but he did not admit kicking her. He trusted that the Bench would deal with him as lenienly as they possibly could. Mr. J. Rymer Young, who presided over the Bench, described the assault as a most brutal one, and as one of which any man ought to be ashamed. He would have to go to prison with hard labour for four months, and he might think himself very lucky that he was not sent for the full term.

div.head: SEPARATED!
div.p: SEPARATED!
Husband Who Left Home And Never Came Back.
Elizabeth Thompson, 16, Heaton-square, applied at the Warrington Borough Police Court on Friday for a separation order from her hus- band, Wm. Thompson, on the ground of deser- tion.
The applicant said that her husband came home the worse for drink on October 15th and commenced to abuse the children. He left the house the same day, and had never been there since.
Mr. T. S. Steel, who defended, admitted the desertion, and pleaded that the husband had gone away in consequence of the applicant's drunken habits.
An order for 7s. 6d. a week was granted.

div.head: DISAPPOINTED "SURER."
div.p: DISAPPOINTED "SURER."
Charged With Smashing Window
‘‘,7hen Refused:

On Friday, befdre Aldermen Bolton (presid- ing), Smethurst and Evans, and Messrs. S. Wright, A. J. Jolley and W. Furness, George Donnelly, a stranger to Warrington, was remanded until Monday on a charge of wilfully breaking five panes of glass at the works of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, thereby doing damage to the amount of ss. From the evidence it appeared that he was casually employed by the firm, and on Thursday afternoon applied for a " sub " from one of the under-managers. He had only worked an hour and a half, and had left his work. On the re- quest being refused, he picked up a clinker and smashed the windows.

div.head: NINE-YEAR-OLD
div.p: NINE-YEAR-OLD
Boy-Offender 'Who Tried To Escape
From Lock-Up.

At the Borough Police Court on Friday a boy, aged nine years, was ()barged with breaking and entering the lock-up shop of Wilfred Burgess, newsagent and stationer, 761, Knutsford-road, on October 27th, and stealing therefrom 18s. 11d.

The Chief Constable that that for some time the Director of Education had had the boy under his supervision. On Wednesday the boy and two younger brothers were sent by their mother to school. Instead of going there, how- ever, they went to Grappenhall, and returned at about 12 o'clock. Shortly after one o'clock the boy went to the shop of Mr. Burgess and gained admittance by taking down a protection which was against the window. He then rifled the till. The shop had been closed and left. It seemed that the boy then went down town and made numerous purchases, the articles he bought including torchlights, sweets and cakes. Altogether he spent about 4s. Gd.
Stayed Out All Night.

At night he went into the Latchford district and stayed in an ashpit. He was found by a workman and taken home to his mother at about three o'clock in the morning. The mother, on searching the boy's pockets, found 12s. 11d. She reported the matter to Mr. Moore Murray., the director of education.

• The Chief Constable went on to tell of the conduct of the by whilst in the cells. He said that one of the officers heard a movement in the detention-room and on asking the boy what he was doing, was told that the form had been placed nearer the pipes because it was warmer. Later another noise was heard, and on going into the room the officer found a chair on the top of the form. It was quite evident, concluded the Chief Constable, that the boy was making an attempt to reach the fanlight and effect an escape in that way. • The boy was remanded for seven ,days.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.. F.C.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.. F.C.
Resuscitation Of Club With A Fine
Record.

It will be welcome and very interesting news to the many followers and supporters of the Great Sankey F.C. to learn that the club has been restarted, with their heath' uart?rs at the Rose Inn, Hood-lane, aad a very I,,iitable ground has been obtained to play upon. Mr. E. Bullen, who is very well-known and popular throughout the district, is taking a 'very active interest in the club, and through his ipfluence there is every probability of some very at- tractive fixtures being decided on the Hood-lane enclosure.

At the present time fixtures are arranged with several Lancashire Combination. Clubs, includ- ing Hurst, Atherton and Altrineham. The cofrtmittee have been successful in obtaining the services of several well-known players in the town, including W. Siddall (Eccles Borough), Leah (Northwich Vies.), and Geo. Whitfield (Altrincham) ; these players assisted last week, and it is expected that Hay- ward (Manchester United and • Cartwright (Manchester City) will give their services. The following players of last season can be relied upon Glover, Ditchfield, T. Whit- field, E. Foster, T. -Ilidge, Kelley, F. Millington and probably 'Banner. From the above list the committee will be able to put a very strong team in the field, and one which should gain the con- fidence of the supporters of the club. The secretarial duties are again taken up by Mr. E. Clarke, Oakleigh, Great Sankey, who has had much to do with the successes gained by the club in the past three seasons, when the team has won the Widnes Alliance the War- rington and District League and , the Widnes Alliance alternately. Mr. E. Bullen is the treasurer and a very strong committee is being elected to ensure the successful management of the club.
People who are positive of their amiability are often hard to get along with. • Our bad qualities are hereditary. Our good ones are our very own.
When a man begins to feel his importance the rest of us begin to doubt it. The man who knows his limitations escapes many a nasty jar that the other fellow doesn't.

div.head: INTERRIEDIATE LEAGUE.
div.p: INTERRIEDIATE LEAGUE.

The Intermediate League results last Satur- day were as follows St. James', 3 points; St. Thomas', 3 points. Heathside, 16; Wycliffe, 0. Beamont, 7; St. Mary's, 5. Parochial, 3; Sacred Heart, 0. Rylands's Recs., 12; Whitecross, 3, Bolton, 5; Silver-street, 5.

div.head: RYLANDS'S RECS. v. WHITECROSS.
div.p: RYLANDS'S RECS. v. WHITECROSS.

This match was played on the Gorsey-lane enclosure. Both teams we well represented. Dumbell winning the toss, izy:ands's elected to play with the wind in their favour. White- cross kicked off, Archer re!urning. Rylands's forwards took the ball with them and Mulvey scored at the corner. The goal-kick failed. Rylands's scored from the drop out, and again attacked, but Whitecross saved. The home team again attacked, Archer scoring a good try. Half-time arrived with the score :—Rylands's, 3 tries, 9 points; Whitecross, nil. Rylands's began the second half with the wind in their favour. Whitecross played better and kept their opponents on tile defence, only the play of Archer saving the home side. White- cross persevered and their efforts were rewarded with a good try, the goal-kick failing. This aroused Rylands's. and Sutton scored. Dumbell failed at goal. Time arrived with the score :—Rylands's, 4 tries, 12 points; Whitecross, I try, 3 points. SILVER-STREET DRAW WITH BOLTON. Silver-street and Bolton met on the Wilders- pool ground in the presence of a fair-sized crowd.

Silver-street kicked off, and for a time play hovered in midfield, but eventually the Bolton men got into their stride, and for a time pressed most strenuously. The Silver-street lads, how- ever, by good defensive play, kept them at bay, and after a time managed to retaliate with an attack on their own. The game was played at a very fast pace. The Bolton boys managed to break away and the Silver-street fall-back Jailed to gather the ball properly, whereupon a Bolton forward managed to get control of it and dribbled it for a considerable distance along the touch-line and finished up by scoring a fine try at the corner. A magnificent goal was kicked from off the touch-line. In the second half the Silver-street forwards came away with a great rush', and several times the opposing three-quarters were not able to gather the ball quick enough, but, for long, always managed to rectify their mistakes in the nick of time. Silver-street kept on persevering and at last Callon scored a good try, and, in the doing thereof, was so badly injured that he had to leave the field and was unable to take further' part in the game. Ratcliffe converted Callon's try and thus made the scores equal at five points all, at which figure they stood when the game closed.

div.head: HEATHSIDE TROUNCE WYCLIFFE.
div.p: HEATHSIDE TROUNCE WYCLIFFE.

The other game on the Wilderspoot ground on Saturday was between Ileathside Old Boys and Wycliffe Old Boys, and it proved to be a some- what one-sided affail. The Heathside lads were in great form and, from first to last, they did the bulk of the pressing; in fact, it was rarely indeed that the Wycliffians trot over the half- way line in the second half. They were lament- ably lacking in attack and. although their defence was energetic it proved to be ineff.?,etnal against the strenuous onslaughts made by their opponents. In the end the Heathsidians won by 16 points to nil. PAROCHIAL v. SACRED HEART.

On No. 3 Field, Victoria Park. Sacred Heart, the only team to register a try against the League • winners last year, came very near accomplishing the same feat again last week, aS the Parochial line was at times very hard pressed. If the Sacred Heart lads can only retain the same team there should not be many defeats to record.

Parochial played indifferently at times, and when favourably placed near the line were un- able to effect any good result. The play dur- ing the first half was always quick, and both lines were frequently visited. A cross-kick to the Parochial left-wing resulted in Challinor scoring the only points of the match. The goal- kick was a failure. The passing movements of the Parochial lads were excellent and once when the ball passed along their three-quarter line, the result must have ended in a certain try but for Baker (the Hearts left wing), who ran across and stopped the performance. Half-time came with the score 3 points to Soon after the interval play was carried near the Parochial line and Baker had hard lines near the corner. Brears and Clarke, the respective full-backs, kicked into each other's hand for fully five minutes. Brown receiving the ball altar a scuffle, passed to Broadhurst, .who was brought down near the Hearts' line. Both teams played a good, clean game, and when the whistle blew for time the _score ended in a victory for Parochial by 1 try to nil. YEAMONT JUNIORS v. ORFORD JUNIORS. Played on No. 2 ground. Following up their victory of 29-0 on the 9th inst. over Orford Juniors, Beamont again accounted for them in the return match last Saturday, winning by 8-6. Anderton and Armitage scored tries for Belmont, the latter converting one. Farrell went over for Orford, but the try was disallowed. Bibby and Johnson scored for Orford. Result: Beamont Juniors, 8 points ; Orford Juniors, 6 points. .
