div.head: ENTHUSIAST.
div.p: THE ENTHUSIAST.

It was after the football game. Amid the plaudits of 50,000 enthusiastic spectators the full-back of the victorious team had been carried from the field on the shoulders of his joy-crazed cohorts. He was the hero of the hour. By his unaided efforts defeat had been turned into glorious victory within one minute of the call of time. _

_ Ile was in the hands of his rubbers when his chum entered the dressing room. "I had the pleasure, of sitting next to your best girl during the game,'; said his chum. "Did she enthuse over my playing ?" askikl the star full-back with that beautiful modesty so characteristic of the modern gridiron gladi- ator.

_ " Well--er—" replied the chum, not without a certain hesitancy, "when you made your run for the last try, and the flags were flying, and we were all yelling ourselves into a state of idiocy, and everybody felt sure of your place on the International team, she turned to me and said: "Hasn't he beautiful hair?"

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

In the Warrington and District League there was only one game decided last week, and this was on the King and Queen ground, where the Paddington team gained an easy victory over the Elmwood Congregationalists.

The Great Sankey F.C. opened their season's fixtures on their new enclosure in Hood-lane with a friendly game against the British Aluminium F.C., the proceeds of the " gate " being devoted to charitable purposes. The home team was a very strong one, and obtained a very easy victory by .eleven goals against one.

In the Warrington and District Junior League fixture between St. Elp.hin's and the ittockton Heath Scouts a very keen game was antlcipated, as both teams have been doing well and won all their engagements. Unfortunately for the Scouts, they were not able to place their b-zst eleven in the field owing to several of their players being on the sick list; and the .game proved to be all'in favour of St. Elphin's, who eventually ran out easy winners, and enabled the Saints to strengthen their position at the head of the League chart.

The Orford JuniorS have now settled down to their game, and ,are going strong. On Saturday their opponents,.the Padgate C.L.8., were-easily defeated, and the Juniors are now welt placed in the table, having won all their games.
Rowley United had their reputation badly damaged last week when they were in opposition to the Fairfield Juniors. It must have been their day off.

The Latchford Cadets have strengthened their ranks by the inclusion of Daniefs, who has been transferred from .the Mersey Juniors. They gained their first victory at the expense of the Bewsey Albions.
The Mersey Juniors are not praying up to their reputation, and at the present time they have played four games, and have not been able to claim a victory.
The Padga,te C.L.B. occupy the bottom' pbsi- tion on the dub chart, and on their present form they wilT take a let of removing:
Keep your eye on St. Elphin's for the' cham- pionship. Boyle is their star artiste. He per- formed the. "hat trick" last week against the Scouts.
On Saturday the Seouts were badly scouted by the Elphin's.
No drawn games up to date in the Junior League. •

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
ELM WOOD CONGREGATIONALISTS v. PADDINGTON.

These teams met in the above competition on ,the King and Queen ground. The home cap- tain won the toss and Rothwell set the ball in motion for the visitors, who at once invaded tilt home territory, Hazelaine clearing a dan- gerous rush, in fine style. The home forwards broke away and a good opportunity was spoiled by Kendrick getting into an off-side position. Both.teams having now got into their stride, the game was very fast and keenly contested, but the visitors proved more p_recise in their move- ments, and Rothwell opened their account with a splendid shot. The Congregationalists retali- ated in stirring fashion, and the scores were made equal with a shot that Horrocks had no chance of saving. Both teams became excited, and many opportunities of scoring were missed. Weak clearances by Holmes were nearly disas- trous for his side, Horrocks proving equal to the emergency. The visitors became aggressive, and after Several futile shots. Taylor obtained the lead with a hard drive. The Congregation- alists made several attempts to equalise, but failed to penetrate the visitors' defence. Half- time: Paddington, 2 goals; Elmwood Congre- gationalists, 1 goal. The second portion opened in favour of the visitors, and in a few minutes Rothwell in- creased the lead. After good midfield play by the Congregationalists their final shots were weak, and Horrocks had not much difficulty in clearing. Derbyshire scored the fourth goal for the visitors. Play was now confined to the home half and off-side was .very frequent. The home gbalkeeper was making some good saves. War- ren, taking a corner kick, placed it so well that it went between the posts before being played by a second player, and the point was not allowed. Rothwell, Warren, Horrocks, Garnett and Derbyshire were the pick for the visitors, and Roberts, Wells and Kendrick did well for the home team. ,
Result: Paddington, 4 goals; Elmwood Con- gregationalists, 1 goal.

div.head: ALUMINIUM JOIN THE LEAGUE.
div.p: ALUMINIUM JOIN THE LEAGUE.

At the monthly meeting of the Warrington and District League, held on Wednesday at the Lion Hotel, Mr. E. Bate presiding, the Secre- tary read the application for membership from the British Aluminium Co. F.C. The applica- tion was accepted and fixtures were ararnged.

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCHES.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCHES.

GREAT SANKEY v. BRITISH ALUMINIUM. The above teams met on Saturday in the opening fixture of the Great Sankey Club on their new ground in Hood-lane. The home club were strongly represented and the visitors were at 'full strength. The following players turned out under the control of Referee Woods:—

Great Sankey: Brindle;-Glover, Kelley; Mil- lington, G. Whitfield, Leah; Illidge, T. Whit- field, Siddall, Ditehfield,and Foster. Aluminium: Bond ;Foster, Northall ; Wells, Davis, Bamford; Walker, Titehard, Llewellyn. Edwards and Banner.

Before a fairly good crowd the home captain won the toss and played up the slope, with the wind in his favour. The visitors set the ball in motion, and the home team, gaining possession, were soon in front of the visitors' goal, where Foster conceded a corner in attempting to clear 1 under heavy pressure. Illidge placed wide. ' After even exchanges in front of .the visitors' goal, E. Eoster was given off-side when well placed. From the free k kick the visitors made several good attempts to break away, but were well held by the home backs, and were soon act- ing on the defensive. T.'"Whitfield opened the home score, after ten minutes' play. The visit- ors now made a raid into the home quarters, when Edwards shot past the post. Operations were quickly in front of the visitors' goal, when Ditchfield scored the second point. Even play followed, in which the visitors showed up well against their more experienced opponents, and then their defence broke down, the backs mak- ing many misikicks, and Bond was called upon to clear some strong shots. Eventually Siddall beat him with a thirty yards'. shot, and directly after the same player missed a very easy chance. G. Whitfield headed. through from a corner kick, and a few minutes later increased the lead with a ldw shot. Illidge added a sixth goal from what appeared to be an off-side posi- tion, the defenders' appeal not being upheld. Just before the interval the visitors made an attack on the home goal and put the ball be- tween the uprights, the point being disallowed for •off-side. Half-time: Great Sankey, 6 goals; British Aluminium, nil.

The opening exchanges in the second half were in favour of the home team, and after an attack on their goal had been repulsed by Fos- ter, the visitors were seen to-better advantage. From some good . passing movements Walker caused Brindle to handle for the first time in the game. After this brief attack the game was again in the visitors' half. Siddall scoring. The same player added to the score from a corner kick. The visitors made another attempt to capture the home citadel. Titchard shooting straight for goal, brought Brindle to his knees to effect a clearance. Then Siddall and Ditch- field added goals in quick succession. Banner was playing a very strong and individual game

for the visitors at this time and caused Kelley to concede a corner, from which Llewellyn scored for the visitors. Ditchfield again re- sponded for the home team, and at the call of time they were easy winners, the final score being: Great Sankey, 11 goals; British Aluminium, 1 goal. EMMANUEL INSTITUTE v. WALTON.

Played on Victoria Park. The visiting team included Cartwright, of Manchester City, as centre-forward. The opening exchanges were mostly in favour of the home team, who were being assisted by the wind. The Emmanuel for- wards swept down on the opposing backs, and after a good centre from the right wing, Oakes secured, and, after beating the full-back, scored with a grand shot, giving the goalkeeper no chance to save. For some minutes the home team attacked, and then Cartwright raced away, and with a Ede drive just missed scoring. Wal- ton pressed hard, but the home backs cleared splendidly. The Walton forwards were play- ing well, but the good form of Crozier and Parr kept them out. Emmanuel forwards repeatedly broke away, but just as often were they hunted back. Cartwright put in a clever piece of play, and just as he was about to shoot, T. Knight, the home goalkeeper, dived at his feet, and made a grand save. The game was full of interest, and Booth made an unexpected rush, but An- drews stopped him, and put the ball well up the field, where Gregory fastened on to it and put in a fine centre. Siddall's shot was again saved by Knight. The pace was fairly fast, and W. Knight made good progress on the right wing, but Gosling checked him. Towards the interval the visitors were put on the defensive. Half- time: Emmanuel, 1 goal; Walton, nil. The visiting forwards, with the wind in their favour, made tracks for the home goal, but could get no further than the full-backs. The Walton right wing dashed away, and lifted the ball right in front of the home goal, where Siddall and Cartwright tried hard to score, but the home goalkeeper effected a fine clearance. After a quarter of an hour's play in the second half Emmanuel went further ahead, for Oakes took the opportunity of a poor kick by the op- posing full-back, shot hard and put the ball, out of the goalkeeper's reach. Walton attacked vigorously, and only the sound defensive work of the home backs kept them at bay. Play was exciting, and Walton were awarded a penalty through Crozier handling, and Cartwright was entrusted with the kick. He shot hard, but Knight got down to the ball and saved, but the leather went loose. Cartwright again tried, but to the home team's delight Knight made a beautiful save. A few minutes afterwards they were awarded another penalty, and this time Andrews took the kick, but Knight again saved his side by getting ..the ball just as the visiting forwards were pushing him through. Walton were now playing well, and Cartwright was dis- tributing the ball in excellent fashion. Both sets of backs were tested in turn, and on one occasion Oakes put in a good centre. The for- wards overran the ball and a good chance was missed. Towards the end the game was very exciting, and after a fine centre by Cartwright, the visiting left inside scored with a beautiful shot. Emmanuel were put on the defensive for the remainder of the time, and when the whistle blew for time, had won a hard-fought game by two goals to one. T. Knight, the home goalkeeper, was the out- standing player for the home team, for the way in which he dealt with the shots from Cart- wright was a treat to watch.
WARRINGTON SECONDARY SCHOOL 2nd v. LYMM GRAMMAR SCHOOL 2nd.

Played on Wednesday afternoon at Padgate. Warrington kicked off, and at the end of three minutes Bennett scored for them. Barton added a second, and other points came rapidly. Half-time: Warrington 9 goals; Lymm, nil. In the second half Lymm -scored three well-de- served goals, but Warrington were the better side by far, and when the whistle went the score read: Warrington, 15 goals; Lymm., 3 goals. The scorers for the winners were Bennett (4), Elwell and Barton (3), Jones (2), Simeock, Critchley and Farrington. Mr. Hoyle was the referee.

div.head: tRRINGTOI-N & DISTRICT ASSOCIATION JUNIOR LEAGUE.
div.p: tRRINGTOI-N & DISTRICT ASSO- CIATION JUNIOR LEAGUE.

Results to October 23rd. Goals. P. W. L. D. F. A. P. St. Elphin's Orford Juniors Stockton Heath Scouts 4 3 1 0 7 9 6 Howley United Fairfield Juniors Bewsey A.F.O Bewsey Albions ' Latchford C.C.3 1 2 0 3 8 2 Mersey Juniors Padgate C.L.B.
ST. ELPHIN'S v. STOCKTON HEATH SCOUTS.

On the Arpley ground. Unfortunately the .visitors were not able to -put their best team out owing to sickness. The visitors won the toss and the home for- wards kicked off with the wind in their favour. The home team were soon aggressive, and forced an unproductive corner. From the goal- kiek the "Saints'" returned to the attack, and an accurate Centre from the left was handled by _Johnson in front of goal. Boyle was entrusted with the kick and he made no mis- take with a- hard and low drive. From the centre-kick the Scouts made a raid on the " Saints' " goal, but were quickly forced back to defend their own -citadel, and after several corner-kicks bad been successfully cleared, a miskick by Hampson allowed Boyle to nip in and score his second goal. The Scouts, were still on .the .defensive, and further goals were scored by Hough and Sankey. Half:time:—St. Elphin's, .4 goals; Scouts, nil. On resuming, the Scours had the wind behind Ahem, and they made a spirited dash on the Saints' ,'< goal, a fine attempt by Haslam 'being just wide of the uprights. Keeping up the pressure, the Scouts were unlucky with several 'fine efforts, after Which they were gradually forced -back to their own defensive area, and HampsOn. receiving a warni shot, only partially cleared, the ball rebounding through the goal off Morgan. The " Saints " further increased their lead from a free kick close in, Boyle con-
verting, the final score being :—St. Elphin's, 0 goals; Stockton Heath Scouts, nil.
MERSEY JUNIORS v. BEWSEY.

On the Lovely-lane ground. The game opened very quietly, and after a brief visit had bees paid to each end Thompson opened the score for the Merseyites. The visitors continued tO have the best of the exchanges, but the home defenders played a sound game, and would not yield again. A few minutes before the interval the home forwards rallied, attacked very strongly, and succeeded in equalising. Half- time :—One goal each. The home team gave a much better display on resuming, and gained the lead after five minutes' play, and directly after Roylance in- erea3e4 the lead for the Bewseyites. After a, spell of give and take play the home team again asserted themselves aml Roylance 5....,red. As the close of play was drawing near the visi- tors made another effort and gained a penalty- kick, from which Smith scored their second goal. Result :—Bewsey, 4 goals; Mersey Juniors, 2 goals.

div.head: ORFORD JUNIORS v. PADGATE C.L.B.
div.p: ORFORD JUNIORS v. PADGATE C.L.B.

- - - - - - - - On the ground of the former. From the kick- off the Juniors soon showed their superiority. After fifteen minutes' play Belshaw was injured and could not take any further part in the game. Half-time :—Orford Juniors, 4 goals; Padgate C.L.8., nil. The second portion was mainly in favour of the Juniors, and the game proved to be a very one-sided affair. Result :—Orford Juniors, 10 goals; Padgate C.L.8., nil.

BEWSEY ALBIONS v. LATCHFORD CADETS On the Arpley grdund. The visitors set the ball rolling and ttit once advanced towards the Cadets' goal, where faulty play by Jones nearly caused the downfall of his goal on two occasions. At the opposite end Walker made fte splendid attempts to lower the visitors' citadel. After a spell of even play in midfield, the Cadets again advanced and forced a corner- kick. The kick was not improved upon, but from the clearance Davenport made a fine return, from which Howard scored the Cadets' first goal. Encouraged by this success, the Cadets were soon swarming round the visitors' goal again, Howard heading against the cross- bar. The visitors now made a temporary raid on the home quarters, when Daniels cleared with a huge kick towards the visitors' goal, when the goalkeeper completely misjudged the ball and allowed it to pass between the poets. Half-time :—Latchford Cadets, 2 goals; Bewsey Albions, nil. The second half was evenly contested, both sides gaining several corner-kicks, which they failed to .ml‘rove upon. Snlith, the Cadets' centre-forward, made several individual efforts, but was defeated by the visitors' backs, whilst Miller indulged in some long shots. Result Latchford Cadets, 2 goals; Bewsey Albions, nil
FAIRFIELD JUNIORS v. HOWLEY UNITED

On the Orford-road ground, before a good company of spectators. The home team at once began to press, and at the end of 10 minutes' play England opened their account. The visi- tors replied with a strong attack on the home goal, and were unfortunate not to make the scores equal. From now to the interval the game was keenly contested, and each goal was attacked in turn. R. George scored a second goal just before fte whistle blew. Half-time:— Fairfield Juniors, 2 goals; Howley United. nil. From a scrummage in the second half in front of the United goal, England added the third goal. The visitors were unable to make any headway, while the home forwards added three more goals in quick succession. Result :—Fair- field Juniors, 6 goals; Howley United, nil.

The elements last week-end had the effect of stopping many from visiting their favourite fisheries, and those who made their journeys on Saturday-at noon had not much to boast about when they returned on Sunday evening. The condition of the weather spoiled sport all along the line. Chirk seems to be the best roaching ground at present. Mr. J. Sherratt was responsible for one last week scaling 11b., but we know of one crack angler who belongs to Ashton Centre who was there for three days without doing anything worth mentioning. Lately the canal from Llangollen Cefu, Chirk, and up to the prohibited length on the Main- waring estate, has been almost choked up with leaves, that made angling very difficult. The fresh we have had lately should improve mat- ters and also put a little colour in the different waters, especially the Gowy. This is what we have been waiting for during several weeks. Given fair conditions, the Gowy should yield better sport than it has done lately.

div.p: VOLUNTEER ORDERS.
SOUTII-WEST LANCS. VOLUNTEER
REGIMENT.
Warrington Company. • Headquarters: Drill Hall. Orders for the week ending November 7th :
Parades. Monday and Thursday. at 8 p.m. Company Dill and Route March. ,Saturday, November 7th, 3 p.m., Outpost Duty. Recruits' Class. Drill Nights, 8 p.m., Band Room.
Class Firing. . No 3 Section, Tuesday November 2nd, Drill Ilan, 7..30 pan.
Musketry. To-day, Range closed. Saturday, November 7th, 4.15 p.m., Muni- cipal Rifle Range.

Trench Digging. SPECIAL: To-day, at 2.30 p.m.; disperse 4.30 p.m.; westerly* side of the Old River. This Company, together with the Stock- ton Heath Company (Cheshire Regiment), will parade for instruction and practice in modern trench construction, under the supervision of one of the Staff from the Depot, lately returned from Flanders. If wet, Lecture at Headquarters.
MEMOS.
1. Area Commandant.—Mr. W. Peter Rylands is appointed Area Commandant from October 27th, and takes command of this Company from that date.

2. A move forward must now be 'made to bring the Company' to full strength, and a special appeal is issued to every Volunteer to make it a point of duty to canvass for new recruits. Old members are asked to rejoin and follow the excellent lead of one of its most Prominent townsmen. 3. As the offer of further assistance by the Depot Staff will be largely influenced by the number present on parade, every Volunteer that can must turn out.
Sandbags and spades, on loan, received at 4, Bridge Foot, or Headquarters.
THE VOLUNTEER TRAINING CORPS.

Mr. Cecil Harmsworth having asked the Under Secretary of State for War whether he can state what is the present strength of the Volunteer Training • Corps, and whether any arrangements have yet been made by the War Office for the employment of members of. this force on less important military duties that aro now being discharged by soldiers of the Regular and Territorial Armies, Mr. Tennant, in a written answer, says :—I understand that the membership of the corps affiliated to the Central Association amounts to 183,415, but it is be-
lieved that this is not by any means the com- plete return. The answer to the second part of the question is in the negative.

div.head: N.VTIONAL DUTY.
div.p: N.VTIONAL DUTY.
One Man In Ten Thousand !
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—nro months ago the Lord-Lieutenant of the County circularised the chief magistrates of the boroughs in the county, stating that the Lancashire Volunteer Brigade had been formed, and requested their assistance to bring about the formation 'of Volunteer Corps in their respective towns. St. Helens, Widnes and Warrington were grouped together, and the South-West Lancashire Regiment was formed, Warrington to act as the Headquarters Com- pany, a most important position. On Wednes- day, after due notification in the local Press, His Worship the Mayor presided over what was purported to be a town's meeting, to consider the best means of furthering the scheme, and also to appoint an area committee. It is computed that there are 6,000 men in the town eligible for this movement. Of that total, apart from officials and members of the local company, one man, and one alone out of that vast number attended. Gallant man! We salute you! This total failure of response is a studied insult to the intelligence of the band of earnest men, who, despite all obstacles, ridicule, and cold water theorists, have •struggled along at great personal sacrifice, preparing for eventu- alities that may possibly happen. It will be claimed that this movement is of no military value, and that with an unbroken Navy, valu- able time would be lost championing a worth- less cause. There is on the face of. it some justification for these claims, but let us go deeper into the question. Everybody places im- plicit confidence in our Navy, but we know that the unexpected has happened in many quarters of late, and it would be foolish to state that invasion was not possible, though highly improbable. Our Third Line Of Reserve.

There are 350,000 Volunteers in this country (15,000 in Lancashire alone), and taking the extraordinary margin of 80 per 'cent. unfit, leaves 70,000 men as a third line of reserve. There are many additional facts which one could write about which would be sufficient vindica- tion of the objects of the movement; but out weighing all these considerations the greatest factor of them all is the principle involved. Countless thousands of pounds are now being spent in bolstering up the Voluntary system, bands, posters, speeches, threats and cajolary are being used to induce men of the military age to join the Forces. Mostly violent Con- scriptionists are men over the military age, urging on the younger men to the great sacrifice in blood-soaked Flanders and 'Gallipoli, and denouncing them as slackers and shirker:3 if they do not join up.
Have Done With Cant.

Sir, let us have done with all this cant and humbug. The greater proportion of men over the military age physically fit are the t,r?ateit slackers in this country, and liken unto a, go me of bridge, ever ready to "leave it to your partner." What sacrifice do the major portion of these older men give in return? A few miserable luxuries less and volumes of empty verbiage of how to direct, control and end the war. Here they have an opportunity (one of many) of setting an example to the younger men, and they fail miserably. Appeal ,to them to put in a minimum of one hour's drill per month and it is treated as a personal favour and condescension to listen to you and end in failure. In this category can he placed the man who almost weeps because he is too old for the Colours. "Had he been five 7,-ears younger he would have gone long since!" Simple soul! Then the man who "if he join anything he will don the proper thing, khaki," and he joins nothing. One, "too busy with golf!" Shades of the brave lads lying in Flanders! Oh, the pity of it! Do not the casualty list and the silent grief reach you older men? Are you for ever going to sit round and. gossip like old women? It's up to you to do some little service to the country which protects you, so "do it now !"

To the members of the company to which I have the honour to belong, I say "Carry on, undaunted, the work which you have taken up, fortified by the faith that your efforts, however humble they may he, you are , following the dictates of your conscience, and that you are setting an example for others to follow."
BRASSARD.

div.head: WAR-FUND AUCTIVN.
div.p: WAR-FUND AUCTIVN.
How Nearly £lOO Was Raised
In Good Causes.

A sum closely approaching £lOO was realised in aid of the local War Funds by a novel sort of auction sale which was held in the Parr Hall on Thursday afternoon. The sale was novel in that all the almost-three-hundred " lots " offered to the many bidders and buyers were the gifts of local ladies and gentlemen, who were desirous of "doing their bit" to help along a real good cause. The goods were sold "under the hammer" by Mr. Herbert Johnson, the well-known local auctioneer, and his per- suasive tongue and business perspicacity re- sulted in over 0t95, being raised; a total which was, at one and the same time, a credit to the business abilities of the vendor and a testimony to the good sense and public spirit of the pur- chasers, who' entered completely into the spirit of the sale and realised that it was not a bargain-hunting sort of business, but an effort to help " Tommy " in his crucial work at the Fropt.

div.head: 'ALL SORTS AND CONDITIONSn OF 'GOODS.
div.p: 'ALL SORTS AND CONDITIONSn OF 'GOODS.

The articles sold were of infinite variety, ranging from choice china to the cabinets to hold and display the same, from utensils for the kitchen to pictures for the drawing-room or parlour; from—well, practically everything was on sale; everything, that is, that one could reasonably want for his home, save eatables. But stay, even eatables Nftere on sale, but not by the auctioneer. On the platform stood daintily-laid. tables and thereat daintily-attired ladies dispensed afternoon tea and other re- freshments to exhausted bidders, thus enabling them to reinvigorate at reasonable cost. The refreshments were provided by the Mayoress (Mrs. Peter Peacock), Mrs. Firth Lindley and Mrs. T. •Locker, and every cent. received for them went to swell the funds. At tea-time— for the sale lasted quite a long while—there was a rush for the tasty viands and the delect- able cup that cheers—and does not do the other thing!
THOSE WHO ORGANISED THE SALE.

The deserving objects that will benefit are the Red Cross Funds, at the Raddon Court and Thelwall Heys Hospitals, and the lands;o9k- the local Tobacco ~Fund for providing smokes for the wounded soldiers in the War- rington district; and the local Prisoners of War Fund, for the purchase of comforts for prisoners from the South Lancashire Regiment, who were residents of Warrington and district. The sale was organised by a representative committee consisting of the folloWing :—The Mayoress (Mrs. Peacock), Lady Crosfield, Lady Greenall, Mesdames Roscoe Brunner, E. G. Davies, Dodds, Fox, F. A. Frost, Henry Greenall, F. Lindlei", T. Locker, Lyon, Nicholson, C. E: Parker, J. C. Parr and ,Stewart Smith, and Miss Sylvia Broadbent; and the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), the Town Clerk (Mr.. J. Lyon Whittle), Alderman James Evans, Councillor Wilson, the Rev. Irvine Lister (lion. secretary), Colonel Simpson, and Messrs. A. Bottomley, J. J. Crosfield, J. Hewitt, T. Hewitt, H. S. Page, W. Peter Rylands, J. H. Smethurst, Herbert Johnson (lion. auctioneer), and J. Fairihurst (hon. treasurer). ,

div.head: MAYOR'S THANKS FOR DONORS.
div.p: MAYOR'S THANKS FOR DONORS.

The sale was opened by the Mayor, who humorously observed that though the usual printed conditions of sale were laid down, if anybody acquired an article for which he or she did not feel they had paid enough, they had the Mayoral permission to break the con- tralt•terms and pay as much more as they felt in dined to. Hearty thanks, his Worship added, were due to the whole of the donors of the articles sent for sale, and he was sure that they would never regret what they had done for the causes which that sale was designed to bene- fit. His Worship added that a wagonette sent for sale by Mr. Parker would be sold at the Stockton Heath Red Cross effort, and that a ' water-colour picture painted and given by Miss Broadbent was sold for £5 before it reached the hall. (Applause.) The sale was then proceeded with, Mr. John- son getting through his big task with his usual business-like promptitude and alacrity; prices, on the whole, being as satisfactory as could be expected.

div.head: ANOTHER WAR SALE NEXT WEEK.
div.p: ANOTHER WAR SALE NEXT WEEK.

So many gifts were received by the committee responsible for the promotion of the auction that it was found impossible to sell them all in the one afternoon and evening, and conse- quently Mr. Herbert Johnson is going to offer the unsold silver, silver-plate, china, pictures, &c., for sale in the Parr Hall at 7 o'clock on Wednesday evening next.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO SANKEY WIRE MILLS MANAGER.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO SANKEY WIRE MILLS MANAGER.

• "A Chip of the Old Block." Mr. John Houghton, chairman of the firm of Messrs. W. D. Houghton, and Co., Ltd., Sankey Wire Mills, in handing a presentation gold watch to Mr. John Forster, the manager, last Monday, said that gentleman's father preceded him as manager and worked for the firm many years. It was quite evident the son was a chip of the old block. He had now worked for the firm 43 years and they all appreciated the zeal, tact and true patriotism with which he had thrown himself into his work, espeCialli dur- ing the 'present national crisis. Mr. Ernest Houghton endorsed all that his brother had said. He was' pleased to say that Mr. Forster had won the esteem of the major- ity of all whom he came in contact with his genial courtesy, good judbment and fair con- sideration.

Mr. George Steeples, chairman" of the pre- sentation committee, spoke in pleasing terms of the manner in which the workmen had contri- buted to the fund, considering the; many calls that were being made upon people at present'. After referring to the pleasant manner that they had worked together, he expressed the hope that Mr. Forster might be given a long life to enjoy the wearing of the watch, and the • .9orl feeling of the directors, staff and workmen. Other speakers in praise of the recipient were Messrs. Saint, Graham and V% illiams. Mr. Forster acknowledged the gift and the good wishes of the givers in suitable terms. The watch bore the inscription: "Presented to Mr. John Forster by the Directors, staff and his workmen at Messrs. W. D. Houghton and Co„ Ltd., Warrington, as a token of respect. 4 lie gets little out of prayer who prays only October,l9ls." when he would get something. • Mr. Forster 's populapity was reflected by the number present who had contributed to the The average person can get more genuine joy coat of the watch, out of a grievance than out of a blessing.

div.head: Medical.
div.p: Medical.
CLEVER "LANCASHIRE LASSES"
AT THE 'HIPPODROME:

The principal attraction—amongst the many— provided at the Hippodrome this week is the "turn" given by the Little Lancashire Lasses, a bevy of delightful and youthful entertainers of the fair sex, who sing catchy songs and choruses as charmingly as they look—and that is saying quite a lot ! One of the most juvenile of the winsome sextet is a particularly promis- ing artiste.. and captivates the hearts of her audiences with her song about " Tommy "; whilst the dancing of the whole half-dozen is decidedly one of the features of a most excel- lent entertainment. The Little Lancashire Lasses are, no doubt, one of the best combina- tions of their kind "working the halls." The Poppescus provide a gymnastic "turn" that is by way of being' unique and every night the echo of the whole-hearted plaudits of the crowd follows them to their dressing-rooms. Their feats on the horizontal bars Lire as daring as they are clever; indeed, the trio are positive breath-catchers. Williams and Warden are a "merry and bright" and, withal, original pair of patterers—and to meet original patterers is something to be exceeding pleased about in these days, when even the newest joke seems to be growing whiskers. Wilf. Burnand delights with a clever character study of a Somerset rustic and most f. cleverly impersonates that quaintest of quaint comedians, George Formby, in one of his "latest and best." Levand is a smart mystery man and brings an excellent programme to a close amid enthusiastic ap- plause; whilst Cissie Lupin°, a pretty and clever dancer; Phillip Williams, in humorous and topical sketches at the piano; and Albert Voyee, described as the new monologue come- dian—and all of them excellent in their respec- tive departments of amusement-making !—go to complete a really Al evening's variety enter- tainment, not forgetting the latest issue of the " Gaumont Graphic."

div.head: Fine Fare Next Week.
div.p: Fine Fare Next Week.

The world-famous Harmony Four will bp next wieek what promises to be one of the finest bills ever presented at the Hippodrome. Ethel and May will present an artiitie musical act, and J. G. Grahame and Zelinq Trafeington will appear in a sketch entitled "The Crooks." Other artistes booked include the Kavattnaghs (Australian comedy jugglers), Arthur Cliften (an entertainer of note), Miss Audrey C.;oper (a pleasing vocalist), Walter Lintone (a con- certina soloist), and Jubb and Jerome (" two versatile ladies ").

div.head: FINE FILMS AT STAR KINEMA.
div.p: FINE FILMS AT STAR KINEMA.

An excellent programme of pictures was pro- vided at the Star Kinema at the beginning' of the week, a stirring American drama, entitled "Beulah," being the chief attraction. Two good scenic pictures were "Isles of the Zuider Zee" and "Beauty Spots of Italy." In the latter, scenes after an earthquake were shown and some fine pictures of a troublous sea com- pleted a good film. "Pathe's Gazette" re- corded a number of interesting events. A hearty laugh was provided by "John Bull's Sketch Book," in which the inimitable Charlie Chaplin was introduced. "The Kaiser Cap- tures Pimple" was also a great laughter-pro- voker.
The programme at the end of the week was most attractive, the " star " picture being "Her Triumph," in which the famous danseuse, Gaby Deslys, figures. Next Week's Big Films.
For the first three nights of next week the
RAILWAY FARE ALLOWED.
entitled "A Modern Magdalen." On the last
three nights the big attraction will be a filmed version of the famous old novel, "John Halifax, Gentleman."
management have booked a specially fine film
" CABIRIA " COMING.

" Cabiria," a film that has cost .t 50,000 to produce, will shortly be on view at the Grand Electric Theatre, Bridge Foot. " Cabiria" is not, in the usual accepted sense of the term, a film. It is a series of dramatic historical episodes written on .so vast a scale that, the kinematograph would seem to be the only possible means of establishing a link be- tween the mind of the author and the great majority of people. Furthermore, the kine- matograph is the Esperanto of the acre; all humanity speaks its language. Signor Gabrielle D'Annunzio, the author, is one of the most renowned of living novelists, poets and drama- tists. Ile wrote " Cabiria " directly for the screen and received £4,000 for his work. It is he more than any statesman who has led the war movement in Italy, and his burning elo- quence has inspired his countrymen ,to make the great decision. D'Annunzio iS a very wizard of description, and he has already com- menced to write the story of " Cabiria " in book form. The scenario of " Cabiria " is, by general consent, D'Annunzio's unwritten masterpiece.

div.head: WAR HITS PICTURE LOVERS.
div.p: WAR HITS PICTURE LOVERS.
Your kinema Seats Will Cost You More !

The proprietors of the picture houses in the town—the Star Kinema, the Queen's Picture House; the Grand Electric Theatre, the War- rington Picturedrome, the Picture House, the Central Picture Palace, the Park Palace and the Delbarwick Pavilion—announce that owing to the taxation on films recently imposed, added to the heavy railway dues for the conveyance of the same and other increased charges that have to be met, they are reluctantly compelled to make certain alterations in the matter of prices of admission, B:e., in consequence of which the minimum charge for adults will be threepence, whilst bill exhibitors will be ex- pected to pay half-price for the seats that they may occupy. Railway privilege tickets twill be abolished.
Home Leather Trade.

There is very little change to report in the situation here. Business continues to move on quiet lines, and the 'orders have been mainly of the nibbling kind, the only real interest shown being in light bends, for which the, inquiry has been strong but the. results poor, for there seems to be very few on offer. At present practically nothing new is being done in Army sole leather, but there has been more done with equipment leather, and sales con- tinue to be made at late prices. The bulk of the new business is for the home trade, and the prospects of a brisk season in this direction seem good. Many manufacturers' who were busy with Army footwear are now looking up their old connection, and, as boot stocks are admittedly low, there is confidence in the ex- pansion of trade in this quarter. The demand - for strap butts is very good, especially for the lighter averages, and the inquiry following is important, indicating a strong call for 'these goods in the near future. The quiet tone of the market is naturally reflected in the prices of the day, and buyers are out for lower figures all round. I fancy the tanner is rather shy of• offering at all for future delivery, except in small bulk, since we are all in 'the dark re- garding the future conditions .of labour. Some yards have already lost a considerable propor- tion of their hands, and there is a very un- certain attitude about the younger men re- maining, the prevailing feeling being that it. is better to enlist now than wait to be forced —Warrington correspondent of the "Leather Trades Review."

RIFLEMAN A. FIEESOM. One Brother Dead, Other's Where- Abonts Unknown. I Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Heesom, of 128, Knuts- ford-road, Latchford—whose eldest Eon, Rifle- man William Heesom, of the King's Royal Rifles, succumbed in hospital to wounds received during .the big advance—were on Wednesday afternoon officially informed that their younger son, Rifleman Arthur Heesom, also Or the King's Royal Rifles, is missing. LOCAL AMUSEMENTS. TIP-TOP FARE AT THE ROYAL COURT. "Lancashire and Proud of It !" proves to be a tip-top medley of mirth and melody, and small wonder is it that it is doing excellent business at the Royal Court this week. The piede is sent on the road by a trio of the best- known comedians in the land—Harry Tate, Joe O'Gorman and Wal Pink—and the fun in it is worthy of their big reputations, the piece being full of hearty laughs. The principal fun- maker—and he is a past-master at the game— is Joe Tennyson as William Henry Wiggles, as humoursome a Lancashire lad as ever cracked a joke. Miss Sara Rosebury, as Mary Ellen, plays up to him well, and Marie Ault is excel-, lent as Lizzie Piggies. Jimmie Hooper is highly amusing as a domineering. millowner, and Babs Helm, as his d-aughter, sings charm- ingly and dances prettily. Charlie Jerome is good as Old Pete. From beginning to end the piece is refresh- ingly original. When the curtain., goes up on the first scene the stage manager steps up to the footlights and in apologetic tones announces that he is afraid there can be no performance, as, for some reason or other, the company have failed to turn up. The explanation is speedily forthcoming, a quaintly attired figure rising from among the audience and announcing that the fault is his, as he is the "knocker-up" and forgot to arouse the members of the company. He speedily makes good his omission and soon the audience are revelling in merry music and mazy dan4s, and are making their sides ache with laughing at the drolleries of the playful comedians. Grand Opera Next Week. Warrington music lovers will have.placed be- fore them next week a great treat in the visit of the Harrison Frewin Opera Company, a mag- nificent and superbly equipped combination. The management of the Re-al Court Theatre are to be complimented in arranging a visit of such magnitude, and it is to be hoped that their enterprise will be generously supported. The
